A well-known challenge in robotic perception is finding a suitable point to grasp an object, largely due to the scarcity of large-scale grasp datasets with diverse object shapes. Current grasp datasets, though extensive, suffer from one or more of the following issues: limited object varieties, insufficent points per object, and lack of ground truth data for point-based grasp in a 3D point cloud. To address this gap, a research group has developed a massive dataset with over 1.3 million objects, 45.6 million grasp points, and 72 million scene meshes. This dataset, named DexGraspNet, is unique in its vast scale and comprehensive object diversity. Combining simulation and deep learning methods allows DexGraspNet to provide high-quality results, surpassing current datasets in quality and quantity. To ensure practical applications, a semi-automatic method was used to generate this dataset, reducing production costs. Evaluating DexGraspNet against existing datasets has confirmed its superior quality and vast object diversity. Moreover, by applying DexGraspNet to a specific task, a group demonstrated successful point-grasp translation on a physical robot platform, achieving high success rates. Relevant source code, dataset files, and video tutorials are freely available online. This research has been financially supported through two research grants. We've developed a novel technique to capture motion-compensated T2-weighted MRI data without relying on braking pauses. By incorporating a particular reconstruction method and using a specific gas mixture in breathing training, the technique aims to minimize respiratory movements during data collection. MoldarX, a novel image processing method, is used to precisely detect and correct variations in chest circumference while suppressing unwanted signal distortions. In a study involving 30 volunteers who underwent MRI scans with no breathing restrictions, the technique successfully captured a detailed 4D image of the body. For expert assessment, the resulting images were compared with a standard method of reassessed respiratory MRI. In a qualitative evaluation, the quality of the technique's images was comparable to that of a standard method. Furthermore, the technique was capable of producing high-quality T2-weighted images at a much faster rate than the standard method, with an average time of around 20 minutes. In conclusion, the technique provides high-quality images of the entire body without requiring patients to halt their breathing. This method has the potential to significantly expand the scope of applications of reassessed respiratory MRI, with implications for a wider range of medical research and applications. Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers can be topologically equivalent in relation to their level curves. This means that there exists continuous monotone transformations of the domain that maintains the topological properties of the functions' respective sets of level curves. Our study proves that if two submersion functions are topologically equivalent in relation to their level curves, then they can also be topologically equivalent in relation to their foliations. Ecosystem models often oversimplify nutrient movement by assuming it occurs locally, neglecting distant nutrient sources. In arid environments, plants draw nutrients from long-distance sources, such as groundwater, to sustain growth. Our research extends a well-known plant-herbivore model by incorporating nutrient movement from a broader source and plant migration. Through analytical and numerical techniques, we find that incorporating global nutrient sources and plant movement leads to a nonlinear relationship between plant density and vegetation coverage, resulting in higher maximum carrying capacities and complex non-reversible transitions between deserts and savannas. These results suggest that large-scale processes like groundwater flow and plant dispersal crucially influence ecosystem behavior. Using a simplified model, we map out the shift in plant density across various parameter settings. Our research, published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology, showcases the significance of considering large-scale processes in understanding and interpreting ecological data. By accounting for these processes, we can apply existing models to forecast arid ecosystem development. The model's complex behavior also indicates that these ecosystems might exhibit state-dependent irreversible dynamics. While our model is fairly basic, it effectively captures the importance of long-distance nutrient sources and plant movement in forming the patterns seen in these unique ecosystems. Finally, by comparing our model's predictions to theoretical concepts like bifurcations and bifurcations-induced iridescence, we find that incorporating global processes and movement into ecological models has the potential to yield valuable new insights. A versatile Python framework, ipie, has been introduced for performing auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) calculations. This framework enables seamless integration of various wavefunctions, importance sampling schemes, and orbital projections. It includes a language-agnostic JUPYER notebook interface and is compatible with both CPU and GPU devices. Furthermore, ipie supports mixed language development and is integrated with the PySCF electronic structure library. This framework's adaptability and integrability are demonstrated through a range of benchmark examples, showcasing its performance on small systems. These examples highlight the importance of orbital optimization for achieving convergence and the exponential complexity of the algorithm, which can be exacerbated by poor orbital quality. However, the framework's ability to mix phases and amplitudes, as well as its flexibility in choosing importance sampling variables, is shown to be effective in accelerating convergence. Additionally, the framework's contribution to developing more general AFQMC algorithms and its potential to expand the library's functionality are discussed. In high-frequency trading, a trading strategy that exploits temporary market discrepancies to generate profit, implementing this approach on a quantum level presents a complex challenge. Due to the inherent randomness of quantum mechanics, generating revenue through high-frequency trading in a quantum environment could be a feasible and impossible task simultaneously. To explore this concept, a simplified model based on the quantum prisoner's dilemma game is proposed to illustrate the theoretical foundations of high-frequency trading in a quantum cloud. The model employs a green-energy trading strategy as an exemplar of this concept. The profitability of trading is evaluated through the game's score, represented as the physical quantity's expectation value. A two-qubit entangled state is utilized in this game to model the exchange of market information through correlations between qubits. The analysis also demonstrates how the exchange rate of the quantum exchange (XQ) influences profitability and reveals that, in a quantum context, unconstrained trading may actually decrease potential gains compared to traditional random trading methods. Nevertheless, when incorporating constraints on the QCD game, the quantum exchange (XQ) can generate substantial profits exceeding those of the classical exchange (XET), especially under specific conditions of score asymmetry. The study concludes that utilizing quantum mechanics for high-frequency trading offers unique opportunities for optimized performance, but a deep understanding of quantum mechanics is required to differentiable between profitable and unprofitable trading strategies. Furthermore, future research on quantum finance is encouraged by acknowledging the implications of measurement-induced wave function collapse, particularly in high-frequency trading, due to its potential influence on market information processing. The study concludes by speculating that future implementations of quantum computers in finance may discover that the principles of quantum mechanics provide advantageous frameworks for decision-making and trading strategies. The paper draws to a close by acknowledging Microsoft's Quantum Development Experience, a pioneering effort in high-speed quantum information processing, which serves as an essential resource for exploring quantum exchange (XQ) and other quantum-based trading methods. The study's findings offer an initial look at how quantum concepts and quantum computing may be applied in financial markets, and it is hoped that future research will delve deeper into these fascinating quantum-based strategies. We investigate how income and wealth are interconnected when some individuals act as intermediaries between the originators and recipients of goods and services. Within a framework of a recurring game involving strategic repetition, each player's position is defined by specific properties, including the amount of goods and services they offer to their clients, the terms of the agreement, the level of compensation, and the frequency of transactions. By exploring the concept of quasi-polymorphism, which emerges when players' characteristics result in varying activity frequencies, our study demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of a stable equilibrium in which players' strategies do not rely on expectations about the future. Additionally, the theory developed applies broadly to various contingency types regarding the players' characteristics. Moreover, the legacy of slavery in economic decisions is examined using a particular type of contingency - racial preferences - to illustrate its practical implications through data-driven analysis of a leading online marketplace. The data show that more affluent users tend to have distinct, yet minimalistic, preferences, whereas less affluent users are generally less pickier but also more likely to cheat in transactions. Consequently, a positive correlation is found between a user's social status and optimal income. We conclude that the interlinked nature of wealth and income, influenced by distinct characteristics, gives rise to a multi-faceted equilibrium structure, which explains why income disparities and privileged attitudes tend to coexist. Finally, the originality of the theoretical contributions is assessed using a suitability metric in English language text. The theories developed were found to completely (100% chance) exclude the possibility that lower income might correspond to lower wealth. Moreover, the theories were found to have a moderate and unlikely (34% chance) correlation with the notion that higher income might correspond to greater wealth. Consequently, a multilingual glossary of 230 sentences was used to translate the concepts into Spanish, which revealed notable linguistic and cultural differences in the interpretation of these terms across languages. The study indicates that higher income is widely associated with greater wealth across cultures, whereas the correlation between wealth and income is minimal and unlikely (25% chance) in both English and Spanish

A generalized framework for incorporating external geometry data in motion planning has been developed, addressing one of the main obstacles in robotic planning by efficiently utilizing available extra sensors. This approach is accommodated by various sensor types including cameras, lidars, radar, sonar, and GPS. The geometric constraints of the environment are leveraged to narrow down the motion planning search space, thus the computational complexity is independent of the task's complexity and is only determined by the sensor data resolution. The proposed algorithm is applicable to robots operating in 2D and 3D dimensions and has been demonstrated in experiments using a quadbike on uneven terrain. The results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline planning methods across diverse terrain conditions. Furthermore, the proposed method allows for real-time feedback and can be executed in real-time on low-cost hardware. The corresponding code is openly accessible on the repository https://github.com/behzadrasoul/SimGeometric. The quadbike videos are accessible on https://youtube.com/behzadrasoul. The geometric properties of navigation have significant real-world implications in multiple fields such as robotics, computer vision, and engineering, and have recently gained a considerable amount of research interest. Historically, the research in geometric robotics has primarily centered on reconstructing the environment using sensor data and incorporating the resulting 2D map as an input constraint to motion planning processes. Nevertheless, the environment model obtained through this approach often fails to align with the actual world observed through a camera, with the discrepancy being typically 10 to 100 times larger than the sensor resolution. Consequently, the motion planning process based on this model may result in suboptimal performance and may even disregard crucial elements in the environment. The proposed framework overcomes these challenges by directly utilizing the geometric properties of the sensor data in motion planning, thus avoiding the environment reconstruction process and enabling robots to simultaneously take advantage of available extra sensors and geometric data. The approach is based on the assumption that the world's geometric structure can be described using basic elements such as points, lines, and planes. The corresponding sensor data is preprocessed and incorporated into an on-the-fly data structure named SimGeometric Data Structure. This structure enables efficient detection of geometric intersections that the robot may encounter or pass through during motion, including collisions and reachability analysis. The proposed algorithm has been successfully tested in experiments and has been validated against baseline planning methods in diverse conditions. Results show that the proposed method outperforms existing algorithms and maintains optimal performance in various scenarios, and is applicable for robots with different shapes and sizes.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with its efficient estimation: the effective Kendall's tau statistic. The investigation considers a joint hypothesis consisting of a null hypothesis representing general alternative scenarios and an alternative hypothesis depicting the scenarios' possibilities. The analysis calculates an efficient statistic for this test and establishes critical values through asymptotic distribution analysis. The researcher also creates finite sampling versions of these results and applies them to convey probabilistic certainty in Kendall's tau rankings. The experiments show that using tau with conventional critical values when data is moderately sized yields test decisions essentially identical to those obtained with more complex methods. Moreover, the computations of tau are substantially reduced through the use of simple formulas. The rapidly expanding automotive networking sector is poised to revolutionize the future of autonomous driving systems. A pivotal aspect of this transformation is the capability of edge cognition - a -predictive intelligence system embedded in the network infrastructure that can forecast drivers' and vehicle's future actions. While enhancing the driving experience, it raises serious concerns regarding user data privacy. This is because the data transmitted to the infrastructure involves sensitive information such as location and camera footage. In this article, we introduce a groundbreaking concept for an automotive network architecture that prioritizes user data privacy while utilizing context-awareness for navigation. We leverage techniques like multi-agent reinforcement learning and privacy-preserving technology to maintain a balance between system performance and privacy compliance. Furthermore, we outline the need for standardized privacy protocols to support the decision-making process in future autonomous systems. In conclusion, we highlight the importance of edge cognition in automotive networks and the crucial role of privacy-protecting artificial intelligence in the design of autonomous driving systems. 

Key words: Edge Cognition, Automotive Networks, Machine Learning, Predictive Intelligence, Privacy Protection, Reinforcement Learning.

The increasing demand for better solutions in more complex problems has driven the development of evolutionary multi-objective algorithms that exploit parallel processing capabilities, such as Parallel Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (PAR-NSGA) and Multi-objective Genetic Algorithm in Shared Resources (MOGAS).  As tasks are divided among multiple processors in these algorithms, the performance is improved; however, the speed at which each processor rotates its focus (evaluation time bias) affects the outcome.  This paper proposes an innovative approach, the Frequency-centered Parent Selection method, to lower the impact of evaluation time bias in asynchronous MOGAS, enhancing its overall performance.  The new approach prioritizes selecting parents based on frequency of rotation, rather than fitness, thereby promoting diversity and counteracting evaluation time bias.  The experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this algorithm, demonstrating improved convergence and diversity in comparison to traditional methods, such as PAR-NSGA, especially under conditions of varying processor loads and multiple local optima.  The overall results highlight the effectiveness of Frequency-centered Parent Selection in enhancing multi-objective optimization performance in scenarios where evaluation time bias is a concern. Deep learning model explainability, particularly for graph neural networks, is a demanding and largely unresolved issue. The complexity of graph data and GNN models makes them unsuitable for the application of existing explainability methods. To address this challenge, this study introduces the Graph Explanation Interpreter, a generalized tool that can instantly provide explanations for any GNP model, without the need for modifications to the model parameters. The results of our experiments demonstrate the interpreter's high performance in accurately identifying key graph factors for prediction and surpassing the performance of other explainability methods in generating node-level attention distributions and feature importance maps. Notably, our interpreter can explain models within any of the six possible GNN hybrid layers with a time complexity of $O(n\log n)$. Due to its non-iterative nature, the interpreter is well-suited for rapid deployment in production environments, making it an ideal choice for rapid, parameter-free model explanation. Recent studies utilizing neutron reflectometry have yielded conflicting results regarding the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membrane outer leaflets. This research aims to resolve the discrepancy by re-examining a key assumption underlying many SR experiments, including the neglect of gradient contributions to membrane curvature energy. Through a thorough mathematical analysis, we demonstrate that incorporating molecular bond angles in membrane models significantly alters their curvature energy when certain assumptions are violated. Consequently, ignoring gradient terms is a valid approximation only when specific conditions are met, such as when membrane segments display constant bond angles or when the contribution of bond energies to curvature is negligible. This realization, in turn, enables us to reassess the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes, ultimately suggesting that prior findings of a negative effect may be inconsequential due to inaccuracies in modeling membrane curvature energy. Our study proposes an improved method for assessing membrane properties: comparing experimentally derived parameters across varying membrane models. Applying this approach to recent neutron reflectometry data on DOPC and DPC can reveal membrane thickness modulations induced by cholesterol and validate our earlier observation of a minimal impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes. This research combines theoretical modeling from a Kalashnikov-Kregg-Monroy-Martin framework with experimental findings, the first combining SR and NMR data. The study has broader implications on understanding membrane curvature and its role in cellular processes such as membrane curvature-mediated signaling. Calculations of membrane curvature energy for cholesterol-containing membranes, taking into account both intrinsic and protein lipid interactions, are provided for relevant cellular membrane models like PM and MAM. These results underscore the significance of considering full three-dimensional curvature energy contributions from bond angles to membrane curvature properties. Additionally, they imply that curvature modulations observed in membranes may not primarily be driven by cholesterol but instead by other factors like temperature variations or protein interactions. Furthermore, such variations could influence membrane-associated processes including Ras activation and TREX1 activity. Finally, our study provides a new perspective on the importance of understanding the complex interplay between intrinsic lipid-lipid interactions and protein-lipid interactions that govern membrane curvature. This research has potential applications in understanding biological membrane-associated processes and cellular signaling. In order to overcome these obstacles a unified research framework was established that is based on a hierarchical decomposition approach, in which hierarchical structural features are extracted and expressed from input data through successive stages of feature reduction and representation refinement from global to local. A receptor-based framework was developed to achieve this goal by establishing a hierarchical structural decomposition model, revising feature reduction and representation refinement, and conducting experiments to verify the effectiveness of the new framework. As a result of this research a novel GNN model was established that is characterized by its unique skeleton structure, high degree of expressiveness, local link rewriting technique, fast training efficiency, and superior performance overall. Further analysis of our research also revealed a universally applicable design principle for machine learning in the form of a hierarchical structural decomposition framework, resulting in a nearly 3 hundredfold reduction in training time with our model compared to its counterparts. In terms of performance our model sets new records with its accuracy and F1-score on various benchmark datasets, achieving accuracy rates of 4.0, 3.8, 4.0, and 4.5 percent respectively for CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet. Currently available source code for our model can be found at https://github.com/ArgRobotics/SuperNeuralNet.GNN. As for further applications of our model structure, future research will involve the development of a new paradigm for universal feature extraction and representation through hierarchical structural decomposition and the investigation of novel designs for machine learning through feature reduction and representation refinement from global to local. In a context where data refinement includes correcting matrix deviations, we introduce a newly developed approach for the low-rank matrix fulfillment process. This approach is based on the principles of differential privacy and employs the Huber loss function in conjunction with the soft-imputation technique from the PSSA method. The proposed framework, dubbed PRiME, utilizes iterative iterativeizations of the Huber loss function to achieve private low-rank matrix estimation. In terms of optimization efficiency, we prove that the subgradient method can be used to perform iterations efficiently. Furthermore, under the assumption of proper choice of parameters, theoretical estimates of the method's performance are provided. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through empirical comparisons with several well-known algorithms for low-rank matrix estimation, including NPSV, SPC, and PSSA, revealing that it maintains a balance between low-rank matrix accuracy and data point density in 2D datasets. The source code of the proposed framework is also openly available for review and verification. Theoretical estimates of the method's performance are further validated through numerical experiments and scaling analyses that confirm the findings. One potential direction for further enhancements would be the adaptation of the proposed framework as a CNN layer for low-rank matrix estimation. The contributions of the proposed framework, in terms of both its technical aspects and its potential applications, are extensively discussed. The research is accompanied by supplementary materials, including figures, tables, and a Python codebase for the proposed framework's implementation, which can be freely accessed. This research explores a novel, abstract interpretation-based numerical static analysis, dubbed "decoupled analysis," that calculates both the maximum and minimum values of a program's numerical expressions independently. The key innovation is the decoupling of numerical domains to accommodate both an upper and lower bound in each domain. Additionally, new operators have been introduced for joint and independent evaluations, respectively. Contrary to traditional analysis methods, this approach does not assume that program instructions can't yield equal outcomes based on their intermediate results. It is proven that the upper and lower bounds calculated by this analysis are accurate, and it has been successfully tested on a substantial program with a complex numerical expression. Comparing its results to existing analysis tools shows that it provides more precise numerical estimates for a comprehensive set of test programs. Performance measurements also demonstrate that the decoupled analysis is generally as fast as or faster than existing methods. Finally, an extension of abstract domains has been proposed to accommodate programs with recursive methods that modify global variables. This solution has been verified with experimental results on various test programs. The implicit values associated with this domain have also been studied in detail. Ultimately, a tool called "Decouple" has been developed that integrates the decoupled analysis with other existing techniques. Experimental results have shown that Decouple provides the most accurate estimates for a wide range of numerical programs when compared to other static analysis methods. What's more, Decouple was able to detect a critical numerical error in a real-world program that other tools failed to identify. The decoupled analysis presented in this research has also inspired theoretical contributions regarding the operation of joints and fusions in abstract interpretation. Specifically, a new sufficient condition for preserving numerical domains has been proposed, and it is shown to be more general than existing alternatives. Furthermore, a generalization of existing theories concerning the operation of joints and fusions in abstract interpretation has been achieved. Additionally, decoupling has been identified as a novel, distinct concept in abstract interpretation, and its connection to other techniques, such as fusion and joint, has been studied in detail. Lastly, decoupling's potential extensions were explored, and it is proposed to incorporate it into existing theoretical frameworks for abstract interpretation in the future. The implementation details of Decouple, an associated tool, are also documented, and it has been released to the public under an open-source license. Experimental results obtained using Decouple have demonstrated its capabilities and accuracy, and they provide valuable insights for tool developers. Anomaly detection is crucial in various scientific and engineering areas to identify data patterns that deviate from common trends or standards. Most current methods, however, are restricted to working with specific types of data, particularly numerical data or words, leaving a gap in detecting anomalies in data with complex structures such as lists, graphs, or images. To address this limitation, a new anomaly detection algorithm has been developed that is highly effective for data in metric spaces. Our method, which does not require parameter adjustment, is also characterized by rapid computation, precision, and scalability. To validate its performance, the proposed algorithm was tested on various synthetic and real-world datasets and compared to established methods. Our results demonstrate that, in most cases, the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches, providing a valuable resource for researchers working with such data. Furthermore, the algorithm is publicly available to facilitate its adoption and improvement. A novel concept, closeness, is defined as a structure-driven property of data objects, reflecting their proximity and similarity. Our method leverages this concept to construct a closeness graph, which serves as a graphical representation of the structure to identify anomalies. Specifically, the algorithm identifies data objects that exhibit irregular patterns not captured by the structure, by identifying nodes in the closeness graph that have isolated or distant relationships. Our method has been experimentally evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its effectiveness and practical applicability in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, additional experiments were conducted to assess its performance and robustness across different parameter configurations. Our algorithm was tested on real-world datasets, providing empirical evidence of its utility and importance in real-world settings. For example, in a case study involving university students, the algorithm was used to identify potential dropouts based on their academic performance, offering valuable insights for university administrators. Our method demonstrates a range of potential applications in various fields, providing a foundation for research and development in anomaly detection and structure analysis. To facilitate adoption and improvement, the algorithm is publicly available, and additional case studies are presented in the accompanying technical report. Our method has been validated through multiple experiments and case studies, and additional experiments were conducted to compare its performance and ease of use with existing algorithms. A survey of its competition was presented, and our method is publicly available to facilitate adoption and improvement. Our approach is characterized by its simplicity, as the algorithm does not require parameter adjustment or tuning. A case study was conducted to assess its performance and confidence in real-world settings. Our method provides a foundation for future research and development in anomaly detection and structure analysis

This phenomenon can be visualized by imagining an atom attached to a slender mirror as it oscillates. As the mirror moves up and down, the atom will experience changing optical properties as it spins around, and these alterations will produce electromagnetic radiation in the visible and ultraviolet spectral ranges. The pattern of radiation will depend on the atom's movement and the optical properties of the surrounding environment. Additionally, the movement of the atom will result in the emission of radiation at specific frequencies related to the optical properties of the system. This type of stimulation or emission of radiation will also occur when a slab mirrors an atom's movement, and similar patterns will emerge if we imagine the atom to be located inside the slab. On the other hand, if we place the atom on the other side of a slab, the patterns will reverse their orientation. This theoretical model from a semi-classical perspective corresponds with previous experimental findings. We propose a framework for visualizing and analyzing organized groups of data,
such as social or professional networks, by using a system that simulates the
viewpoint of the group's leader. Our method represents each node with characteristics
derived from its surrounding community, providing a comprehensive view of the
hierarchy. By applying this approach to a dataset of professional interactions, we
obtained a detailed understanding of the relationships and values within the groups. 
Furthermore, we discovered a pattern where individuals tend to support the leadership
of their respective communities in line with the Equitable Solution principle. The
principle, which was first introduced by graph theory, aims to ensure that in the presence
of similar connections, the relationships within the group are treated equally. Through
our analysis, we also identified certain communities as outliers and identified notable
individuals who contribute significantly to their groups. Our method and findings hold
promise for enhancing our knowledge of organized groups and those who lead them.

This research focuses on solving kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and highlights the importance of using distributional initial conditions. For each model, a corresponding boundary value problem is formulated and a fixed-point proof is applied to demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for estimative problems. An estimative solution for boundary value problems involving the Laplace operator is derived from the distributed parameter system approach. For problems with nonlinear operators, an iterative solution is obtained using a decomposition technique and the successive iterative check method. Although the derived methods require approximations, they serve as valuable approximations for practical use. Moreover, as the methods improve, the error decreases, and this research outlines the method's convergence. Ultimately, numerical examples are used to verify the efficacy of these theoretical frameworks. Additionally, the source code for the numerical methods is included in the appendices. Specialists in the field are encouraged to employ these theories to address the challenges of solving nonlinear kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions. With their expertise in linear problems, they can now apply their knowledge to tackle non-linear problems. Furthermore, the paper also explores an innovative approach for boundary value problems involving systems of ordinary and partial differential equations. Although this aspect requires further research and refinement, the theoretical foundations are laid for solving complete nonlinear problems. As such, we anticipate significant future advancements in this direction. An associated GitHub project is available at: https://github.com/TechRamsey/Distributed-Enzyme-Reactions. The search for indications of supersymmetry in proton-proton collisions at a specific energy level is detailed. The analysis is performed on a subset of the CMS detector's sensor data, focusing on final states consisting of missing transverse momentum and at least one jet, lacking a clear transverse momentum direction. Supersymmetry models featuring natural and divided SUSY models are investigated. Two distinct scenarios within the divided model are studied: a situation where the gluino is the lightest supersymmetry-based particle and decays into the lightest neutralino before transforming into a specified particle. Additionally, a scenario where the gluino is the lightest supersymmetry-based particle and decays into a specified particle and then to the lightest neutralino through an unaccounted process are considered. The analysis is based on a dataset collected in 2016, providing 35 to 415 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions. No signs of supersymmetry were detected in various desired regions, with expected masses ranging from 1,000 to 4,000 GeV for gluinos and their decay products in natural and divided models. Masses up to 2,000 GeV for R-parity violating scenarios were ruled out, depending on parameters such as the branching ratio and type of particle decaying to the lightest neutralino. The investigation resulted in the establishment of new, stringent theoretical and experimental upper limits on supersymmetry masses in various particle interactions. In specific interactions involving electrons, muons, and bottom quarks, experimental limits were set on supersymmetry masses up to 1,000 GeV for a particular interaction type, with masses beyond 1,000 GeV remaining within the theoretical realm for another interaction type. Using stochastic dynamics guided by a mean-reverting mechanism, the model is capable of accurately predicting the likelihood of prolonged trade durations and the associated financial gains. Our method incorporates an expectation function formulated in Reversible Jump Mixture of Distributions with explicit expression and optimistically framed to facilitate efficient detection of extended trades from observed data. Further developments involve extending the model to distinguish between normal and prolonged trades, where the distinction is made based on a predetermined threshold. Our experimental results, obtained from two distinct datasets, yield an impressive 32% and 40% increase in predictive accuracy compared to the conventional STT model. A comparative analysis of our model with established methods confirms its high capacity for regulating financial transaction management with robustness, efficiency, and stability. The proposed model demonstrates practical value for traders in achieving optimal QoS factors, including the highest possible returns, shortest transaction duration, and greatest profitability. Our model's implementation is accompanied by newly introduced diagnosticians that make the most of STT's predictive capabilities. Our methods successfully leverage the Reversible Jump algorithm to estimate parameters for multiple mixture components and provide detailed insights of the model's efficiency in predicting termination times. Our model's reliability is further assessed through sensitivity analysis and the design of a autonomous-stochastic terminal time (ASTT) agent, which exhibits stability in multiple scenarios. Through thorough evaluation, the proposed methods achieve a dynamic balance between predicted termination times and financial gains, thus enabling stakeholders to make more accurate predictions and take informed decisions. Our model's performance is notable for its swift training, minimal memory requirements, and efficient processing capabilities. Through thorough evaluation, the proposed methods achieve a dynamic balance between predicted termination times and financial gains, thus enabling stakeholders to make more accurate predictions and take informed decisions. However, existing methods have yet to fully utilize the insight-packed nature of evaluation data due to its relative neglectation. This paper seeks to address this gap by introducing a novel interaction-based recommender, called SIFN. Inspired by the success of interactive models, SIFN interacts with both users and items to adaptively learn a user's sentiment towards various items. Crucially, SIFN uses a unique data augmentation technique to effectively combine the user's feelings with comprehensive item descriptions that are grounded in factual data from knowledge bases. When deployed, SIFN demonstrates superior performance on large-scale real-world datasets from two online platforms for shopping and travel recommendations, outperforming all comparators. Our analysis reveals that the predictive accuracy of SIFN's auxiliary sentiment learning component is remarkably robust. Furthermore, the underlying code for SIFN will be made freely available to the public. Overall, the contributions of this research are multi-fold: First, we successfully introduced a powerful interactive recommender, SIFN, that harvests the rich predictive value of evaluation-based sentiment. Second, we compiled two comprehensive evaluation datasets with extensive item-related information that was augmented from various sources for the benefit of the community. Last but not least, the underlying code for our approach will be made freely available to the public. The technique of information augmentation through text translation is widely employed, yet difficulties arise when dealing with code-switched texts due to their dual language composition. As a result, direct translation of these texts poses problems in utilizing augmented data, particularly when training models. We address this challenge by examining the potential of lexical substitutions in place of direct translation for augmenting code-switched texts. We present initial findings from an automated evaluation, indicating that lexical substitutions are a viable alternative to generate augmented data that can be utilized efficiently. To date, there has been a lack of research focusing on lexical substitutions in information augmentation, especially in the context of neural language models. We hope that our research sparks future investigations in this area. We also make our project resources available, encompassing data, scripts, and experimental sets, in the hope that they might be useful to other researchers. A mirror of our project can be found at https://mimirsoft.github.io/LexAugCS/. We believe that further investigations are necessary to fully realize the potential of lexical substitutions in the long run. A type of generalized lambda transformation, applied to a hyperbolic Liouville integrable equation, results in inclusions of certain soliton equations and their integrable pairs. A specific lambda transformation yields a new integrable equation, describing a membrane in two dimensions, with a notable property - it's not a conventional soliton equation. We examine the equation's symmetry properties and quasiconformal automorphisms. Furthermore, we provide two solutions methods to the equation and discuss the connection to an existing Cosgrove ring, with a focus on the integrable pairs of KdV-SKdV and CH. Moreover, by employing lambda transformations, we derive a new integrable equation for an L-shaped membrane, existing within three-dimensional space. This is achieved by combining a known condition, expressed as a lambda transformation of a hyperbolic Liouville equation, with a corresponding lambda transformation of the equation describing a hyperbolic membrane. Finally, some further perspectives on the integrable equation and its solutions are provided. A thorough classification of the equation, in terms of integrable pairs, remains an open question and is still under investigation. The present research represents a first step in exploring the possibilities of general lambda transformations. Such a transformation could lead to the discovery of further, previously unknown integrable equations. Notably, lambda transformations can be applied not only to the Liouville equation but also to the hyperbolic sine-Gordon equation, resulting in the discovery of a new integrable equation for a curved, membrane-like surface, although this will be detailed in a subsequent study. A significant challenge with hexahedral mesh generation arises from hexahedra having a large number of degrees of freedom (DoFs), making efficient optimization of the mesh difficult due to the high computational complexity. Breaking down the optimization process into smaller, unique hexahedral sub-meshes with fewer DoFs allows for efficient refinement of each individual mesh. Building upon this concept, a generation of extensive hexahedral meshes is proposed. In this approach, a initial coarse mesh with reduced DoFs is first optimized, and then subsequently enriched by adding new tetrahedra to specific hexahedral sub-domains, with each having a lower number of DoFs than the previous ones. By iteratively refining the DoFs throughout the mesh, a final high-quality hexahedral mesh with an increased number of DoFs can be achieved. To accurately model the conversion delay in power converters, we need to account for components such as inverter and switch-on delays. Since manufacturers don't provide precise product information, we must rely on measuring the devices' characteristics themselves. Using analytical functions from Matlab's Curve Fitting Tool, we can model these individual delays and combine them to represent the actual conversion delay. Our approach is demonstrated using a SiC power module, discrete diodes conversion, and a 12V to 15V converter. By analyzing the measured turn-on and turn-off waveforms, we can identify the relevant delays and accurately model the conversion delay. Our method allows for reliable conversion delay simulation without the need for specific simulation software or knowledge of the devices' internal workings, making it particularly useful for embedded systems developers who don't have access to specialized software. Furthermore, our analytical model can be easily scaled up or down to accommodate various devices with different operating voltages and frequencies. Ultimately, by adjusting the simulation parameters, we can determine the impact of conversion delay on the overall system, which enables valuable delay-to-performance tradeoff studies to be made without the need for actual hardware testing. Using this delay model, we have conducted some preliminary testing which showed significant performance improvements for a conversion loop controller, which would have been difficult to achieve through mere simulation, underscoring the importance of this rigorous testing and validation process. Our research highlights the value of thorough validation and testing, particularly in complex embedded systems design where over-reliance on simulation and testing may lead to a lack of understanding of the underlying physical phenomena. Our goal is that this work will inspire other designers to adopt similar analytical and experimental methodologies in their own work, leading to enhanced insights into the various physical and technical aspects involved in the design. Moreover, by employing a rigorous experimental methodology, we have successfully overcome a common design challenge, namely the difficulty in accurately modeling the conversion delay of modern power converters with their various amplifier and switch configurations. Our experiment represents a classic example of a cause-effect relationship in engineering, where an in-depth analysis of a local phenomenon (the converter delay) helps to understand a broader, complex issue (conversion delay measurement and modeling). Our work through careful analysis, has identified the critical factors contributing to the converter delay, which are crucial for developing an effective delay estimation strategy. Our model is compatible with a wide range of modern power converters that utilize various amplifier and switch configurations. We introduce a concept of rough-grained smoothness, an adaptation for function functions in metric frameworks suitable for reinforcement learning. This new concept is linked to the option metric, initially proposed by Sutton et al. (2001), demonstrating its usefulness in optimizing parameterized policies using just one gradient update with episodic validation. The episodic update can be applied to policy gradient methods when the base policy is chosen randomly from a metric space. The results we obtained are inclusive of previously studied methods within the field of reinforcement learning, such as episodic policy optimization (EPO), using the option metric to measure policy variations. The application of rough-grained smoothness is not limited to reinforcement learning as it is applicable across general supervised learning scenarios with high dimensionality. For instance, it is observable that conditional on specific features, rough-grained smoothness is beneficial for policy verification problems involving parameterized behaviors. The arrangement of animacy, defined as the capacity to act intentionally, varies significantly in the human ventral temporal cortex, encompassing the occipito-temporal junction and nearby regions.  In this research, we present a novel, empirically-driven animacy arrangement, utilizing a broad range of stimuli that challenge the traditional notion of animacy.  By designing a framework that automatically classifies the animacy of local brain signals, we identified a dynamic network, consisting of the superior lateral occipital gyrus, posterior fusiform gyrus, and parietal posterior gyrus, that consistently responds across different animacy categories.  Notably, the parietal posterior gyrus was found to contribute uniquely to the animacy arrangement, highlighting its essential role in integrating visual and motor memory aspects to distinguish animacy.  Moreover, the posterior fusiform gyrus, specifically in the left hemisphere, was found to play a critical part in integrating visual and motor information to recognize animacy in social stimuli.  These findings demonstrate the intricate dynamics of the animacy arrangement in the human ventral temporal cortex and its subtle nuances in distinct contexts.  They also underscore the significant challenges in defining animacy and the necessity of moving beyond a simplistic dichotomy between living and non-living objects, as well as humans and animals.  In this perspective, we explore the multi-faceted nature of animacy and investigate the possibility that some intermediate entities, such as robots, could be considered animate.  Ultimately, we highlight the central role of cognitive neuroscience research in informing the development of animacy, as reflected in the animacy arrangement, and the broader implications for artificial intelligence and robotics.  A technical demonstration of the animacy arrangement is available at https://github.com/grassynetworks/animacyarr.  A comprehensive interactive visualization platform for the arrangement is provided at https://grasml.com/animacy-arr.  In addition, a detailed dataset is included at https://osf.io/dj3gn/ as well as the dataset used in extension as https://osf.io/6e7fc/ and https://osf.io/df8ja/. The extensive computations required for multidimensional simulations in fluid dynamics, like 2D Euler equations, often necessitate sophisticated filtering techniques, particularly when dealing with non-regular grids or short timeframes. Traditional shock-capturing techniques aim to stabilize computations at the grid scale while preserving the solution's accuracy and its inherent structural properties. This study proposes a novel, convex optimization-based approach to filtering that maintains the solution's monotonicity and discontinuity preservation properties. It applies a divergence-based method for preserving shock waves and is evaluated against alternative methods such as Sullivan's and Wong and Mullen's non-dissipative schemes. The efficacy of this technique is demonstrated through comparison with established methods in multiple scenarios, including steady-state and transient simulations with various test cases. The availability of open-source code for this method is also provided online. Overall, this technique shows great potential in complex simulations where it can help avoid the numerical dissipation that often accompanies shock simulations. Its high efficiency, being nearly as accurate as more sensitive methods while requiring only a minor increase in computational cost, makes it a valuable tool. Additionally, its versatility extends to one-step methods where it can help enhance algorithm performance. Further development of this technique is recommended. Its potential applications are vast and could potentially be expanded to 3D simulations in the future. Using the Insight-HXMT, we investigated quasi-periodic oscillations in the MAXI J1535-571 corona, which exhibited unique type C behavior, characterized by a rapid pattern of both soft and hard photons. Through a fast-time analysis, we linked these patterns to a pattern of pulsating radiation lasting 4-12 seconds. This phenomenon occurred repeatedly when the source was in a low-hard state and the source's accretion rate was relatively low. A primary beam of soft photons is likely produced by the Lense-Thirring precession model, which might help explain transient X-ray flashes during this process. This Insight-HXMT study marks the first time these fluctuations have been linked to coronal dynamics, which could significantly influence understanding of these fluctuations and the coronae of transient low-mass black holes. Furthermore, we propose that these fluctuations may be associated with a dynamic coronal structure formed through a series of slow-mode shocks. This unique coronal structure could significantly impact models of QPOs and afterglow phenomena in low-mass black hole binaries. Moreover, detecting these fluctuations during a low-hard state suggests a role for coronal precession in transitioning between the two states. Finally, observing these fluctuations as prolonged patterns of coronal precession could significantly extend our understanding of the rapid evolution of transient soft and hard radiation in low-mass black hole binaries. A particular bonus of this discovery by the Insight-HXMT satellite was its ability to substantially revise previous classification schemes of QPOs, which had previously distinguished between two distinct patterns of coronal activity. To date, the fastest coronal precession observed in low-mass black hole binaries is approximately 1.5 seconds, which could significantly impact theoretical models of these phenomena. By analyzing the Insight-HXMT dataset, we were able to identify a distinct spectral component of these fluctuations, which displayed a relatively low break energy of approximately 4.9 keV. This distinct component, which was not apparent during coronal precession, demonstrated a unique correlation between soft and hard photons, which may be associated with a distinct physical mechanism. As automation increasingly performs tasks previously managed by humans, the goal of trust-worthy and adaptable interaction between humans and robots is becoming more crucial. The capacity of robots to understand and respond to social cues is a vital element in achieving safe and efficient robot operation within environments shared with people. Traditional approaches to robot learning and decision-making frequently neglect the significance of associate benefits, assuming solely the perspective of the primary agent. By incorporating the social aspect of associate motivations, we've developed a model-exclusion method that enables learning robots to respond appropriately to the actions of associates. Through this approach, we've addressed two primary challenges: ensuring the robot's response is trustworthy and consistent with its program, and ensuring its program incorporates diverse associate motivations. Experimental results obtained from a pilot study confirm that humans perceive robots functioning with our motivation-based response strategy as more accurate and attentive than those controlled by conventional algorithms. Moreover, we've demonstrated that incorporating various associate motivations leads to enhanced performance and versatility in robot behavior. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of considering the social and relational dimensions of human-robot interactions in environments shared with people. The presented research forms the groundwork for developing learning robots that are attentive to and responsive to human behaviors and social relationships, enabling safe and efficient coexistence in shared environments. A cutting-edge method employing contrastive learning is used to train a video-based detector that can identify unknown substances from a single frame. The detector is trained using a vast, unrestricted source dataset comprising various substances, resulting in a generalist detector with superior performance. To aid in troubleshooting, real-time object labels are generated through informed data augmentation, providing users with precise annotation. The trained detector is publicly accessible at https://object-detection.org. Evaluations were conducted using a substantial, yet unofficial dataset, as the original training data is not publicly available due to existing patents, and a novel metric was introduced to assess single-shot performance. The study demonstrates the largest known gap closure between few-shot and general bare-bones models in a physically meaningful sense, with the trained model performing near-perfectly on new, unseen materials after observing only five examples. The study also highlights the significance of understanding the algorithm's reasoning via physics-informed visualization. The public implementation is compatible with existing optical-based sensors, including cameras and lidar, providing users with the ability to train customized, effective detectors. The study shows the distinct advantages of employing contrastive learning with image sequences to enhance object detection accuracy. Two-algebras, which are the basic components of Lie 2-groups, have been thoroughly explored in a distinguished school. A crucial paper that introduced the concept of Lie 2-groups through the adjoint method has been celebrated for its originality. Building upon this foundation, the current work aims to provide an in-depth, systematic, and expansive review of the field, encompassing both classical aspects and cutting-edge developments. Key topics covered include the definition and differentiation methods of Lie 2-groups, their fundamental properties, classification, advancement in homogeneous spaces, group-valued functors, and the latest developments in weakly Lie 2-algebraic structures, which serve as the base of Lie 2-groups. The chapter also explores a range of emerging topics such as bi-differential systems, one-dimensional Lie 2-algebras, the linearization of Lie 2-algebras, the infinite series of differential equations that arise from homogeneous spaces of Lie 2-algebras, and the differential ideals corresponding to Lie 2-algebras. Finally, the current work acknowledges and draws inspiration from a notable paper that introduces the concept of coherent Lie 2-algebras and their generalizations to higher degrees. The chapter also includes an introduction to the Lie module 2-algebra, which is a crucial recent development in the field. The writing style is supplemented by numerous examples, examples, and their corresponding illustrations. A comprehensive bibliography is also included with detailed descriptions of the included papers. The current work is structured into twelve sections, with some of the sections providing a historical perspective on the development of the subject. The remaining sections are dedicated to presenting the latest advancements in the field. A detailed index of the included terms and definitions concludes the monograph. The current work is distinct from a previous survey on the subject due to its expanded scope, which now includes a wide range of Lie 2-algebraic structures. A previous survey on the subject primarily focused on Lie 2-algebras and their cohomology, which is a crucial aspect of the field, but it failed to explore other important areas. In contrast, the current work not only covers the mentioned area, but it also introduces a new set of important topics related to the subject, which are the bi-differential systems and the linearization of Lie 2-algebras. These topics are directly linked to homogeneous spaces of Lie 2-algebras and serve as an important area of study. We introduce a novel method for local feature matching, where instead of a detector, we utilize a pairwise feature matching algorithm leveraging the capabilities of the Transformer model. Our approach, LoFTR, employs a hierarchical, rotationalally-invariant patch matching framework to bypass the limitations of traditional detectors, such as their reliance on fixed grid-based structures and susceptibility to rotational errors. By enabling the efficient and accurate matching of features from two images, LoFTR facilitates consistent performance across various frequencies and rotational scenarios. Furthermore, LoFTR benefits from a reduced computational complexity thanks to its reliance on a sparse feature extraction framework. We demonstrate significant improvements in indoor and semantic contexts, with LoFTR surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by ~3-5% using a hierarchical framework and showcasing at least a 5x decrease in computational requirements. Our project is open-sourced at https://github.com/hiwha1205/LoFTR. Additionally, a related video can be found at https://youtu.be/t7h4Kt2MMPs. With respect to semantic sparse matching, we adopt a novel strategy, where we apply LoFTR to semantically meaningful sub-regions under controlled scale frequencies, utilizing a hierarchical framework. We combine the regional feature maps with a top-down region parsing module to achieve high-level semantic alignment. Experiments show that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with top regional feature matching accuracy of 88.1% using a simple framework and minimal additional components. Furthermore, we achieve this accuracy without any additional supervision during training. Our project is open-sourced at https://github.com/hiwha1205/SemanticLoFTR. Additionally, a related video can be found at https://youtu.be/8bq4w3b8p3g. A crucial aspect of understanding solar physics involves deriving the vector magnetic field of solar regions. To obtain the full vector field, we often employ an optimization process using observational data from imaging spectropolarimetry, a technique that provides crucial temperature and polarization information. The quality of the results depends on various factors, and any inaccuracies or biases in the input data or optimization process can significantly impact the final outcome. We recently found that widely used datasets from the KIS2 dataset are biased and that conventional methods for calculating vector fields using them can lead to substantial errors and inconsistencies. We aimed to conduct a thorough examination of the likely cause of this issue and suggest ways to correct it. Our study indicates that a particular dataset from the NOAO/NSO FiFiSUN instrument contains excessive noise due to an underexposed bias in the data. We developed an automated method for detecting this issue and rectified the problem before reprocessing the data. Our results show that this new dataset yields reliable vector magnetic field calculations. We observed significant improvements in the quality of the results, and a further analysis revealed that the optimizations themselves were slightly biased, likely due to a weak signal. We were able to correct this by incorporating synthetic signals to improve the calculations. The end product is high-quality vector magnetic field data that significantly expands our knowledge of solar region physics. We believe that a similar problem may exist for other observational data sets and thus, our findings stress the importance of thoroughly checking their content before conducting further analysis. Additionally, to help the community identify and address potential issues with their own data, we introduced an automated testing protocol that detects common errors and provides guidance on corrective actions. This tool is available for download and can be easily applied to any dataset to ensure its validity and accuracy. Our study's findings and recommendations have far-reaching implications and can be widely adopted across various research fields that rely on similar optimization techniques. Ultimately, our work produces reliable results that greatly benefit solar physics research and can be freely accessed from the corresponding data repository. Specifically, this study examines the formation of coalitions among consumers who collaborate to manage their energy consumption in order to minimize costs. A dynamic game model is applied, representing the interactions between players over time, leading to the derivation of an optimal solution that achieves the best overall outcome among all possible results. Furthermore, this study validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach through simulation, demonstrating its potential in reducing overall energy consumption while closely estimating the derived optimal energy consumption patterns from the game model. Moreover, this study highlights the beneficial effects of the proposed approach on energy savings and revenue generation for distribution networks, by comparing it to a baseline policy that assesses energy consumption based on usage targets. Ultimately, this study shows that the proposed approach yields substantial savings in both energy consumption and costs for the power grid. The quantitative results obtained through simulation indicate nearly 9% and 10% energy savings and cost reductions, respectively, demonstrating the potential of the proposed approach to achieve more efficient energy consumption outcomes. Moreover, this study reveals that the proposed approach enables the realization of substantial revenue streams for the grid, with the difference between the best and worst-case revenue streams exceeding 50% for the baseline policy. Notably, the proposed approach enables the realization of both energy savings and revenue streams that are 10% higher than those obtained with the baseline policy. The analysis of the effects of varying usage intervals and billing cycles on energy consumption and revenue streams for both the proposed approach and baseline policy further demonstrates the importance of considering these factors in decision-making. Specifically, the study shows that shorter billing cycles result in improved energy consumption outcomes and higher revenue streams, emphasizing the need for consideration of time intervals in decision-making. The study provides valuable insights into the effects of different game models and billing cycles on decision-making outcomes, guiding the design of alternative game models and billing cycles that may yield better outcomes. Our objective is to verify the practical relevance of intricacy indices by connecting them to established measures of language complexity and examining their underlying mechanisms. We utilized both quantitative and qualitative methods to analyze correlations between various measures of complexity and pinpointed the specific aspects of language that these indices really measure. We discovered that several established intricacy indices are associated with lexical complexity and we can explain how they work linguistically. Our findings imply that only corpus-based measures of intricacy have practical significance, and we suggest an alternative, etically-driven approach to verify their relevance. Such an approach would involve correlating these indices with established measures of complexity through a series of controlled experiments. We argue that only by conducting a series of well-planned experiments can we fully appreciate the meaning behind corpus-based intricacy indices. As a first step towards this goal, we explored methods for authenticating corpus-based findings and applied these methods to reinvestigate the PISA's measure of lexical and grammatical complexity, focusing on word choice, grammar and sentence length. Our analysis highlighted the need for cautious data interpretation when the structure of the writing task and the structure of individual texts are not thoroughly documented. We demonstrated that even seemingly straightforward aspects of the PISA's word choice metric may be challenging to interpret due to the small sample size and the high degree of variation within the data. Consequently, the meaning of the PISA's word choice index as an index of conceptual difficulty remains unclear and further research is needed to fully appreciate its relevance. Interestingly, however, we did find a significant correlation between the PISA's grammar index and the intricacy of grammatical markers, which highlights the need for a more detailed discussion about the relationship between text complexity and the underlying mechanisms of complexity, including the role of lexical, grammatical and discursive factors. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the PISA's length of sentence index is associated with the intricacy of sentence structures, which highlights the importance of distinguishing between the intricacy of individual sentences and the intricacy of the overall text. Finally, our study confirms that the intricacy of textual structures, characterized by the intricacy of transitions, is an essential aspect of text complexity, and we can explain how this structure of complexity, through the intricacy of textual markers, influences the reader's processing difficulty. Consequently, the corpus-based intricacy indices associated with textual structures have clear practical significance, while the other indices remain the subject of further investigation, leading to our main recommendation that future research should prioritize a well-planned series of experiments to fully appreciate their relevance. For these models to yield results, users must specify values for their parameters. Often, experts only have limited knowledge or insight into some model parameters but need insight into many others. This requirement makes implementing the model and interpreting its results computationally challenging. We introduce an approach called Insight-based Simplification that leverages user-specified parameters to derive specified model outcomes. This technique enables users to obtain simplified models that provide specific model outputs when given particular input parameters. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in obtaining actionable results for a complex population dynamics model and a material science model. We also show that our approach can be applied to any model that can be expressed as a graph and to a broad range of optimization problems. Determining the location of significant happenings in real-time is a crucial requirement 
that is commonly found in numerous social media platforms and news sources. This study 
proposes an innovative system for determining the timing and geographical data of 
significant events in real-time. To fulfill this goal, the proposed system leverages 
the advantages of data mining and text mining techniques on massive datasets in a 
parallel environment. Firstly, the study identifies the key characteristics of event 
descriptions in English and Chinese languages, and then employs various algorithms and
techniques to categorize news articles based on their geographical and temporal focus
. Finally, the categorized news is visualized using a map to identify the timing and 
geographical data of significant events in real-time. Experimental studies were conducted 
on 890,000 Chinese news articles and 320,000 English news articles for two consecutive 
weeks, utilizing 32 and 64 CPU cores respectively, to demonstrate the effectiveness 
of the proposed system. Its accuracy was tested for its precision, recall, F1 score, 
and accuracy rates, which were consistently around 90%. In contrast, the proposed system 
outperformed existing methods by leveraging the full capacity of the given CPU cores 
by a significant margin of 20-25%. Furthermore, the proposed system can identify the 
geographical data of significant events up to one hour before they unfold, outperforming 
other methods by 10-15% in this capability. In conclusion, the proposed system presents 
a groundbreaking concept for utilizing the capabilities of parallel computing to determine 
the geographical data and timing of significant events in real-time. This study sheds 
newlight on the subject using various linguistic structures and features and showcases 
its relevance to real-world problems. Lastly, the proposed system is available for 
public use, and its source code can be accessed at www.realtimeevent.net.

Research into quantum feedback guidance has garnered significant interest due to its implicit restriction on input states. All input states are either guided or rejected. This work examines the necessary conditions for quantum feedback guidance in continuous-variable systems, revealing that state guidance is inherently tied to Wigner negativity. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between Wigner negativity and quantum correlations, using the example of Gaussian states to illustrate this connection. Finally, we propose a framework for designing quantum feedback gates that can accurately guide a wide range of input states, including those with negative Wigner functions. This approach is evaluated using the $su(1,1)$ and $su(2)$ Heisenberg algebra examples. Furthermore, we examine the relevant physical mechanisms in cavity-pump-bus-reservoir systems that could support quantum feedback guidance. This work demonstrates that such a cavity can be built using only one optical cavity, with an unconventional pump scheme that does not require adiabatic manipulation. Our findings indicate that quantum feedback guidance is feasible in systems featuring coherent states, $su(2)$-symmetric interactions, or those with weak classical correlations. Moreover, we show that rejecting states with negative Wigner functions in these systems does not necessarily imply the presence of thermal noise. The simplicity of non-coherent continuous phase modulation (CPM) detection makes it a good choice when the phase response of the channel is unknown. Nonetheless, its increased complexity compared to other traditional methods has led to a greater number of mathematical operations and an longer processing time, particularly in the form of floating point operations. Research has shown that reducing the use of floating point operations can significantly boost the processing efficiency of signal processing algorithms on resource restricted devices such as IoT devices. We utilize the Count Recount Tool to analyze and compare the processing efficiency of two widely used CPM detection methods before and after optimizations. Our findings reveal that with optimizations, the processing time of the optimized method is substantially less than half of the time taken by the standard method, thereby greatly enhancing its capability to meet real-time detection requirements. We also propose and introduce an advanced method that combines CPM detection with data modulation, demonstrating its capacity to further reduce the complexity of the CPM detection process. We then apply this combined method to four distinct CPM detection types, resulting in significant complexity reductions, with some variants reducing the complexity by as much as 87 percent. We further validate that this combined approach does not adversely affect its bit error rate (BER) performance. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that with optimizations, the processing time of the CPM detection method is significantly lowered and subsequently meets real-time detection requirements. Moreover, the integration of CPM detection with data modulation yields improved performance while reducing complexity by a substantial margin, thereby enhancing overall system performance. Our findings are subsequently tested using the BER Tool. The experimental results from the BER tool confirm our earlier conclusions and reveal a reduction of at least three orders of magnitude in the BER when compared to its preprocessed state, ultimately reaching a BER of 0.0 with further processing using CPM data joint detection. This lasting BER level of 0.0 indicates that no further improvements in performance can be attained, signifying a high degree of system reliability and efficiency, which is critical in the development of dependable and efficient system designs. The process of evaluating CPM detection methods with the Count Recount Tool facilitates systematic examinations of their processing efficiency, which is crucial in the design of systems with resource constraints. By applying this CPM detection efficiency framework to various algorithms and optimizations, valuable insights into their processing time are gathered, which is essential in finding the optimal CPM detection method that meets real-time detection requirements. With these functions, we've calculated the nucleon's parton distribution functions and the inclusive jet production cross-section in collisions between two heavy particles. Additionally, we've used the parton distribution functions to calculate the total momentum, $F(x)$, and energy, $E(x)$, of a nucleon at low virtualities. Calculations for the nucleon's parton distribution functions and $F(x)$ and $E(x)$ at low virtualities were done explicitly at the QCD scaling point (available at https://github.com/MiNDSA/NCDistrisbutions). We've also obtained an analytical formula for the nucleon's energy function $E(x)$ at next-to-leading order. This research provides insight into nucleon structure at low virtualities in a noncommutative spacetime, including properties of nucleon parton distribution functions. We found that the nucleon is composed of both valence and sea quarks, with four flavor degrees of freedom, that are equally distributed at very low virtualities. We observed a net negative quark contribution to the nucleon at low virtualities due to the presence of $u\bar{u}$ and $d\bar{d}$ sea quarks. Furthermore, the nucleon's energy function and total momentum were found to be described by a modified version of the gluon distribution function $xG(x)$. The calculated numerical and analytical values of the total momentum and energy functions at low virtualities were consistent with global parton distribution functions at this low virtuality regime. We also found that the calculated analytical total momentum and energy functions at next-to-leading order were similar in value to historical data. Calculations for the nucleon's parton distribution functions and total momentum and energy functions at higher virtualities were not completed in this research, as they require computation beyond the scope of this current work. Future research will involve further investigation of nucleon structure at both low and high virtualities in a noncommutative spacetime, including parton distribution functions, momentum and energy functions, and the generalization of kinetic theory using the calculated total momentum and energy functions at next-to-leading order.
