A core capability for engaging in conversational interactions is comprehending the meaning of dialogues. Current models excel at predicting probabilities for pre-defined categories based on textual input, but they lack a deep understanding of the underlying semantic structures essential for sophisticated conversational responses. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel, meaning-centered training paradigm tailored for conversational data. Our method encompasses three key areas of improvement: Firstly, we develop a novel task to guide the learning of sentence meaning representations that incorporate implicit contextual connections between sentences. Secondly, we create a novel learning objective to teach models the task of uncovering semantic structures within sentence collections. Thirdly, we introduce a new training objective to promote text-to-text generation of detailed, explicit meaning structures enriching the underlying semantic structures. Our proposed method is successfully evaluated across various benchmarks, demonstrating substantial improvements in performance. Notably, it lays the groundwork for applying large language models to more complex tasks, such as filling gaps in conversational datasets, as well as more ambitious tasks, like generating conversational data autonomously. To facilitate future research, we provide open-source code and the extensive dataset collection, the Meaningful Conversation Dataset. Our dataset spans 1.3 billion training samples, covering diverse human languages, and complements the Meaningful English Conversation Dataset with human annotations collected via crowdsourcing and automated techniques. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearnEngland/LaMDa-LEISegments. As machine learning and interpretability go hand-in-hand, experts are seeking ways to measure and evaluate algorithms based on how well they can be understood by humans. While there are existing methods to assess data quality and identify areas for improvement in algorithmic transparency, they lack a universal metric to gauge cognitive complexity, or the difficulty in comprehending a model. In this paper, we introduce a new approach to interpretability that focuses on how well algorithms can be learned by humans, proposing a framework and a specific metric, the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS). The CCS measures algorithmic clarity through a method that combines its logic and logic in relation to the target data. Additionally, we propose a learning curve metric to assess how easily users can adapt to an algorithm's changing conditions. By evaluating and demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method, we found that the CCS identifies complexities in algorithms that other methods miss, providing a more complete assessment of interpretability. Importantly, the CCS offers actionable suggestions for improving algorithmic clarity. Our research emphasizes the importance of understanding an algorithm's learnability in order to improve its transparency. In order to validate the practical value of the CCS, we conducted and published a study involving 25 data science experts from 5 different countries, who tested and refined the effectiveness of the CCS. A related video showcasing this study's methodology and results can be found at https://youtu.be/GQPpYcUfO6Y. In addition, the study's code and a live demo of the CCS are available at https://github.com/learn-interpretability/learn-interpretability.com. Extreme events and their resulting severities are crucially important to understand, particularly for accurate risk assessments and mitigation strategies.  The traditional Extreme Value Theory approach constructs a model by assuming a geometric connection between return periods, event counts, and the maximum extreme event observed, which is based on an extreme event probability distribution.  This fundamental relationship is often broken by the statistical method of Maximum Likelihood Estimation, leading to significant biases in parametric models when dealing with rare and record-span phenomena.  This paper introduces a new Bayesian estimation technique that restores relationships intact, allowing for an objective prior distribution that maintains geometric connections, which in turn provides accurate Bayesian posterior inferences.  The methodology is based on a Poisson processes reparametrization that offers several benefits, including maintaining statistical independence between events, descreasing occurrence rates as events get more extreme, and facilitating straightforward Bayesian inference and model comparison.  The theoretical framework is supported by various numerical experiments showing the approach's capacity for correcting biases and improving model selection and prediction capabilities.  As an application, the methodology is used to study the extreme events of Hurricane Katrina.  The findings suggest that the reparametrization provides an effective way to establish reliable relationships between event counts, allowing for accurate risk assessments and statistical inferences. Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths in orbit have traditionally struggled with accurate photometry due to the intense Lyman-alpha line emitted by the Earth's atmosphere. Engineering prototypes known as Lyman-alpha filters are being designed to block this line and enable global UV spectroscopy missions to achieve reliable flux calculations. Although the concept has been around for decades, we are creating a new filter prototype through collaboration with Teledyne and the NASA Godard Space Telescope and Instrument Center, with the goal of achieving a level of precision that meets scientific standards. Our prototype will focus on the 1216.0-1216.1 Å band, aiming for an error margin of less than 1% by utilizing multi-coated MkII silicon nitride coatings to optimize the optical properties of the band. Testing of the prototype will involve measuring the filter's transmission and reflectivity under various vacuum and x-ray conditions, as well as testing its ability to block Lyman-alpha radiation generated through interstellar transmission, hydrogen gas transmission, and artificial broad-source radiation. By analyzing data from a spectrometer with the prototype in place, we can accurately determine any residual transmission within the filter, with the ultimate goal of fulfilling NASA's Godard SPT definition for this photometric instrument. Success in this endeavor would make it possible for future space missions to compute precise spectra and photometry data from various UV sources, taking a significant step forward in ultraviolet astronomy research. The prototype's development could potentially be applied in future extraterrestrial-based photometry endeavors, allowing these missions to capture a deeper understanding of the far-UV spectral properties prevalent across the universe. Moreover, a new technique of calculating photometric accuracy by modeling the optical properties of the filter using vacuum, residual transmission, reflectivity, and transmission of the Lyman-alpha line could be established, providing scientists with a useful tool for predicting a telescope's photometric accuracy before it's deployed. This technique could then be applied in various astronomical research contexts, yielding crucial data essential for a precise measurement of various stellar's and galactic's spectral properties. Lastly, a study on the statistical precision achieved through repeated measurements of a stellar star's spectral properties could be conducted, providing scientists with a more detailed understanding of the theoretical models they can use to create more accurate galactic mass, stellar mass, and star composition forecasts. In computer networks, the management of graphs plays a vital role in ensuring efficient network operation. Effective graph management requires a symmetry-checking process, which can be computationally intensive and time-consuming, especially with the increasing presence of low-cost, energy-efficient devices on the network. These devices, or 'graph calculators,' can perform simple operations, such as XOR operations, at very low power consumption. By leveraging these devices to perform symmetry-checking tasks, we can reduce the load on the network and prevent unnecessary data transmission. In this study, we introduce a novel protocol that utilizes a minimal number of specialized graph devices to verify symmetry in graph networks in a distributed manner. The protocol ensures that each node's local view of the network contains a symmetric subgraph without requiring direct node-to-node communication. The study provides a mathematical analysis of the probability of incorrect symmetry assumptions in nodes and offers a practical solution to minimize the risk of such errors. The proposed protocol demonstrates a significant reduction in power consumption and latency compared to alternative methods, with results verified through simulation testing. In a typical scenario with 1000 nodes and a symmetry probability of 0.1, the protocol reduces power consumption by 26.7% and latency by 65.1%. Moreover, the protocol achieves substantial latency reductions of up to 71% and power savings of up to 28% in specific network configurations. The study showcases the practical application of the concept of graph devices for enhancing the performance of computer networks. The test data and graph device models are made available for further research. The research was conducted with the support of the Fundacao para a Computacao Cientifica (FCC). We're investigating the quantum statistics of a charged impurity moving freely on a 2D plane with zero spin, subject to no external influences, within a environment of the vacuum field with nonzero spin, which gives rise to a interaction between the impurity and the quantum void due to their opposing spins. This interaction is called the angular Casimir effect, and it includes terms dependent on the impurity's kinetic energy and its relationship with the surrounding quantum void. Calculations indicate that the angular terms of the Casimir effect and the kinetic energy terms demonstrate a linear relationship, while the angular terms are directly proportional to the impurity's charge, and their magnitudes decrease as the distance between the impurity and the boundary increases. Furthermore, at a distance of 2 away from the plane's perimeter, the angular terms cancel each other out. Analysis of this system's behavior under different constraints that could influence the angular Casimir effect reveals that even though the system is not in thermodynamic equilibrium, the angular terms are still constant and independent of temperature. This is because the system's symmetry precludes any variation in the angular terms due to temperature changes. This research extends the FGNET model by integrating reparameterization techniques in hyperbolic space to improve its encoding capabilities for detailed tasks. This theoretical work provides the foundation for developing efficient tree search algorithms in hyperbolic space, (iii) leading to improved sample efficiency in few-shot link prediction tasks.  Experimental results validate the advantages of integrating hyperbolic space with FGNET, while demonstrating the universality of these improvements across various FGNET datasets and different encoding architectures. This study's results showcase the enhanced capabilities of FGNET-RH across various FGNET datasets, and its adaptability across distinct encoding architectures and hyperbolic space implementations, establishing it as a robust improvement over existing approaches. Predictive models for games are essential in determining likely outcomes
and understanding the impact of various actions. The issue with modeling the
Nash Equilibrium (NE), the most established concept of game equilibria, is
that it's not feasible for large-scale and dynamic games due to its computational
intensiveness and lack of generalization capabilities. The NE concept alone
is insufficient in capturing various types of non-cooperative and online game
scenarios where multiple NE states may exist, potentially switching over time.
This paper introduces the study of a different game equilibrium, the Generalized
Nash Equilibrium (gne) that can represent multiple NE states and is applicable
to large-scale and dynamic games. The gne has the advantage of its composition
ability, enabling us to develop a special type of neural network, the Fixed Point
Network (FPN), capable of directly learning the gne of large-scale and dynamic games. 
We provide theoretical justifications for the unique properties of FPN and show
its practical potential in learning various types of game equilibria. The experimental
results confirm that FPN outperforms the alternatives significantly in a variety
of test cases. The framework presented in this paper can potentially expand to
other types of game scenarios, encompassing large-scale and dynamic games with
various types of equilibria. The data and the code for the study are available
at: \url{https://github.com/RunProb/GneFlowing}. \uff0c

Due to the inherent complexity of these systems, only a limited set of green measures can be effectively monitored in real-time. Therefore, we employ model-based predictive monitoring to identify which green measures should be prioritized within a given timeframe, utilizing a developed model to optimize the selection process. The proposed effective predictive monitoring (EPM) method systematically schedules surveillance for crucial metrics in real-time, prioritizing those most essential for operational safety. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of covert attacks on a linear time-invariant system, where the system operator is unaware of the compromise, and derive conditions for their detection through directional search. Notably, EPM can function seamlessly with any set of search algorithms, including the currently available ones. Although promising results have been achieved, problems still exist, particularly with regards to overconfidence in the encoded representations achieved by the minimum square Kullback-Leibler divergence. For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which include a wide range of hyperbolic systems, we've established a significant principle: For a sufficiently small, C2 perturbation, the leading eigenvalue of the transfer operator will experience a decrease. In systems exhibiting uniform expansion, this transfer operator has a finite dimension, and corresponding properties for perturbed systems follow from this, involving exponential behavior and smooth, dominant eigenfunctions, which also demonstrate a decrease in norm. In systems exhibiting nonuniform expansion, this transfer operator does not have a finite dimension, and corresponding properties for perturbed systems follow from operator perturbation theory. These results will be crucial in the future for proving the transfer operator's hyperbolicity, and specifically, for a universality principle in this context. An crucial part of this involves intervention impact identification - a procedure that determines which interventions have led to notable effects at a controlled false discovery rate (FDR) across various scenarios. This method uses a temporary FDR of 0.1 level in the initial rounds to strip away interventions with unimportant effects and subsequently applies a more stringent FDR of 0.05 in the second round to identify significant interventions. Furthermore, our method exhibits a nominal FDR that is close to the specified threshold in all cases. This proposed strategy is both computationally efficient and scalable for large datasets such as those encountered in extensive experimental settings. Feedback from instructors is essential for students's success in any educational setting. Yet, incorporating feedback from instructors can be time-consuming and impractical for large student groups. Moreover, students may struggle to incorporate instructors's feedback due to varying levels of understanding and feedback scope. This study compares a novel learning approach, called RAINIER, which provides software testing students with instant fundamental feedback based on their task submissions, versus a traditional detailed feedback system. Our analysis of 138 students over two academic cycles revealed that those using RAINIER performed better and demonstrated more confidence, completing additional tasks and creating more test cases, while consuming less instructors's time and resources. Notably, our empirical findings show that RAINIER's immediate feedback is just as effective as conventional detailed feedback provided by instructors. This research uncovers that less frequent but in-depth feedback might not be necessary for achieving similar results, and highlights the benefits of feedback frequency, proximity to feedback, student confidence, task scope and completeness, and multi-modal approaches that complement each other in the education of software engineering. Domain adjustment, which involves adapting a model's performance across different domains, is a crucial task in many applications. However, when the target domain is fully restricted, a novel and interesting sub-task, known as source-free domain adjustment, arises. The key requirement is that the target domain is not accessible for training purposes. A naive approach to resolve this challenge is to utilize data-efficient supervised fine-tuning methods. Nevertheless, they are expensive to implement and can't be used when the target domain is fully restricted. To overcome this limitation, we propose a semi-supervised learning approach to transfer a self-supervised model trained in the source domain to the target domain. The approach minimizes both pseudo-label losses and information regularization to adjust the model. The practicality and effectiveness of the proposed method are demonstrated through extensive experiments, which show that it successfully transfers a model trained in one domain to another without requiring training data from the target domain. Moreover, the results indicate that it outperforms existing domain adjustment methods by a significant margin. The code for the proposed method is publicly available at this GitHub link: https://github.com/sterliloo/STA. With its reliability and strong performance, our approach has the potential to effectively utilize large-scale unlabeled data, thereby facilitating model adaptation without requiring label-rich target data. Furthermore, the results highlight that the proposed method successfully generalizes to more challenging scenarios, such as adjusting a model's performance from a domain with non-ID background variations to another domain with rich variation in background content. Ultimately, the proposed method effectively solves the difficult task of source-free domain adjustment. In various life science studies, researchers often work with complex time-series data. This paper proposes a new neural network-based approach called monitored supervised learning for short-time series (MOTSalt) to tackle the challenge of learning from noisy, high-dimensional temporal sequences. MOTSalt combines a residual monitoring system with an online deep learning method, allowing the model to adapt quickly and improve information recovery in real-time. Using simulated biological signals and real-world E. coli single-cell data, our experiments demonstrate that MOTSalt can effectively reduce noise and reveal previously hidden details from time-stamped data, even when certain data points are suspect or missing. This capability is particularly valuable for studying rapid cell processes, such as rapid signaling events or Ca2+ dynamics. Our code has been made available on GitHub to facilitate future applications. In these scenarios, we explore the connection between a class of algorithms based on neural networks and a theory of how people make decisions that involves subconscious steps and subconscious conflicts. Our research is in two parts. In the first part, we demonstrate that finding an effective strategy for these scenarios is equivalent to solving a complex network of subconscious steps and can be challenging even when the substeps are simple. In the second part, we compare the different strategies that a realistic computer system uses to solve these scenarios with the decisions that a realistic human would make in these scenarios and highlight the limitations of computer systems in these environments. Current state-of-the-art action detection models, which identify every single frame in an animation, are plagued by several issues. Notably, they require intense labor and fail to capture the overall story. This work presents a framework for action detection by focusing only on decisive moments. Unlike prior approaches, our system is not reliant on users labeling specific scenes. Instead, it uses a simple three-way annotation scheme that asks users to identify the subject, action, and setting. This subject-action-context triangle enables the model to grasp the story in videos by combining the information from all moments in an animation, where every instance is viewed as an extension of the preceding one. Our system consists of two distinct modules. The first module utilizes a hidden state in a self-supervised manner to filter out unimportant scenes and retain only the pivotal ones. The second module integrates all moments in an animation to extract key frames that represent the story in an animation. This story is then used to determine the start and end points of actions in an animation. Our spot-train-graph-based method, which trains the model using the self-learned key frames, outperforms other approaches on activity detection tasks, according to our tests. Our code is available for public viewing at https://github.com/asharakeh/spot-train-graph-clips. Nevertheless, safeguarding the confidentiality of this sensitive information in such a system poses a significant challenge. A potential solution to this problem is the development of a secure graduation ranking system that complies with the privacy protocols of federated learning. Despite advancements in this area, existing methods often fail to effectively protect student data and provide consistent ranking results. To overcome these issues, we introduced the DP-REC system, which uses a robust training strategy and robust neural network design to effectively and securely train a ranking model in a distributed educational setting. The DP-REC system utilizes a unique training technique to ensure that the model's training process meets strict data confidentiality requirements. By integrating this approach with a robust neural network framework, DP-REC is able to provide reliable graduation rankings while ensuring the privacy of student data in accordance with the strictest privacy protocols. In our evaluation, we found that DP-REC is capable of achieving the same level of accuracy as a non-confidential model, while providing reliable graduation rankings and strict data confidentiality. To validate the effectiveness of DP-REC, we conducted several experiments to test the model's accuracy, reliability, and data confidentiality. The results of these experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DP-REC and provide valuable insights into its potential applications. Notably, DP-REC was found to be more accurate and reliable than a non-confidential model that was trained on real-world student data. To the best of our knowledge, DP-REC is the first federated learning system that is designed to provide reliable graduation rankings while ensuring the privacy of student data in accordance with the strictest privacy protocols. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DP-REC and provide valuable insights into its potential applications in the field of educational data mining. These insights can be utilized by researchers and practitioners to develop more efficient and effective data mining solutions for educational institutions. In particular, we found that DP-REC is capable of handling large amounts of sensitive data in real-world educational settings, making it a valuable tool for educational data miners. By designing a reliable data ranking system, DP-REC is able to provide valuable insights into the behavior and performance of students, which can be used to inform various academic decisions. The first cognitive structure we calls 'C1', which involves incomplete information about an opponent's specific actions, and results in probabilistic transitions to the next phase. The second, 'C2', involves incomplete information about an opponent's parameters, which results in deterministic transitions. Our paper investigates how these cognitive structures impact two types of multi-phase games: binary and hybrid games. In binary games with two pure strategies, we show that 'C1' leads to the existence of unique pure equilibria in each phase. However, 'C2' may not guarantee such equilibria. We prove that under 'C1', players can employ a straightforward strategy of maximizing expected payoffs in each phase. The lack of analogous results for 'C2' under incomplete parameter information necessitates the introduction of a new concept of 'uniqueness' for 'C2', which we call 'uniqueness of expectation'. designed to enhance internal data flow through sequential refinement steps.

such as UNet, TransUNNet, TempUNet, and TempTransUNNet.
Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets, 
including ClimatePrediction, WeatherATLAS, WeatherUNet, and TMSGLUE,
reveal that Hopper significantly enhances predictive accuracy and overall efficiency.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been a prominent model for layered neural networks due to its distinct benefits, yet its full potential could not be harnessed because of an unresolved optimization challenge. A straightforward algorithm was able to perform well initially, yet it failed to reach the optimal solution in larger-scale networks. To overcome this issue, we present a novel algorithm that significantly improves upon the previous state-of-the-art in MoE network optimization, enabling consistent convergence at any network size. A variant of the algorithm was also formulated to mimic non-convex optimization methods like gradient descent, as confirmed by theoretical proofs and supporting numerical experiments in datasets of varying difficulty. When applied to image generation and compression tasks, our algorithm outperformed existing solutions, achieving state-of-the-art results with significant improvements in computational efficiency and network size reductions. Moreover, the latter task's challenging subtask of image compression was successfully solved for the first time. Analysis of the algorithm's properties reveals that it shares certain beneficial characteristics with dynamic neural networks, such as non-monotonicity and non-stationarity. However, we also establish that the algorithm converges to a stable point, unlike some non-convex optimization methods that converge to random variables instead of a well-defined point. Finally, the efficacy of the algorithm was demonstrated through successful applications in reinforcement learning tasks, specifically in the challenging game of chess. When combined with a pre-trained MoE network, our algorithm was able to play this game continuously for the first time, playing at a level of medium competence. Details of the algorithm's performance in this game are available at https://github.com/lyst/official_moels_improvements/, as it has been open-sourced for the benefit of the research community. To sum up, our contributions are threefold: presenting a novel MoE optimization algorithm for large-scale networks; successfully applying non-convex optimization to MoE for the first time; and improving the performance of MoE networks through a deeper comprehension of their regularizing properties. Ultimately, the main advantage of MoE networks, which is their capacity to learn diverse representations, has been unlocked more effectively than before. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the belief that certain deep neural networks are inherently robust against overfitting due to their architecture. However, research has revealed that well-established architectural patterns commonly seen in natural image datasets can influence transferability, which is contingent upon the training and testing dataset in question. Our investigation delves into this phenomenon by examining two widely accepted assertions within the deep learning community: firstly, that convolutional networks benefit from spatial invariance thanks to data augmentation, and secondly, that symmetric datasets exhibit superior transferability. Our findings indicate that both of these claims require revision. Instead, the key to achieving transferability lies in the creation of similar local representations through data augmentation methods or feature extractors. Furthermore, the assumption that datasets with symmetric properties exhibit higher transferability was also found to be unfounded. Our study demonstrates this concept using a variety of counterexamples and supporting experiments. Our research contributes towards optimising transferability by identifying the most effective data augmentation methods and incorporating these into a method for determining optimal preprocessing techniques. Our method, referred to as the Relative Feature Similarity Search (RFSS), searches for an optimal preprocessing technique to enhance transferability. It achieves this aim by (i) conducting a comprehensive search for the most effective data augmentation technique across a range of potential techniques, and (ii) applying a dimensionality reduction method in order to identify similar representations. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of the RFSS algorithm by achieving transferability rates of 85% using MNIST on test CIFAR10, and 80% using CNIST on test CNIST. By exploring transferability, our study contributes towards a deeper understanding of the underlying architecture of deep neural networks. It has far-reaching implications for the development of ensemble learning methods, particularly in terms of creating robust inter-ensemble connections. It also raises crucial questions regarding the design of inter-ensemble architectures, prompting a challenge to conventional wisdom. Our study provides key insights of value to the inter-ensemble learning community. It also sheds light on the broader societal consequences of deep learning advancements, prompting reflections on the dual uses of AI. Finally, the accompanying code for our study has been made publicly available at https://github.com/azee/Transferability. By promoting reproducibility, our code contributes towards fostering research transparency and advancing knowledge in the field of deep learning. In order to disseminate information across complex networks, which connect vast populations, arrays of sensors, or digital systems, it is crucial to comprehend how information-generating entities respond to stimulations and share this information with other nodes. The inception of an information-generating event is typically characterized by a rapid increase in activity, during which the information spreads among neighboring nodes at varying propagation speeds. Past research has thoroughly documented the impact of network topology on task propagation, revealing that dense networks facilitate faster information dissemination than sparse networks. However, a crucial aspect of network architecture, namely modularity, which represents the degree of segregation within a network's communities, has not been extensively evaluated for its effect on information dissemination speed. Using task propagation experiments on artificial small-world networks, we have demonstrated that a higher modularity significantly impedes the propagation speed. Moreover, we have demonstrated that a highly segregated network architecture hinders fast information dissemination just as it hampers efficient task propagation. Consequently, network architects designing new systems, researchers studying task propagation, and individuals setting up information-sharing systems across diverse nodes are advised to minimize network modularity and enhance node connectivity to enhance propagation efficiency. The findings, based on a comprehensive analysis of a large model network consisting of over 88 million nodes, are universally applicable and may as well be relevant to vast arrays of sensors, social networks, or populations connecting across the globe. The presented research lays the groundwork for future studies on information dissemination speed in relation to network architecture. Research has thoroughly documented the phenomenon that heavily overparameterized deep neural networks achieve excellent performance even when their underlying architectures remain unsophisticated. Although this phenomenon has sparked significant controversy across the scientific community, the underlying cause remains unclear. This study presents evidence suggesting that excessive overparameterization in successful neural networks is, in fact, a direct consequence of limitations in machine computation and data encoding rather than an inherent property of the data itself. Furthermore, the study introduces an innovative perspective on the role of overparameterization in successful neural networks. It demonstrates that, under certain computational constraints, heavily overparameterized neural networks with relatively basic architectures achieve excellent performance. Additionally, the study shows that the underlying signals present in the data can be reconstructed by extremely narrow minima, which is in contrast to the prevailing notion that the successful neural networks were associated with broad minima. To support this hypothesis, the study performs computations using a low-setting M1 chip and achieves comparable results with a typical CPU. Moreover, the study investigates the impact of data encoding methods on the performance of overparameterized neural networks. Interestingly, the study finds that the underlying signals present in the data can be reconstructed more effectively using bit-precision models rather than the typical floating-point models used in conventional deep learning applications. The study initiates an innovative research paradigm that deviates from the conventional finite sample perspective and instead focuses on the implications of infinite-bit precision data encoding. This research paradigm may facilitate the development of novel insights into the behavior of overparameterized neural networks. Finally, the study demonstrates that the reconstruction of signals from the data can be leveraged to decrease the required overparameterization in successful neural networks. This approach may lead to a potential solution to the long-standing issue of gradient vanishing problems encountered in overparameterized deep neural networks. The dial-a-ride problem is a service route planning problem where a transporter responds to non-committed requests from customers within a set service time limit. Each customer request consists of a trip starting from a specified location and ending at another specified location, within a certain time frame. We modify the dial-a-ride problem by incorporating a service area constraint, prohibiting drivers from deviating from their assigned routes. In this modified context, we label the problem as the dial-a-ride metropolitan problem (DRM). We propose a branch-and-bound algorithm to solve DRM, involving a lower-bound estimation and an efficient branching strategy. Computational tests show that our algorithm effectively solves small DRM instances within a reasonable time frame, yielding a high-quality solution close to optimality. Additionally, a variation of the DRM with multiple drivers has been investigated. We further analyzed the properties of DRM solutions and conducted a study on the performance of our algorithm using a range of instances, gathering important insights along the way. We observed that under specific conditions, a DRM system may not always have a solution, as demonstrated by the presentation of counter-cases. Furthermore, through computational analysis, we established the existence of DRM optimal solutions in certain, somewhat restricted scenarios. We also evaluated the quality of approximate solutions obtained from a range of standard heuristics for route planning and discovered that they are effective in finding a substantial proportion of the optimal cost (averaging between 70% and 80% of the optimal cost) in our specific test cases. We derived a lower-bound limit of 3/5 of the optimal cost for the DRM using a specific method and demonstrated that this bound is indeed asymptotically unattainable in certain scenarios. Lastly, computational results showed that DRM can be efficiently solved by the branch-and-bound algorithm within a reasonable time frame, as long as the number of customers does not exceed 20. We also observed a considerable reduction in solution computation time when employing a pre-processing method to reduce the number of possible solutions. The analysis further showed that the branching priority leads to the most time-efficient solution search. We propose a strategy to reduce the number of possible solutions during computation, resulting in a considerable reduction of solution computation time when implemented. Additionally, we observed that the approximate solutions obtained from the heuristics are such that each vehicle makes the most of its capacity, as well as that the number of possible solutions for each vehicle is substantial, as it is proportional to the number of customers and exponentially increases with the number of vehicles, as it is proportional to the number of vehicles.

Our work is further facilitated by its publically available code and detailed replication documentation. In computational models used to study DNA's structural and functional aspects, active site constraints are essential, especially for processes such as transcription and replication. We developed an efficient and localized method for applying constraints similar to those found in real systems, utilizing a 'rigid foundation' concept adapted from techniques used in building structures. This approach, effectively minimizing unwanted degrees of freedom, allows us to study molecular systems, including long DNA polymers, in an efficient manner. We have successfully demonstrated our method's effectiveness by applying it to a simulation system consisting of a DNA molecule containing 12 bases in solution. In comparison to a 'fixed atom' method, our approach, the 'rigid foundation' method, exhibits improved overall efficiency while simultaneously allowing for accurate bond lengths and allowing the system to freely move in other aspects. In general, the 'rigid foundation' method performs operations within a 2-3 times CPU factor in comparison to the 'fixed atom' method, depending on the system in question. In addition to these findings, 'rigid foundation' method constraints have proven to be compatible with the AMD force field and are suitable for a range of computational simulations. Ultimately, the results from our tests show that the 'rigid foundation' method constraints work well in facilitating the creation of various structures found within DNA, including A-DNA, B-DNA and a hybrid PNA structure comprising non-natural nucleic acids. In summary, the 'rigid foundation' method represents an important constraint type capable of being easily integrated into existing simulations in order to expedite an understanding of the complex processes involved in DNA's structural and functional aspects. The Active Natural Sampling (ANS) algorithm has been proposed as an efficient and effective solution for deep learning, particularly for training, where large datasets are readily available. It works by systematically exploring the full parameter space and selecting only the crucial data points to label, utilizing a novel bias that favors learning from key data variations. This has been achieved through the development of an analytical model and theoretical proof, demonstrating the algorithm's ability to balance training complexity with the efficiency of selecting representative data points. Crucially, ANS achieves comparable accuracy as other leading methods, but significantly outperforms them by efficiently reducing the number of labeled data points required for training, resulting in substantial time and computational savings. This is accompanied by a proportionate reduction in energy consumption, thereby highlighting the algorithm's dual benefits of environmental friendliness and significant resource cost savings. Moreover, the feasibility of implementing ANS on edge devices has been demonstrated. Upon reviewing the current literature, a notable research gap was identified, which is the absence of an in-depth analysis on the complementary and mutual benefits of model efficiency and energy efficiency, which is proposed to be investigated further in the future. Research into the sound production of flying objects dates back to several decades, primarily focusing on the characteristics of their acoustic signals rather than their underlying decision-making processes. Similar research on the sound production of flying devices with brains, such as drones controlled by autonomous movement strategies, is largely missing. Our paper describes a quantitative method for analyzing acoustic pressure over time and assigns a comprehensive set of signal characteristics to each decision made by the autonomous system. We apply this approach to two military swarm drone scenarios: one with two and three drones, each controlled by different decision-making processes. By exploring the decision-making strategies of these systems over extended periods of time, we reveal the impact of various parameters and how their behavior can be identified in their sound production, even when there's no external influence. Despite the limitations of their individual capabilities, these systems have developed a level of complexity in their decision-making, enabling them to adapt to challenging situations. Their decision-making processes over time are marked by the appearance of specific patterns and transitions, along with recurring patterns in the changes they undergo. These findings open up new avenues for investigating the capacity of central brainless entities, whether they're individual or group-based, to adapt and respond to their environment. Moreover, our ability to extract and analyze this information has significant implications for the study and monitoring of autonomous systems, both in their natural state and as observed through sensory inputs like sound. Finally, our research highlights the need to carefully consider the potential for autonomous entities to cause harm, whether it's intentional or not, and the importance of establishing guidelines for their use. As such systems become more capable, both individually and collectively, they are capable of producing a diverse range of sounds that not only signify their own internal workings but also possess aesthetic value. Therefore, it is essential that their sound is continuously monitored and analyzed in order to interpret their behavior correctly. Our research demonstrates that even autonomous systems producing sound in a complex and variable manner can be successfully assigned a set of consistent characteristics, which in turn facilitates their detection and classification. Of course, our current methods for analyzing these systems have been developed and tested primarily through analytical work, so more practical applications remain to be found. One potential application, for example, could involve identifying the decision-making strategies of autonomous drones by listening to the sounds they produce during a drone chase. Our research may also inspire the development of new methods for analyzing sound, potentially leading to new applications involving auditory perception. In any case, our ability to interpret the decision-making strategies of autonomous entities relies on their sounds exhibiting a sufficient level of repetition and variability

A crucial metric for measuring system complexity is entropy, as it can capture inherent order, reveal hidden patterns, and assess the amount of uncertainty within a system, whether it's a liquid or a random crystal. Entropy can be measured in various ways, such as specific entropy concerning certain parameters or redundancy entropy, which compares system-specific entropy to its minimum possible value. To examine the role of detail in driving self-organizing systems, we applied entropy measures to Boltzmann networks with a energy function. We designed these systems to exhibit geometric closure, often leading to the formation of clusters, rings and hyperlinks. We found that in systems where details play a significant role in organizing, the redundancy entropy reaches its minimum value much faster than specific entropy, indicating that in systems where details matter, order develops quickly from initial states of high uncertainty. These results align with experimental observations on protein structures, as well as the development of geometric clusters in natural bird flocks. Additionally, we found that in systems where details play no significant role in organization, the specific entropy outperforms the redundancy entropy. We support our numerical findings with analytical models by modifying the eigenvalue distribution of the network, such that the laplacian matrix no longer dominates the eigenvalue spectrum. This modification leads to substantial differences in the redundancy and specific entropy measures, which can now more closely resemble each other than they do the thermodynamic entropy. Notably, the redundancy entropy becomes insensitive to the direction of flow in these systems, which is not the case for specific entropy. These results, in combination with previous work on Boltzmann networks with random edges, reveal that in systems where details matter, the redundancy entropy reaches its minimum value much faster than specific entropy, and in systems where details play no significant role in organization, the specific entropy outperforms the redundancy entropy. Importantly, the analytical models confirm these numerical findings, which can now be used to evaluate the organization of biological systems, such as geographic clusters in bird flocks. The application of entropy measures to Boltzmann networks may also inform the development of computational models for geometric self-organizing systems, as well as aid in the analysis of temporal systems. Ultimately, the integration of entropy measures and geometric constraints may offer the most effective approach to understanding the complexity of systems that transition from disordered states to ordered states within geometrically related subsets of their parameter spaces. This work is documented at https://github.com/asharkey/entropy-boltzmann-networks. A related movie is available at https://youtu.org/jV8

Our hand gesture recognition system, developed using a combination of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks, demonstrates high accuracy levels on a large dataset featuring diverse and rapid hand movements. This accuracy enables our swarm of robots to make informed decisions, allowing them to successfully complete various tasks, such as package delivery, object manipulation, and exploration within these challenging environments. Our experimental results, derived from extensive evaluation on a large dataset, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, a series of real-world experiments, conducted outdoors over an area spanning 8 square meters, showcase the capabilities of this technique in facilitating swarm behavior. Ultimately, these findings contribute to the solution of the "symbolic communication problem" afflicting multi-robot systems and highlight the benefits of distributed human-swarm interaction. Our proposed method's source code, associated data, and detailed simulation environment are freely available on public code repositories, aimed at fostering future research in this field. With these findings in tandem, multi-robot systems may now successfully engage in communication with humans in a wide range of diverse, high-complexity environments. Our research also addresses the broader issue of communication between humans and robotic systems, posing a pressing need for autonomous vehicles and robots to interact with humans in a more intuitive and recognizable manner. Our study has also received a Registered Report designation. This research has also received an Best Paper award at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Distributed Intelligent Systems (ICDIS). Additional information can also be found at the website of the NavSys research project. Our approach to human-swarm communication addresses a long-standing issue, the symbolic communication problem, affecting multi-robot systems. In the analysis of microscopic images representing blood cell morphology,
a persistent problem for experts is accurately categorizing various cell types.
To overcome this issue, a cutting-edge deep learning technique called ensembles
has shown significant potential in enhancing classification accuracy and reliability.
This method involves uniting multiple neural networks, each trained on distinct
segments of the same image, to robustly identify the target cells. Below, the
ensemble model for categorizing white blood cells is presented, along with
our investigation of its efficacy in accurately classifying these cells when
compared to a trained individual model. Moreover, the importance of incorporating
expert feedback into the traditional supervised training process is highlighted
in order to improve the accuracy of the neural networks. Finally, a systematic
evaluation is conducted to demonstrate how the accuracy of the ensemble model
can be further improved by varying the proportions of expert-labeled and
self-labeled images used in the training process. Experimental findings validate
that more expert-labeled images, although in the minority, significantly outperform
those provided by the expert, thereby offering greater stability to the ensemble.
Conversely, scenarios primarily involving self-labeled images may experience
degraded performance due to increased noise. The research's conclusions are then
applied to a practical application: assisting in the diagnosis of certain rare blood
diseases. All necessary code and descriptions have been documented in a GitHub
repository for ease of replication by the scientific and medical communities. 
This research is part of a larger initiative focused on rare blood disorders,
led by Professor G. V. M. Barp, at the Federal University of Rio Grande do
Sul in the Porto Alegre region of Brazil. 
Ultimately, the accuracy of the ensemble model is verified to be 99.16% for
accurately identifying the five main types of white blood cells, thereupon
achieving a milestone that opens doors for diagnosing rare blood disorders. 
For further details on this project, please visit the website at 
https://github.com/bueno/Neural-Network-Ensemble. 
This resource serves as a comprehensive repository containing all documentation,
images, and code necessary for reproducing the research. 
The research received funding from the Brazilian agency CAPES, grant
Process: 8888.200736/BNDESPA, as well as the Universidade Federal do Rio
Grande do Sul, UFRGS, through its Programa de Posgraduate em Computacao. 
The research received partial support from the CNP

A novel method for quantifying the high-velocity decoloration of moving particles or gases offers an innovative approach to researching tinted matter in atmospheric systems. A color model utilized in this research combines hue and temperature variation to represent changes in color and temperature, respectively. A new high-velocity decoloration parameter, $\chi$, is introduced to characterize the rate of color change in relation to velocity and temperature. Results from computer simulations reveal complex patterns of color alteration resulting from the interaction of particles with differing initial colors as they move at various velocities. A range of velocity intervals was investigated, from 0 to 5 $m s^{-1}$, and the effectiveness of the $\chi$ parameter in accurately predicting color changes at high velocities was verified. A non-linear relationship between the $\chi$ parameter and velocity intervals was found, and the effects of temperature variations on color change were also considered. Interpreting the research results in terms of the physical processes driving particle interaction at different velocity intervals provided new insights, and the applicability of this method to real-world applications such as tints in atmospheric observations was discussed. A possible limitation of this research was identified: accurately predicting tint color at high velocities requires advanced numerical modeling, whereas at lower velocities either simpler models or observations can suffice to make predictions regarding tint formation processes. Overall, the novel approach to measuring the rate of color change in moving objects has broad implications for atmospheric science research. We've analyzed the influence of $m_{12}$ on the mass of this chargino, discovering that experiments currently have limited reach in this model due to a lack of sensitive observables. We've found that, in general, precision at the 1 TeV level in chargino mass is achievable only in a very small region of parameter space. However, we've also identified a specific measurable with the potential for significant improvement: the difference between the electron and muon decay rates of a $Z$ boson. We've found that this difference may be influenced by $m_{12}$ with an uncertainty as low as 1%, and that the LHC could make a substantial contribution to enhancing the present experimental sensitivity to this effect. We've also examined the theoretical constraints on $m_{12}$, discovering that a thorough investigation of the dark matter sector can effectively restrict this parameter throughout the entire global fit. We've further demonstrated that, in many cases, experimental data will be sufficient to bound $m_{12}$ across most of the parameter space. We've also highlighted the notable point that $m_{12}$ can be completely constrained by the LHC and ferminos-only direct detection searches, with no contribution from DM searches, Higgs data or electroweak precision data. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this method and reveal that the majority of existing mainline relational databases can benefit from this technique with minimal additional processing required. Ultimately, the aim is for this method to serve as a basis for creating tools supporting the task of RDF data replication. Such tools could be particularly useful in scenarios like public health or social media monitoring, which frequently involve replicating data from various sources. Furthermore, the introduction of Shape Expression techniques is anticipated to increase developer productivity by blocking excessive data adjustments after a transfer has occurred, thus streamlining the process. Finally, the proposed technique aims to facilitate the creation of tools for data analysis, such as those supporting scientific research in machine learning. Measuring Performance (MP) is an essential phase in any Investment Management process, where the main objective is to evaluate the management's ability to generate returns while taking a specified level of risk. The MP stage typically involves various methods for calculating risk and performance measures, with the square root of variance (Volatility) or expected short fall being the most widely used risk metrics. Due to the different characteristics of Volatility and Expected Short Fall, their applications differ in financial contexts. Volatility is considered a limited risk measure as it fails to account for scenarios where the return is not linear, whereas Expected Short Fall is an absolute method that considers all investment scenarios. Despite their differences, both metrics find extensive use in the creation of aardly measurable indices, where the ratio of returns over Volatility is applied to evaluate the calculated risk. The process of their calculation is known as Performance measurement through Volatility or Expected Short Fall measurement (StoNED). The combination of risk and performance measures creates a two-dimensional graph known as the StoNED Frontier, which is used to compare performances of distinct investment strategies or management funds. Due to the complexity of generating Volatility and Expected Short Fall surfaces, which require solving for and interpolating numerous scenarios resulting from stochastic simulations, the process can be time-consuming. The Python library 'pyStoNED' is used to speed up the processing of Volatility and Expected Short Fall surfaces by leveraging a strong CVXPY algorithm for the calculation of the surfaces' gradients. Furthermore, pyStoNED allows for the simple extraction of the frontier from the StoNED surface through the use of a regular surface polygon. The Python library pyStoNED is demonstrated through its application in the Italian stock market of the Milan Stock Exchange (MFTP fund). The MFTP fund is a collective investment investment fund that invests exclusively on the Milan Stock Exchange, specifically in small and mid-cap companies, where the MFTP fund is considered a benchmark index. The MFTP fund analysis serves as an empirical case study to test the functionality of the pyStoNED library. Language model pretraining offers a robust understanding of general language patterns, allowing for broad applicability and reduced task-specific adjustments. This study examines whether large language models hold essential knowledge that can be directly applied to new and unrelated tasks with minimal supervision. Furthermore, we investigate whether models trained on smaller datasets, comprising only a handful of examples, can draw upon this general knowledge to enhance performance. To answer these queries, we propose a novel method that extracts and combines task-specific and general unsupervised signals from text to augment few-example supervision, resulting in the UFE method. Using the UFE method, we evaluate its utility in conjunction with semi-supervised models on the sentiment analysis task and find significant advantages in terms of both semantic richness and efficiency of analysis. Notably, the combination of UFE and semi-supervised models achieves comparable results to fully supervised models on the SST-2 dataset, surpassing its performance on the more challenging SST-5 dataset. This study ultimately demonstrates the substantial efficacy of large language models in providing general knowledge and facilitates their effective integration with semi-supervised learning to tackle unsupervised sentiment analysis. The proposed UFE method presents an innovative approach to harnessing general knowledge in pretraining models and systematizes its extraction and combination with specific supervision to boost few-example tasks. Notably, the proposed UFE method excels in its simplicity, as it operates without requiring fine-tuning, and is compatible with a variety of pretraining models and supervised distillation methods. Lastly, the experimental findings and datasets (including sentence-level annotations) are made publicly available to foster replication and promote pretraining-based unsupervised sentiment analysis. The code for the UFE method is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-TNLL.git. The dataset is hosted at https://www.interspeech2022/fu2022-research.pdf. This study examines the feasibility of improving text standardization using large datasets by leveraging a pre-existing transformation is applied across all samples before statistical analysis can take place. This approach draws on the success of inverse covariance matrix standardization, which utilizes a pre-existing matrix to normalize residuals by calculating deviations from the mean. Similarly, a data-driven method has been developed that automatically identifies and adjusts for irregularities in data distributions without requiring any prior knowledge. This method involves creating a reference dataset, which is then used to normalize the target dataset by comparing it to the reference using a pre-defined metric. The study compares various data enhancement techniques as methods for creating the reference dataset and evaluates their effectiveness across a range of datasets differing in size, diversity, and structure. The results indicate that a data-driven method outperforms the existing inverse covariance matrix approach and highlight the importance of the reference dataset in data standardization. The developed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of data enhancement as a data standardization technique and its potential to simplify statistical analysis across various fields. The findings also illustrate how data standardization can reveal important insights about dataset normality and bias. Ultimately, the study contributes to the existing research in inverse covariance matrix standardization by introducing an alternative method and providing a more comprehensive understanding of data standardization best practices. The research further expands upon the theories of covariance matrix and inverse covariance matrix by providing a rigorous empirical comparison of data enhancement and standardization techniques across a diverse range of datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of data enhancement as a data standardization technique and its potential to simplify statistical analysis in fields such as information retrieval, machine learning, natural language processing, and data mining. The research provides a rigorous empirical comparison of data enhancement and standardization techniques across a range of datasets and structures, and highlights the importance of the reference dataset in data standardization. We examined the integration of speaker traits in synthetic speech through the evaluation of four male voices with varying levels of formidability (firm, moderate, soft) and agreeableness (unfriendly, neutral, friendly). We conducted a crowd-sourcing study where human listeners received conversational transcripts and responded to questions about speaker traits, as well as expressed their overall preference for the voices. We discovered that distinct voices yielded distinct perceptions of speaker traits, but these attributes did not significantly influence participants' perceptions of the speaking voices themselves. This investigation of speaker traits in spoken interactions explores their potential application in generating more realistic and engaging synthetic speech. We also analyzed the impact of speaker traits on human preferences for the voices and found that voices conveying higher levels of friendliness tended to receive greater liking, while those conveying a moderate level of friendliness were more favored than those with a more assertive tone. These findings demonstrate the importance of integrating speaker traits in speech generation to produce more authentic and interactive conversations. In doing so, we sought to develop a voice generation pipeline that not only produces natural-sounding speech but also accurately conveys the intended speaker's personality and interpersonal characteristics. We discovered that this attribute-based model effectively predicts speaker traits and their effects on human perceptions in both a lab setting and a social media context. Moreover, we demonstrated that modifying voice properties in specific dimensions can systematically alter speaker attributes and their effects on human attitudes, while attributing personalities to speakers leads to more pronounced effects on human emotions. This investigation of speaker attributes and their effects on human emotions highlights the importance of integrating emotional traits in speech generation to produce more engaging and natural conversations. Conversely, we found that voice properties were not sufficient to accurately infer speaker attributes and their effects on human emotions in most cases. For 23 different model potentials, our results show a positive relationship between remaining entropy and high-density viscosity, with a correlation appearing when using a reduced state space. However, such a relationship was not found when examining the low-density viscosity values. A study on the flexibility of water models' water bodies, with 51 different components, also yielded a positive correlation between remaining entropy and high-density viscosity. Our work further demonstrates how high remaining entropy within molecules affects their fluid-like behavior at high pressures, which is reflected in their property of temperature-dependent viscosity. With a positive relationship established between remaining entropy/ flexibility and high-density viscosity, it follows that increasing these factors could lead to larger deviations of viscosity from ideal conditions, with potential applications in such a modification being investigated (e.g., to create room-temperature ferroelectricity). Our work also highlights that remaining entropy can serve as an important characteristic to optimize the performance of both molecular and empirical components. Furthermore, a positive relationship between remaining entropy and high-density viscosity has also been discovered in some real materials, with examples including hydrogen-bonded liquids (ammonia and hydrofluoric acid) and ionic liquids (EMIM$^{+}$-based). Inspired by recent discoveries in condensed matter physics and reaction-diffusion systems, we develop a straightforward method to analyze two-dimensional fermions interacting with a bosonic field within a lattice framework. We demonstrate this approach by applying it to the Ising model and the Dirac fermions with a time-dependent gauge field background introduced by Polyakov, and derive a precise equation governing fermion and anti-fermion correlation. Furthermore, in the presence of a time-dependent gauge field, we calculate the probability of fermion presence, their distribution function and the current flowing through a system, and find that the results resemble those of the dimer model. We also discuss the behavior of current flowing through a system at different temperatures and find that it exhibits a thermal anomaly akin to a jump in value at a specific temperature. A short investigation into the origin of the fermion's thermal anomaly is provided in the context of the effective mass concept. In addition, we present an alternative to existing methods for determining the critical temperature of the Ising model by utilizing the probability of fermion presence, and verify that it leads to the same critical temperature value as determined by other methods. We rely on the concept of the effective mass to analyze this critical temperature verification process. To further validate our approach, we compared the distribution function of fermions obtained in the Ising model and the Dirac fermions with a time-dependent gauge field to the distribution function of particles in the 2D free Fermi gas model. We achieved a satisfactory agreement between them. Ultimately, we established a straightforward correspondence between two-dimensional Ising models and various systems containing fermions with time-dependent gauge fields, and verified that the results obtained are consistent with those of the dimer model and the free Fermi gas model. The approach to statistical physics developed here could be a valuable tool for studying various systems containing fermions interacting with a bosonic field within a lattice framework. Moreover, in the context of the tendency towards universality, we discovered a straightforward means of analyzing fermions within gauge field backgrounds through a comparison with the dimer model and the free Fermi gas model. Finally, in the context of the concept of the effective mass, we investigated the thermal anomaly phenomenon that occurs in the critical region of various systems containing time-dependent gauge fields and the probability of fermion presence in the 2D free Fermi gas model. In various embedded systems, real-time software interactions are essential to ensure timely and predictable operations. Many modern embedded systems employ software virtualization techniques to enhance real-time performance, often combining this with other virtualization methods. For such systems to effectively use virtualization, the real-time software run-level must be minimized, making it necessary for a real-time aware virtualization solution. To address this need, this research introduces a new real-time embedded hypervisor called T-Visor, designed to support both kernel and user-level virtualization. T-Visor provides hardware virtualization assistance for critical real-time tasks and efficiently manages context switches to minimize real-time performance overhead. A case study examined the performance of T-Visor on an iMX8-based development board, demonstrating that it can perform 30000 context switches per second with a 12.8-microsecond average latency, making it suitable for low-latency and high-throughput applications. Furthermore, T-Visor was found to provide 4-12 times better real-time performance isolation compared to existing solutions, with a significant reduction in overhead when running the LAMDA CPU scheduler on an iMX8-based development board. To facilitate practical applications, a new development platform was created to support T-Visor, featuring an x86-64 and ARM64 SoC, as well as various peripherals commonly used in embedded systems. Contemporary robot controllers are typically defined as fixed, deterministic equations with parameters that can be adjusted. However, the traditional method of developing these controllers, which involves designing them based on predicted behavior, can be problematic as it does not account for uncertainties that may arise in real-world situations. As a result, there is a possibility that even an optimized controller may prove ineffective when encountering unforeseen obstacles or unexpected changes in its environment. To address this, we propose using a adaptable, probabilistic controller that takes into consideration a range of potential uncertainties. In this study, we develop an algorithm that combines a probabilistic model with a policy-based search method to create an adaptable controller. This algorithm generates a set of controllers, each with a level of effectiveness that can be evaluated in advance. This allows a robot to be equipped with an optimized controller tailored to the specific situation it encounters. Our framework is particularly suitable for controllers that operate using reinforcement learning, where the uncertainty most often arises from the quality of the data used during training. Furthermore, our method outperforms an alternative strategy that involves testing a fixed controller in various scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this is a novel strategy that has not been proposed before. Our study demonstrates that using a probabilistic model to create a policy-based search method offers a solution to the problem of developing effective, deterministic robot controllers that can handle a range of uncertainties. Multi-layer graphs are a type of graph structure that contains multiple interconnected layers, representing different groups of nodes and their connections. To analyze such graphs, we develop a mathematical framework using elevated slice algebras, derived from the decomposition of nodal functions into simple, fundamental elements, and demonstrate how certain graph properties can be computed as products or compositions within this framework. Building on this concept, we generalize the structure of graph algebras to apply to multi-layer graphs, and show that such algebras are fully embedded in a larger, more complex algebra system, with the more complex algebra capturing relationships between different graph layers. To illustrate the benefits of this approach, we show how the computational efficiency of this algebra system can be used to reduce the computational complexity of certain graph algorithms. Specifically, we show that some operations, such as maximizing graph clique sizes and computing the top K most connected nodes, can be performed in O(n log n) time, a significant improvement, and that more complex problems, such as maximum flow and bipartite matching, can be performed in a time proportional to standard graph algorithms. Finally, we identify an upper bound on the time complexity of graph operations within this new algebra system. To support the validity of our approach, we reference related research in the fields of graph property algorithms and elevated slice algebras. Furthermore, for higher-dimensional tensors, we find that paired entropies do not align as the sum of mirrored entropy may exceed the original entropy, leading to a discrepancy. The principles underlying these findings are that mirrored entropy represents a negative (positive) shift, and the sum of entropies includes an negative (positive) excess, respectively. When the system mixes its components, a pattern persists only in systems with long-lasting elements, retained through a natural decay. Continuous learning is becoming increasingly important as machines learn from experiences over time. One major challenge is that the subjects they're learning from often change over time, with some aspects becoming irrelevant and new information emerging. To address this issue, we're developing a framework for learning collectively, where multiple agents work together to share knowledge and stay up-to-date with new information. To this end, we've designed a neural framework for online collective continuous learning, incorporating feature extraction, feature selection, and classification. To test this framework, we created a dynamic, ever-evolving dataset that reflects real-world learning scenarios, where agents learn from a diverse set of changing topics over time. Our results indicate that the agents' performance improves significantly when working together, outperforming individual agents in continuous learning tasks. Moreover, the collective agents are more resilient to temporary collaborative disruptions and recovers quickly when working together again. Notably, when the collaborative period ends, the agents regain their individual accuracy and do not be hindered from it. To overcome the problem of online information overlap, we've also developed methods for identifying and separating overlapping information for each topic at its changing point. Interestingly, when the agents work together, they're able to identify overlapping information more effectively than individual agents, demonstrating greater knowledge diversity and independence. Ultimately, the results indicate that the agents' performance improves significantly when working together, offering promising prospects for collective continuous learning in real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a significant advancement in the proximal gradient method (PGD) for nonlinear programming, incorporating the dual simplex method as a perturbed gradient calculator to optimize stochastic dual dynamic programming problems with complex constraints. We've developed the stochastic dual simplex method (SDSM) which calculates a perturbed gradient while maintaining the and non-negative property for some variable vector. This approach also utilizes a genetic filter to address the diversity issue in local optimization. We've applied the proposed method to the full and steady flight problem, achieving a 9% overall success rate on random problems, with the steady flight variant allowing for a predetermined flight speed. Experimental results indicate that our solution's constraint violation average is typically around 2 millionth of one, with the solution's diversity also noticeably increased. In comparison, the proposed method outperforms existing techniques such as genetic filter proximal gradient (GFGD) and genetic filter dual simplex (GFD) with a success rate of 7% and 5% respectively. Notably, the proposed method has demonstrated a substantial improvement in constraint violation and tailing off, consistent with our theoretical predictions. In terms of computational complexity, a temporal decomposition of the proposed method yields an time complexity of O(n^2 * N) and a space complexity of O(n^2) where n is the number of variables and N is the number of samples, both in the diversity and filter scenarios. The study also confirms via experimental evaluation that our method can achieve an arbitrary close solution to the optimal using the dual simplex method (DS) with a reasonable violation of no more than the square root of N. Consequently, the proposed method has the potential to tackle more demanding problems, with its diverse solutions displaying a lower variance for the same mean error compared to other methods such as genetic filter dual simplex (GFD) and genetic filter proximal gradient (GFGD). The source code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/LinearProgramming/Proximal_Genetic_Filter/tree/2022a/PI.... Following rigorous testing, the proposed method has successfully demonstrated its capabilities on various high-dimensional problems of up to 250 variables with a 95% confidence level. In the future, the goal is to extend this method by incorporating the simplex method as an efficient solver for big data problems, particularly in the sparse and imbalanced data scenarios. Moreover, the method could be enhanced by incorporating the dual fem method as a perturbed gradient calculator to optimize stochastic dual dynamic programming problems with complex network constraints

The work also explores potential implications for calculations of nuclear mass excesses and elastic scattering cross-sections using the non-relativistic Schrodinger equation. The work then concludes by considering various possibilities for accounting for the resonance phenomenon within a relativistic formalism for scattering reactions.
