We have developed a groundbreaking machine learning-based method to classify and quantify the morphological structures present within compact galaxies redshifted due to their internal motion. We have successfully applied this method to a dataset of 176,111 galaxies, which was extracted from the XMM-LSS field of the First Year Depth Hyper Suprime-Cam survey. This field provides accurate photometric redshift estimates for a significant percentage of galaxies within the 0<z<5 range. By using our morphological classification scheme, we are able to analyze the morphological structures present in 126,691 galaxies within the redshift range of 0<z<1 in great detail. This was possible due to the high resolution and accuracy of the HSRC galaxy images, which is approximately one to five times the size of a galaxy's effective diameter. We are able to analyze the physical properties of the overall galaxy structure, as well as the structures of its central and surrounding areas. Furthermore, our model's ability to distinguish between discrete galaxy structures, including bulges, centers, and major/Minor arcs, reveals valuable insights on a galaxy's internal dust distribution. Notably, we found that approximately two percent of galaxies within this sample exhibit dust hiding (i.e. a face-down bulge aligned with a cone) within their central areas. We are able to make direct comparisons of our results with those of morphological classification schemes developed for more local galaxies and those observed through the CANDELS survey. While our results do not exhibit any statistical differences with these other classification schemes, we do notice a significant increase in a particular type of morphological structure in our sample, which could be attributed to a selection bias associated with the HSRC survey. This new machine learning-based method provides an essential tool for automatically classifying and quantifying the morphological structures present within large datasets of diverse galaxies across a wide range of redshifts. As such, it paves the way for an extensive analysis of a nearly one million galaxy sample, which is expected to be obtained from the second generation of the HSRC survey in its final stage. Ultimately, this dataset will enable researchers to make a detailed comparison of its morphological structures with those of local galaxies observed through the CANDELS survey. A key attribute of this new classification scheme is its ability to quantify the morphological structures present in compact galaxies for the first time through an extensive analysis of a diversity of galaxies across a wide range of redshifts (0<z<1). This innovative detector leverages advanced optical and cryogenic techniques to identify tiny friction generated by weak interactions. The focus is on low-energy neutrinos and the project's ability to open new avenues for investigating nuclear reactions. The prototype will be located in the Borexina Wide Linear Chamber, where it will utilize a 50 kg sample of diamond to enhance scientific outcomes. The diamond's interactions will be recorded using a laser and data analysis will be employed to differentiate signal from background noise. The project's primary goal is to develop a new method for detecting very weak interactions, with potential applications in fields such as astronomy and medical research. The team aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of this innovative technique in solving complex scientific problems. The PALEOCCENE protocol was recently tested in a 12-channel system, with encouraging results. The project is now preparing a substantial single-crystal diamond setup to further demonstrate its feasibility as a detection method. The Encoded Direct Detection (EDD) approach, utilized by PALEOCCENE, has the potential to revolutionize direct detection experiments. Counting on language to define reward objectives in complex environments proves challenging due to the ambiguity of interpretation that can lead to a gap between the trainer's and learner's understanding. Current approaches typically rely on assumptions of unambiguous reference or impose limited, structured reference constraints that don't account for most real-world scenarios where reference ambiguity arises from factors such as lack of universal knowledge (e.g., "pick up the thing that's good for your health"), word ambiguity ("pick up the car"), or reference scope (e.g., "pick up the room"). To tackle this issue, we propose a novel, pragmatic method for overcoming reference uncertainty by translating training objectives into detailed, structured descriptions of desired effects. Experiments across various platforms, including a multi-objective grid world and two different real-world robotic tasks, show that our method effectively addresses reference uncertainty and surpasses the performance of prior approaches that fail to mitigate this problem. Notably, we found that our method is adaptable to settings where the trainer and learner have different knowledge bases and language processing skills. Implementations of the method and a training dataset are freely accessible online. The results suggest that incorporating pragmatic principles can effectively address the challenge of training agents to achieve goals defined through language by mitigating reference uncertainty. Initially, the layers' interaction is scale-invariant; at a specific scale, short-range correlations arise, leading to the development of polaron states and a short-range restoring force. The initial instability is facilitated by long-range interactions, while the restoration of symmetry is attributed to scale-invariant Coulomb interactions in the transverse plane. This leads to the emergence of droplets within the scale-invariant state. The molecular qubit, Sc2TbN@C80, exhibits dual charge states (+1 and +3e) with distinct magnetic properties. This study explores the electronic and magnetic structures of the monolayer and bulk Sc2TbN@C80 on a hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN)/Ni(111) substrate using first-principles calculations. The results indicate that the substrate does not distort the hexagonal structure of the h-BN layer or the spherical cage of the nanocage. The calculations also predict that the ferromagnetic spin arrangement found in the Ni(111) layer enhances the magnetic moment of the Tb atom in the nanocage by 0.18mu_B, but the charge state of the nanocage as a whole does not change. However, the findings reveal that the Sc2TbN@C80/$\sqrt{3}\times3$gR33.75°B-Ni(111) interface experiences a temperature-triggered shift in the conformation of the nanocage from an oblate to a prolate shape under a temperature increase. The research delves into the influence of the substrate and the spin state of the nanocage on its dimensional and orientational transformations. The study provides valuable insights into the design of molecular qubits, which can operate efficiently over a broad temperature range. The results show that the Sc2TbN@C80 monolayer offers great potential as an efficient thermal qubit that can operate at room temperature. The use of the first-principles method in the study allows for a comprehensive understanding of the electronic and magnetic structures of the systems under investigation, particularly at a mesoscopic scale. The method could be widely applied to the study of various molecular and atomic monolayers on substrates. Notably, the study reveals a proton-induced switching of the Tb's spin state between up and down configurations for the bulk Sc2TbN@C80 on the h-BN/Ni(111) substrate. The results of the study can contribute to the rapid growth of the field of quantum computing in the near future. The Ramsey series offers a compelling approach for creating quantum sensors that can detect oscillations in magnetic fields. However, this method's efficiency can be enhanced through strategic planning. A refined strategy is developed by incorporating a Bayesian data analysis process. A key aspect of this approach involves setting predetermined goals for probability thresholds and loss functions, with the aim of optimizing these objectives by adaptively adjusting key parameters. A method for implementing this adaptive approach in real-time is established, allowing for proactive modification of the measurement sequence based on up-to-date information. A comparative analysis is conducted to evaluate the success of this adaptive approach in enhancing magnetic field detection capabilities, specifically when contrasted against a conventional conservative conservative approach that ignores future data and overemphasizes accuracy. A simulation-based study further highlights the benefits of this adaptive approach under various scenarios, including when compared to a conservative conservative approach that shaves off imperfect pillars to prioritize precision. A practical application of the adaptive approach is also demonstrated for a scenario involving the simultaneous exploitation of multiple frequencies. Furthermore, the theoretical framework is expanded to accommodate a more complex Bayesian analysis and the incorporation of further objectives such as minimizing measurement duration and detecting partial signatures of magnetic fields. A summary of the developed methods is collected and presented within a companion paper called the PLA Q. for wide-scale implementation in quantum research facilities. Network centrality metrics form the foundation of graph statistics, used for various applications beyond node ranking. The existing toolbox of centrality metrics is extensive, yet each is tied to a particular network architecture and functional analysis. We introduce a new multi-layer metric, Gromov importance, designed to be robust across diverse network structures. Derived from the minimum surplus of the multi-layer graph's triangle inequality, this metric combines the perspectives of algebraic topology and graph geometry. The Gromov importance enables the quantification of nodal, cellular, and network centrality, demonstrating its potential for statistical analysis and functional characterization. In comparative analysis with established centrality metrics, our results show that Gromov importance is particularly effective in revealing key nodes regulating genetic or chemical neural networks. Furthermore, this metric has been applied to the study of the interplay between neuroscience and artificial intelligence systems. The provided software packages enable the computation and visualization of Gromov importance for diverse types of multi-layer graph input. The Gromov importance statistical approach and its underlying algorithmic tools offer novel insights into the structure and function of biological and technological complex networks. The study of Gromov importance in multi-layer networks reveals its potential for community detection, reveals complex node distributions, and highlights its capacity for non-extensive graph statistics and its relevance to graph geometry and topology. The use of Gromov importance for node centrality ranking in molecular biological systems shows that it offers a general alternative to existing centrality metrics. The study of Gromov importance in the global network reveals its potential for descriptive analysis of complex network characteristics and its application in taxonomy. The correlation between Gromov importance and established centrality metrics or network characteristics provides new insights into the properties of key nodes, demonstrating their potential for functional characterization. The Gromov importance algorithm has a computational complexity of O(n^2 d) with a quadratic dependence on the number of nodes and layers, suggesting its efficiency for small to medium-sized networks with a maximum diameter of 10. The visualization of Gromov importance for layered graphs can be effectively presented using 3D geometry and topology, while its presentation for models with mixed edges requires a separate color coding system. The study of Gromov importance in multi-layer networks with a mix of different edge types suggests its potential for statistical analysis and its general applicability to a wide range of complex network models. The Gromov importance algorithm provides a new tool for statistical analysis of biological and technological complex networks with a multi-layer structure. A research paper introduces the notion of strong equivalence for linear matrix pencils for the first time. This type of equivalence is applied to create specific categories of objects, such as collections of matrix pencils, which are then studied. It is proven that collections of matrix pencils can be fully characterized by a parameter equal in size to the dimension of the space being observed, regardless of the actual size of the matrices. Additionally, this characterization serves as a theoretical foundation for developing algorithms that can strongly equivalently transform any given collection of matrix pencils to the standard canonical form. Another significant finding related to strong equivalence is that it leads to the discovery of a one-to-one correspondence between certain collections of matrix pencils and linearly independent collections of vectors, which in turn is linked to the non-singularity of the pencil. All of these results are likely to be widely applicable due to their simplicity and generality. Lastly, a practical example demonstrates that strong equivalence can be used to effectively reduce the size of large numerical data sets. A cutting-edge computational method known as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has been developed to solve quantum chemistry issues on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. Nevertheless, the current adaptive VQE approach is hindered by a problem: accurate solutions for chemical bonds are difficult to obtain due to the NISQ device's rapid decline in precision with the number of gates. To address this limitation, a new algorithmic approach is presented, which exploits quantum bootstrapping techniques using qubit-excitation states to enhance the precision of NISQ devices. This proposed adaptive VQE variant, referred to as qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQE (QE-AD-VQE), employs a combination of excitation and ground states to tackle quantum chemistry problems. By utilizing CASSCF models and simulations on both quantum and classical computers, the QE-AD-VQE method is shown to outperform the existing AD-VQE algorithm in terms of ground-state precision with fewer quantum gates. Furthermore, the QE-AD-VQE method is capable of accurately solving CASSCF models with increased precision, whereas the AD-VQE approach falls short in this regard. With an increased ability to resolve fine features, the QE-AD-VQE method has the potential to expand the capabilities of NISQ devices in quantum chemistry simulations. Nonetheless, the precision gained by QE-AD-VQE comes at the expense of reduced robustness against quantum noise, as evidenced by noise-resistance experiments on both quantum and classical computers. One key aspect of this research is the development of a new error-accumulation model, which reveals that noise in quantum computers manifests as a complex interplay of hardware and software factors. This study contributes to quantum computing research by providing (a) a novel algorithmic approach to address the issue of infidelity growth in NISQ devices and (b) a ground-breaking analytical model explaining qubit error propagation. Additionally, the results of this research are supported by numerical simulations of quantum and classical computers. Recently, multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEA) have gained significant attention as a fast and efficient approach to multi-objective optimization problems, offering flexible trade-off analysis and often outperforming more conventional mathematical optimization techniques, such as branch and bound methods, especially in complex computational settings. However, certain types of MOEA may encounter difficulty in finding high quality solutions that exactly meet multiple criteria when the related objective functions and constraint equations involve integer decisions. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid algorithm that seamlessly integrates a MOEA, optimized for multi-objective integer optimization, with a convergence-enhancing convergence assurance framework. We test the effectiveness of this novel method against four diverse MONIP scenarios, including the multi-objective non-convex quadratic optimization problem presented by Li et al. (2014), and against three challenging MONIP test problems recently studied by Chakrabarti et al. (2022), confirming that our approach yields superior results, outperforming both the branch and bound algorithm and MOEA alone. We provide in-depth statistical analysis of these findings, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of our technical innovation and suggesting avenues for future research. We also make the source code of our approach available to the research community at https://github.com/UtkarshGajjala/MOCONI. While our algorithm exhibits impressive capabilities for non-convex integer optimization, it still requires further development to tackle such complex problems as computing fixed objective value solutions, where branch and bound algorithms currently hold a logical advantage. In response to this challenge, we outline the requirements necessary to overcome this gap in our introduction. Our experimental results confirm that our approach yields superior quality Pareto front solutions for the multi-objective integer optimization problem of computational tensor decomposition. Interestingly, our experimental analysis reveals that while MOEA excel at exploring diverse solutions, branch and bound algorithms outperform them when it comes to identifying exact, rigorous solutions. We provide recommendations for future research directions in optimizing computational methods, such as tensor decomposition, where precise solutions hold significant value. In conclusion, our optimization algorithm yields outstanding results in optimizing computational methods, demonstrating considerable progress in tackling complex optimization problems. While our approach fails to match the mathematical guarantees of branch and bound algorithms in certain contexts, it far surpasses them in numerical experiments, suggesting its applicability to various real-world applications. To the best of our knowledge, our approach stands out from other available methods, and we encourage its continued development in optimizing computational methods, such as tensor decomposition, to obtain the best possible outcomes. This research delves into the development of resilient transmission designs for reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) that aid secure communication networks with multiple users in a wireless system, taking into consideration the failure rates of RIS elements and receivers. Specifically, we investigate two main problems within two distinct scenarios. The first scenario involves a single RIS assisting multiple secure transmission, where we aim to optimize the phase shift matrix to maximize the minimum value of the minimum mean square error (MMSE) detection error at the receiver, under a constraint that guarantees a specified signal to interference ratio (SIR) at the receiver and reduces the interference received from the authorized transmitter at other receivers. The second scenario involves multiple RISs assisting secure communication for a single receiver, where we seek to optimize the phase shift matrices to maximize the minimum SIR at the receiver, under a constraint that reduces the interference received from the authorized transmitter at other receivers. Both problems are found to be complex nonconvex problems, solved using the projected gradient descent (PGD) method to attain the best possible approximate solution, showcased by means of a numerical example that demonstrates its efficiency. The outcomes show that the proposed designs can still be effective and meet the specified performance requirements even in cases where a subset of RIS elements are malfunctioning. The results also indicate a considerable improvement in the unassisted SIR at other receivers as a positive byproduct of these designs. Furthermore, the resilience of the designs in cases of partial failure is found to generally improve, though it depends on various parameters such as the orientation of the RIS elements, the failure probability, and the position of the receivers, where lower failure probabilities may result in smaller degradation of the output MMSE at the receivers, as shown in the provided example. Theoretical analysis of these findings is also developed. A complementary analysis of the outcomes shows that the output MMSE at each receiver is limited by two values: the minimum output MMSE when no RIS malfunctions and the output MMSE at the clipping level (set by the receiver's amplifier) when all RIS elements are malfunctioning. The theoretical findings suggest a reasonable explanation for these observed general trends. Moreover, the proposed methods are found to outperform conventional alternatives in cases of partial failure, as the numerical example demonstrates. The research presents a comprehensive framework for understanding the trade-offs between the resilience of the designs and other important performance metrics such as output MMSE at the receivers and unassisted SIR at the receivers and the authorized transmitter. Despite decades of research in cognitive science, psychology and neuroscience, there has been a lack of a comprehensive theory explaining executive function's role in decision-making. To address this gap, we propose a value function theory, framing executive function as a strategic choice between exploration and exploitation. Through this lens, we examine various techniques used to analyze and interpret episode tables, discovering connections between these methods and the executive function concept. By recognizing that these methods essentially predict outcomes based on given inputs and then eliminate non-common pathways, we create a simplified framework that mimics their behavior, thus establishing a systematic approach to understanding the role of executive function in decision-making processes. Furthermore, our framework enables us to identify and assess a portfolio strategy that incorporates both temporal exploration and exploitation, effectively integrating the benefits of past and future thinking. After applying the COCO Episode Database to test our theory, we find that a portfolio consisting of prospected, renamed, resampled, and revalued strategies performs better than standalone versions, thus validating our value function approach and offering new insights from the COCO dataset. Ultimately, our framework provides a unified and coherent understanding of the decision-making process and suggests that portfolio techniques may hold the key to improving performance in a wide range of applications from economics to game development. This summary, what we call "hindsight summary," enables us to gauge the degree of epistemic uncertainty present in past decisions and can be utilized in various applications, such as the creation of a digital will or decision support systems. We've used data from the Solar Wind Electrons, Atoms and Ions (SWEAPI) instrument on the Parker Solar Probe to examine the properties of high-speed solar wind streams and their connection to the solar corona's energy production near the star. By studying how densities and energy distributions change over a short distance near the star, we've gained insight into the energy transfer process within these fast wind streams. Our analysis shows significant variations in electron density and temperature within the solar wind, linked to specific characteristics of the coronal energy source. The data also reveal that there's a consistent pattern of high speed streams originating from specific regions of the coronal streamer belt without the usual expected lower-speed solar wind. This behavior is associated with the energy characteristics of the coronal acceleration region, and we're treating these findings as preliminary due to the young age of the mission. Given the close proximity to the star that our data were obtained at, we're looking forward to analyzing more SWEAPI data from closer and higher distances from the star to gain a more in-depth understanding of the energy production processes within the solar corona. These findings are expected to be presented at the 17th International Solar Wind Conference held at 29 June 2020 in Boulder, Colorado. A paper based on this work was published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics on 24 June 2020, volume 125, issue 6. A new class of collective rotational states, termed Adverse R-parity Scissors modes, is introduced within the context of the Double-Rotors Model. These states exhibit unique properties derived from combining R-parity considerations with collective rotation dynamics. Two distinct scenarios are envisioned to potentially yield experimental evidence for these states: (i) R-parity violating interactions inducing slight deformations and (ii) R-parity conserving interactions resulting in minor polarization. Theoretical spectra for a range of even-even nuclei with Z between 58 and 90 and N between 82 and 124 are computed using the Integro-Differential Collective Rotation (IDCR) approach, which underpins the Double-Rotors Model. The calculated spectra are compared to experimental data via an overlay of both energy and reduced gamma-band energy distributions. Numerous instances of adverse R-parity scissors modes have been identified in the computed spectra, alongside a significant number of regular scissors modes. Key characteristics distinguish adverse R-parity states from their even-odd and even-even counterparts, including reduced transition widths, unbalanced prober and emitter ratios, and energy spacings that deviate from the'magic' value of 0.173 MeV. These characteristics serve as crucial criteria for the distinct identification of adverse R-parity scissors modes. Empirical analysis reveals that such states could be within the reach of state-of-the-art experimental facilities, such as FAIR and NSCL@MSU. The present work represents an initial exploration of R-parity related collective phenomena within the context of the Double-Rotors Model. The calculated spectra are provided in supplemental material. Furthermore, discussions on theoretical implications, including possibilities for experimental detection, are presented in a follow-up article (arXiv:2202.00975). Furthermore, the proposed method is straightforward to implement, not requiring any modifications to the underlying numerical scheme or code. Its adaptability is demonstrated through successful application to different types of equations, including the 2D Navier-Stokes equation, Poisson equation, and 1D elliptic equation. The results are validated by comparing them with analytical solutions and conventional finite element method results. This approach holds potential for wide application across various field of continuum mechanics and physics. The main objectives of this study are two-fold: Firstly, it is intended to illustrate the utility of the forward mapping in the investigation of global characteristic structures, with a particular emphasis on achieving a straightforward demonstration of the positivity of these structures. Secondly, the study aims to achieve a more in-depth, yet abstract demonstration of the fundamental theorem of global characteristic structures by building on existing knowledge regarding the properties of global vector bundles and partial differential operators. A fundamental task in Natural Language Understanding is extracting universal tree structures from plain text, a task easily corrupted by noise and ambiguity. The basic approach of generating tree structures from training data doesn't work due to noise and lacks robustness. We introduce an innovative method that tackles these issues by leveraging a robust, noise-resistant framework based on Markov properties. The new method is based on the idea that sequences of tree structures can be modelled across the entire dataset, enabling both syntactic and semantic analyses. We couple this with a unique loss function that mimics collaborative learning, using pairs of experts with contrasting views. This collaborative method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, also achieving faster computation and better scalability on various challenging datasets that were previously unsolvable. Additionally, the resulting model can efficiently handle tasks such as text simplification and sentiment analysis that were previously unattainable. The study's findings are available online, along with the accompanying code at https://github.com/mosamha/clsa. The results were achieved on publicly available datasets, as well as on the recently released GitHub dataset 'treebank'. For demonstration purposes, an interactive visualisation tool is provided at https://cosda.herokuapp.com/. Through experiments, we validated the effectiveness of our novel theoretical contribution, proving the robustness of our method in dealing with noise and showing its applicability to various types of natural language. Moreover, the study's results highlight the importance of collaborative learning when dealing with noisy and ambiguous data. Lastly, the accompanying code at https://github.com/mosamha/clsa provides a versatile platform for solving various NLU problems, exemplified by successful applications in text simplification and sentiment analysis. Overall, the study's innovative theory and its practical applications demonstrate the value of collaborative learning in the field of Natural Language Understanding. The current implementation of the method has its limitations, but it provides a robust foundation for future improvements. A compact object formed during a merger may eventually grow a disk, which could be fueled by a neutrino-cooled accretion disk. The presence of magnetic fields in this disk can lead to their importance in determining when and how matter and energy are released. The study uses a sophisticated computer code to simulate various scenarios of magnetic fields and disk density. In brightness scans, the beam current is measured while the horizontal and vertical beam focuses are simultaneously adjusted towards their minimum values. The resulting data is then analyzed for peaks representing the beam's transverse intensity distributions at various apertures. The full width half maxima of these peaks serve as indicators of the root mean square beam size. The technique does not demand high precision in measuring the beam position or working in a low-emittance working mode. Its major advantages include not requiring a sophisticated data analysis procedure and being able to be fully implemented through machine commands, making it easily accessible at many accelerator facilities. The optimization of quantized neural networks typically involves solving an optimization problem with constraints, particularly the range-constrained optimization problem, to determine the parameters of the quantized networks. Since the problem has a computationally costly subgradient, finding an efficient optimization algorithm is crucial for generating high-quality solutions in a time-efficient manner. We introduce a novel optimization algorithm, AskewSGD, which is an iterative, annealed method for unconstrained optimization with adaptive step size adjustment. We then modify it to solve the constrained optimization problem by imposing minor constraints on the solution. Our results demonstrate that AskewSGD outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a significant reduction in optimization steps of up to $76\%$, resulting in lower error rates on various dataset and network configurations. The source code for AskewSGD is freely accessible and can be used with the provided code on GitHub. Nevertheless, GAN's excellent generative capabilities quickly dwindle when dealing with incomplete or partially obscured input data, particularly in situations like partially occluded images or incomplete medical scans. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Hidden Space Conditioning method (HSC), which effectively propagates visual information through GANs by utilizing intermediate hidden representations within the network. By effectively propagating visual information, HSC enables GANs to utilize this hidden knowledge to produce realistic output data. In this study, we explored four distinct data aggregation techniques based on graph theory and a global solver that simulates local and global interactions. Our analysis is grounded in the hierarchy of social networks proposed by Barabasi and Olsson. A dynamic, multi-agent, multi-step influence model was developed to mimic the processes leading to the formation of social hierarchies as described by Barabasi and Olson. This model consists of three layers: (1) an individual level, (2) a group level, and (3) a global level. Each level uses an agent-level time step, and solving equations at each level requires distinct steps. In the context of accelerators, we investigated the practicality of reusing intermediate data to optimize communication and computation. Our evaluation of these approaches involved a series of hierarchical models, and interestingly, we found that despite computational benefits, our analysis suggests that typically encountered system characteristics may render hierarchical methods non-feasible on current hardware. Consequently, we implore the development of hardware architecture tailored to accommodating hierarchical methods. Furthermore, we propose a set of test cases that exhibit hierarchical behavior and may serve as a foundation for assessing the capabilities of future, custom-designed hardware. The code for our experiments is written in C and comprised part of the XAIN project at GitHub, and our accelerators are implemented using an optimized version of the OpenCL framework. In this study, we examined the theoretical properties of a modified Bose-Hubbard model that introduces disorder and non-linearity, and demonstrated that applying compulsion can facilitate compiling quantum interactions onto a single controllable qubit. Our investigation of the model's behavior included an analysis of how the presence of compulsion affects the quantum states of the system, as well as its impact on entanglement and spectral properties. The results showed that compulsion leads to localized non-Gaussian states and enables a clear separation of spectral and correlation data, revealing entity-specific correlations. The research identified various distinctive patterns in the system's behavior across different regimes, including transitions between localized and delocalized states, and revealed the compulsion-induced formation of a quasi-gap in the system's Hilbert space. Additionally, we found that compulsion is a necessary condition for observing a degenerate four-fold spectral point, thus facilitating the experimental investigation of non-linearity in single-photon driven systems. The findings of this research provide valuable insights for the experimental and theoretical exploration of quantum interactions and could potentially facilitate a deeper understanding of quantum optics and classical computing. The research was published in the December 2021 edition of Physical Review A with the article title 'Compelled Quantum Phenomena in a Causal Quantum Network: Evidence for Quasi-Gap in Quantum States and Spectra'. A previous study by the authors, with the title 'Compelled Quantum Phenomena in a Quantum Chain with Interspecies Interactions', was presented at the International Conference on Advances in Signal Processing and Artificial Intelligence 2021. The associated data with this research can be found on the repository with the title 'Compelled Quantum Phenomena in a Quantum Chain with Interspecies Interactions: Data'. The study demonstrates, through theoretical analysis, the mechanism of compelled quantum phenomena and predicts that such phenomena can be observed in systems with complicated interactions, thus highlighting a novel approach to compiling interactions onto quantum systems using causal quantum networks. The study is autocritical in the sense that it compels localization, thus facilitating a deeper understanding of the quantum states of the compiled system. The associated research demo can be found at the link 'Demonstration of Compelled Quantum Phenomena in a Quantum Chain with Interspecies Interactions'. This distribution does not match any of the commonly found distribution types in statistical analysis and is primarily influenced by the physical characteristics of the fibers. Natural language understanding has progressed significantly in characterizing speech patterns.
However, generating human-like text in response to prompts remains an unresolved issue.
This paper proposes a new structural framework, LEATHER, for producing text in dialogue.
By incorporating a semantic representation of meaning and analyzing syntactic patterns,
LEATHER enables controlled and varied generation of dialogue.
Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through visual thesaurus generation and
unrestricted dialogue generation in multiple domains, outperforming existing methods. 
Notably, LEATHER achieves the highest score in the Open-ended Dialogue Generation track of ALBERT-OD-CONVO 2020. 
Evaluations reveal that a significant portion of its outputs resemble human language for the visual thesaurus task (75%), 
as well as in the open-ended dialogue generation tasks, including restaurant conversation (67%), coffee shop conversation (65%), 
science conversation (64%), and comedy conversation (63%). 
Furthermore, LEATHER's generated outputs exhibit a high degree of fluency, with 75% of its sentences mirroring human sentence structures. 
The study also highlights the advantages of semantic representation over other methods. 
Lastly, LEATHER's potential for natural language instruction is explored. 
For example, it can produce thesaurus entries based on an input sentence, as shown in Figure 1. 
By providing the user with the option to specify meaning, instead of meaninglessly mimicking, LEATHER differs from other machine translation methods. 
Moreover, it can generate text in response to prompts that deviate from its original corpus, much like human language producers, by employing domain-independent words and meanings, as illustrated in Figure 2. 
To facilitate domain-specific training, access to a vast database of text may be necessary, potentially limiting its application in restricted environments, as shown in Figure 3. 
Still, LEATHER remains a versatile tool, capable of producing thesaurus entries, given only an input sentence and the user's thesaurus definition. 
As such, it remains an invaluable asset in the machine translation repertoire, complementing existing methods as an open-ended dialogue generation approach. 
Moreover, it remains an intriguing idea, warranting the construction of a semantic representation to produce text in dialogue. 
To facilitate its development, the source code for LEATHER is available at https://github.com/jeelarky/LEATHER.

Nevertheless, accurately capturing the variability of ocean-related factors posing the greatest risk to the turbines proves highly challenging. Our approach incorporates a statistical methodology that uses probabilistic proxy models to quantify the uncertain loads acted upon the turbines by time-varying ocean actions. This framework relies on a Bayesian factorization technique to identify patterns in data and relates them to stress indicators on the turbines. Social media platforms provide invaluable data for research on natural disasters, their consequences, and public responses. This data can be analyzed to determine the demographics and locations of those affected, as well as providing vital information for crisis management and decision-making processes. The objective of this study is to present a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data in the context of the Izmir earthquake that occurred in Turkey on October 6, 2020. The study encompasses a threefold analysis: first, exploring the relationship between users' posting frequencies; second, examining the geographical distribution of users and tweet origins; and third, exploring the temporal and textual characteristics of tweets related to the earthquake. The analysis was applied to two distinct time periods, one covering 7 days after the earthquake, and another focusing on the 3-day aftermath. The study's findings reveal the demographic and spatial characteristics of Twitter users based on historical data, and the users' behavior following the earthquake, utilizing random matrix theory and network science principles. The analysis also revealed significant findings from the text analysis, comprising keyword extraction and sentiment analysis. The study's methodology can serve as a basis for researching other social media platforms, such as Reddit or Pinterest, with a focus on pinnet, media, or video content. Recent advancements in machine learning are paving the way for significant interactions between physics and computer science. This research explores the application of machine learning techniques to solve longstanding issues in algebraic topology, a field that intersects with topology and category theory. We examine how mapping class group classification can be modified to extract useful data, and we demonstrate that nonlinear neural networks are well-suited to generating representations of topological structures. These findings open up potential avenues for using machine learning in advanced mathematical contexts, leading to possibilities for computational implementations and applications within physics. As an example, we investigate the incorporation of mathematical tools from higher category theory to model quantum systems, and we discuss the potential extension of this approach to more complex scenarios. We also provide an introduction to the foundational concepts and methods in both algebraic topology and machine learning for non-specialists, as well as a detailed review of relevant work in the context of physics. By identifying common themes and challenges, we aim to encourage further research at the intersection of physics, computer science, and mathematics. We analyze the primary obstacles to implementing these ideas technically and offer recommendations for addressing these difficulties in the future. Specifically, we recommend developing more advanced computational tools and methodologies within the Euler characteristic framework, supporting more projects that integrate physics, computer science, and mathematics, and promoting collaboration and knowledge sharing within these communities to establish more robust and unified research frameworks. These efforts could significantly benefit from the development of custom software, dedicated to solving differential equations and topological structures. Such a software could be added to existing projects, such as kwant, but a deeper discussion of its feasibility, development, and maintenance would be necessary. Ultimately, the potential outcomes of these endeavors are worthy of exploration and could lead to the advancement of the fields involved. Our research into how Signal users understand PINs reveals a discrepancy between official guidelines and real-world practice. While the Signal app advises users to share PINs via non-secure channels like social media, many users who receive PINs report confusion as to their purpose. These unclear intentions can undermine users' confidence in the Signal app's security capabilities, making it less likely for them to effectively use the service. Our findings suggest that, to prevent misguided security practices and ensure successful adoption of security tools like Signal, it is essential to clarify the underlying technology and user experience. To address this issue, we propose implementing a unified, secure method for sharing PINs within the Signal app itself, as well as refining the app's content to educate users about PINs and their function. By reorganizing the app's content and introducing a PIN verification process, users can develop a clearer understanding of these links and a more secure user experience can be achieved. Our study focuses on enthusiastic and casual Signal users in developing countries, including Nigeria, the Dominican Republic, and Ghana, exploring how educational content within the Signal app can be tailored to serve these users better and enhance their capacity to use the link without compromising their security. Ultimately, our research aims to ensure that users can safely and effectively use the Signal app's security features like PINs and links without exposing themselves to security risks. The resulting rule is applicable in the case where the solar irradiance model is a piecewise polynomial. The paper demonstrates the importance of an accurate solar filter response function in calculating the integrals, and uses numerical methods to determine the number of quadrature points needed for high precision. The second-order curvature information is a crucial aspect in modern optimization techniques for machine learning. The widespread use of gradient descent due to its efficient computational requirements has made second-order methods less appealing due to their significant computational costs. The development of neural Gaussian Newton method with an approximate Hessian by substituting the last few hidden layers with a low-dimensional Gaussian matrix has made it possible to obtain second-order curvature information while maintaining the standard back-propagation process and competitive performance on various tasks. This replacement allows the optimization of the Hessian's upper triangular tensor to provide second-order curvature information and has been proven effective on tasks involving both supervised and reinforcement learning, as well as on distributed systems. The success of this method has also led to the development of similar approaches for obtaining first-order entry-free curvature information and higher-order tensor optimization. The corresponding implementation can be found on the ViViT GitHub repository. The generalized Gauss-Newton optimization process has also enabled the development of a low-dimensional and efficient end-to-end autoencoder called Scalable Newton system that can perform equally well as larger methods requiring similar computational resources. The designed Scalable Newton system is capable of handling tasks involving various levels of complexity, ranging from a simple MNIST dataset to a more complex Case 12 dataset in fewer than 700 lines of code. Moreover, it achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods such as Szegedy's ImageNet model without pre-training and outperforms other recent approaches across various tasks. The process of substituting the last few layers of a neural network with a low-dimensional Gaussian matrix has also enabled the development of a neural network that provides second-order entry-free curvature information and third-order curvature information and achieves comparable performance to the neural Gaussian Newton method and the ViViT Hessian structure on tasks involving both supervised and reinforcement learning. This new class of second-order entry-free methods requires only two times the computational requirements of standard back-propagation and gradient descent. Many languages differentiate nouns based on grammatical gender, influencing their representations. This study examines how grammatical gender affects noun embeddings in languages that label nouns with gender. The research initial stage involved creating a comprehensive dataset from existing resources for four such languages: French, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. This dataset contains approximately 750 thousand French, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish noun entries, each including its gender and embeddings across various sources. The researchers then conducted experiments to compare gender-based embeddings with a unified gender system. The results showed that grammatical gender affects noun embeddings, and that the gender of a noun can be predicted with considerable accuracy using its word embeddings. This discovery implies that word embeddings can be influenced by a language's grammatical gender feature. Furthermore, the researchers found that a unified gender system can be effectively applied to male and feminine embeddings. The researchers also investigated how embeddings for couples of related gender-class specifications (e.g. masculine in French) deviate from their respective parent embeddings. Lastly, the researchers trained and tested various neural network models using the WordSim Semantics Benchmark and COW datasets, and found that models trained with unified gender embeddings slightly outperformed those trained without. The researchers plan to further develop and apply this findings, and to explore the extent to which other linguistic features, such as morphology, influence word embeddings. The data collected during this research will also be made publicly available to aid in replicating the study's results and enable researchers to examine additional languages in which nouns are assigned based on grammatical gender. Such an exploration could provide valuable insights into the effect of various linguistic features on the embeddings that languages create. The researchers also aim to achieve more by incorporating the results of this study, such as improving lexical query translation by incorporating the gender feature. The ultimate goal is to utilize word embeddings more effectively in that they can be influenced by a variety of linguistic features, such as grammatical gender, and recognize their interconnected nature. This influence and interrelation could offer valuable insights into the world of language and its complexities and help in the process of natural language understanding and generation. We state two fundamental results. First, any finite product of arithmetic groups having a common factor of $2$ in their rank can be characterized as rigid only if the product is composed of rigid individual groups. Additionally, a lattice formed from the product of individual, non-special groups becomes special if its sum of non-specialities exceeds its smallest positive rank. These findings combine to show that a finite product of arithmetic groups having a common factor of $2$ in their rank can be characterized as hyperbolic only if the product is composed of hyperbolic individual groups. Related proof variations are noted for other related scenarios. These outcomes, excepting the last statement's conclusion, were established with slightly relaxed conditions in an earlier paper, however with such conditions fully removed here. Moreover, a special case was considered in: Why Hyperbolic Space is Fixed, by Kanter, March 2016. Furthermore, this paper's conclusions, excepting the last statement's conclusion, extend clearly established theorems of Borel-Tzesin and the Milnor-Serre-Thompson Conjecture, though certain proof variations are offered. Finally, a special case was considered in: How Geometry Informs Theorems, by Kanter, August 2020. Estimating the class-specific position of objects within an image is a sophisticated
task that has significant potential for advanced applications. Unlike typical
object detection tasks, our focus is not on identifying individual objects, but
instead, we aim to pinpoint the location of each class within a single image.
Given the limited availability of large-scale annotation tools for this specific
task, we have developed a new, zero-shot approach to address the associated
challenges. By leveraging text data to build shared semantic spaces for both
textual and visual data, our technique successfully bridges the gap between
cross-lingual and cross-domain embeddings. Extensive evaluation of our approach
on an existing dataset reveals its exceptional performance, even when compared to
other estimation tasks. To promote further research in this area, we have made
available a comprehensive dataset containing 50 classes and 5,000 annotation tags. 
This resource can be accessed at https://github.com/apapadopoulos/posEst. The code
used in our research is publicly available on the GitHub repository:
https://github.com/multigamma/zero-shot-position-estimation. The associated
pre-trained models can be downloaded from:

Predicting precise traffic conditions is crucial for a modern urban transportation system.
However, gathering detailed and real-time traffic data across various roads is extremely difficult and resource-intensive.
To address this challenge, a novel approach to traffic forecasting is proposed, focusing on sparse but detailed observation data.
The proposed method, Similarity-driven Attribute Extraction for Extensive Traffic Forecasting (SAE-EF), leverages the similarities among roads to transfer knowledge and make predictions.
By incorporating an spatio-temporal attention network, SAE-EF improves prediction accuracy by dynamically weighing past road conditions.
Experimental results validate the efficacy of SAE-EF, achieving an impressive 50% reduction in prediction error compared to the baseline model, and outperforming other traffic forecasting approaches such as Deep State Space Models and Spatio-Temporal Attention Networks. Currently, it runs a sophisticated algorithm for fast radio burst detection and is also capable of processing the dynamic spectrum in real-time, allowing for the discovery of various FRBs and GRBs. The development of nanophotonic solutions to tackle the "dark ages" of metamaterials, exacerbated by excessive data generation and the need for efficient data analysis, has led to the emergence of "clever metaphotonics." This new approach leverages artificial intelligence to create innovative photonic devices, paving the way for transformative transformations in the fields of optics and photonics. By combining numerical simulations and machine learning techniques, such as genetic algorithms and neural networks, researchers can design and discover novel photonic bandgap materials and waveguides more efficiently than before. Moreover, the integration of artificial intelligence has accelerated the development of optimized photonic devices, including high-precision lasers and sensitive sensors, which are now being explored for a range of practical applications. As a prime example, the development of artificial intelligence-optimized Bragg modellers has significantly expedited the development of ultra-fast and high-power photonic devices, such as photonic crystal lasers, while simultaneously enhancing sensor technologies and enabling advanced optical manipulation at the quantum level. The filmed sector is a significant source of global income. In the pre-production phase, filmmakers consider various factors such as location, weather, and visual effects when deciding to proceed with a project. This paper examines how different visual attributes, influenced by weather and geographical conditions, impact film gross income. To tackle this challenge, we developed a feature engineering process that extracts multiple characteristics from each film's visual content. This comprehensive approach was applied to the filmed sector, addressing a critical issue faced by filmmakers. To expand our research, we gathered data on 18,875 films from cinema reports between 1994 and 2017. This dataset includes 639 unique actors, 1,852 location sites, and 1,685 cinematographers. Our results indicate that certain features, such as lead actors and location, have a pronounced effect on film income. Moreover, we analyzed the impact of visual attributes on income and discovered that films shot mainly at night tend to earn less, whereas those with prominent visual effects tend to earn more. The key contributions of our research are a larger dataset of cinema reports, an optimized feature engineering process for image characterization, and a comprehensive understanding of the significant features influencing film income. The latter includes lead actors, location, cinematographers, visual attributes, and time of shooting. All our research data, including codes and data sets, are freely accessible on the https://github.com/jpgleiser/multimedia_energy_dataset platform. For demonstration purposes, a mobile application is available at https://github.com/jpgleiser/mobilefilmenergy. The mobile application is also available in app stores under the name 'Film Energy'. The performance of AFR systems is typically evaluated based on their capacity for frequency regulation. However, this approach is insufficient to fully assess their potential to mitigate voltage problems due to the variety of system scenarios and voltage stability criteria, such as maximum power transfer and small-signal stability limits. This study examines the impact of AFR systems on system stability when subject to small sudden changes in power. Utilizing a stability approach, we analyze the effect of AFR systems on transmission lines and investigated their ability to prevent voltage collapse in a linearized model of the problem environment, thus providing an indicator for evaluating their performance. The results confirm the validity of this approach and enable a comparative evaluation of AFR systems with varying characteristics. The validity of this approach is confirmed through simulation of various scenarios on the European electricity network, as well as on a network with renewable energy integration. The study's findings demonstrate that AFR systems have an inhibiting effect on system stability and can cause oscillations when the power transmitted by them exceeds a particular threshold. Consequently, the use of these systems to stabilize voltage is insufficient, and a more comprehensive solution is required, such as upgrading the power transmission capacity. The importance of accurately modeling AFR systems in power flow and stability analysis is also emphasized. It also opens up opportunities for further research and development of more efficient approaches to regulating frequency and maintaining system stability. This allows CPSs to be modeled as networks of interconnected modules, each possessing varying levels of cognitive functionality. A distributed algorithm is developed to optimize network flow and manage distributed cognition within CPS networks in the presence of heterogeneous processing capabilities and data exchange limitations. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and two real-world applications. Initially, the algorithm is applied to optimize supply chains for vaccine distribution within artificial cognitive CPS networks. Subsequently, its capabilities are utilized to enhance the data collection speed of sensor networks in industrial settings. Throughout, the proposed approach is exemplified through case studies illustrating the conceptual framework in practical contexts. The underlying mathematical models serve as a common foundation for understanding and analyzing the trade-offs inherent in distributed cognition within CPSs. A demo is provided to facilitate user comprehension of the presented concepts. The work is supplemented by four additional videos. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/cambridge-caps/dkcps. A comprehensive user guide is available to ensure that the proposed framework is applicable to a broad range of applications. Following a concise introduction to distributed cognition within CPSs, we examine its practical implications in the context of social systems. A novel concept, district citizenship, is introduced as a foundation for capturing the unique properties of CPSs comprising multiple entities possessing cognitive functionality. A model of district citizenship within CPSs is formulated, which informs the development of a cognitive protocol for enhancing public utility in districts. Following an in-depth analysis of the protocol's properties, its implementation is evaluated in terms of optimization within artificial CPS networks. Furthermore, the district concept is illustrated through case studies, which highlight the different forms of citizenship within CPSs comprising entities characterized by their cultural or professional affiliations. The conclusions drawn from these examples inform the discussion of the broader social implications of CPSs comprising entities possessing cognitive functionality. Ultimately, the independence of district citizenship from its individual constituents is established, which informs the two key principles of citizenship in the context of CPSs. Firstly, a principle governing the preservation of district properties is identified, which ensures that these properties are preserved even when individual entities are replaced. Secondly, a principle governing the consistency of cognitive functionality is observed, which ensures that the collective cognition of CPSs is not affected by the order in which their constituent entities are considered. These principles provide a framework for advancing the theoretical understanding of CPSs comprising entities possessing cognitive functionality. Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable excess in the ultraviolet and soft X-ray ranges. This blazar excess can be attributed to an alternative radiation process called the inverse Compton scattering of partially polarized photons. A new method, the MAPPIES model, has been developed to determine the polarization of these photons by using magnetized plasma to interact with them. According to the MAPPIES model, a 1-e-5 mu-G magnetic field present in the accretion disk can account for the spectrum and polarization of the excess emission, assuming the photons originate from a specific radiation zone. Conversely, a 1-e-3 mu-G magnetic field, present in a different radiation zone, can also yield comparable emission and polarization patterns. As this alternative radiation process typically produces lower levels of polarization compared to other scattering processes, the MAPPIES model suggests that the accretion disk is likely bathed in a radiation zone produced by the accretion of protons with gold nuclei at the accretion plate. Furthermore, the model's requirements for the magnetic field strength and radiation zone produce a spectral excess six times more powerful than what is expected from relativistic jets, a fact also supported by the polarization of the excess emission in the case of the particular blazar PG 1116-2. The MAPPIES model presents a new explanation for the nature of the blazar excess, an explanation that can be broadly applied. This new explanation for the blazar excess is expected to not only describe but also predict the polarization patterns of blazars with similar spectral energy distributions. To confirm the accuracy of the MAPPIES model in its current form, future studies aimed at directly measuring the polarization of UV and soft X-ray emissions from accretion disk radiation zones are recommended. Moreover, the model's proposed predictions regarding the generalized nature of MAPPIES to various physical scenarios are also worthy of future investigation. Ultimately, the accuracy of the MAPPIES model in its current form, as well as its potential applicability in its generalized form, will be confirmed through direct measurement. Such a direct measurement of the polarization of the excess emission of particular blazar PG 1116-2 has already been successfully carried out in the case of the particular blazar PG 1116-2, as reported in an accompanying study. This investigation leads to the creation of a corresponding abstract algebraic structure, which is then fully analyzed. Furthermore, this method facilitates the creation of a corollary to Bishop's theorem and allows us to approach the challenging issue of determining whether a given net of contractive maps can be combined to form a contractive metric. One potential area for further research could be its application to the concept of germs. Researchers have discovered a correlation between solar flares and slight changes in the sun's rotation period, as observed through helioseismic oscillations, following the sun's equatorial rotation speed being slowed and then restored. To further understand this phenomenon, scientists have used numerical simulations to find the cause behind this recovery phase. These simulations revealed that a restoration of the sun's rotation speed occurs due to a specific interaction between the sun's internal fluid and the surrounding magnetic fields, as well as the influence of mass movements within the sun's interior and on its surface surrounding the active regions. Specifically, the restoration was found to be primarily attributed to a specific movement of the sun's fluid, known as secondary circulation, which develops in the areas adjacent to the active regions. By analyzing the sun's response to these mass movements, scientists were able to estimate the contribution of these flows to the slight changes in the sun's rotation period. These calculations indicated that the secondary circulation around the active regions could alone account for approximately one-half to two-thirds of the observed changes in travel time relative to the total duration of the sun's rotation period. The remainder of the observed changes was attributed to another specific movement of the sun's fluid, known as deep convection. By understanding the relative impacts of these different mass movements, scientists have gained a more comprehensive knowledge of the sun's interior dynamics, which has implications for the study of the sun's long-term evolution. These new insights might be useful in assessing how these movements contribute to solar activity, which scientists know occurred in the sun in the past and can also be predicted for the sun in the future. Furthermore, the sun is also an ideal model for studying similar astrophysical phenomena that occur in other stars that are known to rotate more slowly. Such examples include stars with low levels of activity or ones that have stopped rotating altogether due to their own versions of mass movements, which similar to what was observed in the sun, result in slight changes in their rotation periods. Our research centers around exploring the interplay between random and planar components of magnetic fields in the early Universe. These fields not only influenced the distribution of electric charges but also warped the fabric of space-time, generating subtle signatures in the motion of nearby celestial objects. Since primordial magnetic fields were likely highly non-homogeneous on a large scale, we develop a model where one type of field is randomly distributed and another is a uniform plane. This unique configuration may have mimicked the non-random, anisotropic magnetic fields in the early Universe. When imposed on a sphere representing the entire Universe, the plane can be imagined as a great circle. We calculate the amplitude of the gravitational wave signal produced by these fields and its potential detection by the MARS and LISA instruments. Due to the spectrum's single power-law component, the predicted signals from individual objects are too faint for direct detection. However, when signals from numerous pulsars are combined, they become detectable at frequencies around $10^{-12} - 10^{-3}$ Hz. This combination could potentially be achieved through the collaboration of various instruments, including those in the MARS dataset and LISA's spectral content. Moreover, we simulate a dataset of 282 pulsars to identify the signatures of these fields in the MARS-LISA consortium's future joint dataset. At a frequency range of $10^{-4} - 10^{-3}$ Hz, the joint spectrum exhibits a $3\sigma$ anomaly in the MARS-LISA dataset, indicating its potential as a pioneering experiment in observing the gravitational wave signal from the early Universe. This signature can be recognized once temporal noise is subtracted and frequency-dependent corrections are applied. Our research opens new avenues for investigating the impact of planar components of magnetic fields in the early Universe, inspiring the development of future analysis methods to detect such signatures in Pulsar Timing Arrays, including those expansion to Pulsar Timing Array expansion to nearly a third of the sky. Moreover, our findings have significant implications for research on primordial black holes and the early Universe, suggesting that these holes may be aligned along great circles, thereby increasing their overall mass in these areas. This hypothesis may be tested through the observation of gravitational wave signals from these holes aligned along these circles. Our research provides insights into the alignment of primordial black holes in the early Universe, offering an explanation for their potential uniform alignment along great circles. These findings demonstrate that planar components of magnetic fields in the early Universe, aligned along these circles, may increase the overall mass in these areas

Light field technology is currently a highly active area of study, despite the significant complexity and computational demands of its applications. This study focuses on the practical aspects of using compressed optimisation methods for light field image compression, and it is the first of its kind to incorporate insights gained from pre-trained, model-optimised techniques. The paper presents a novel model-based approach that is specifically tailored to capture both the structural and statistical patterns within 4D light field images, and it achieves this by combining a disparity-aware image generation architecture with a secondary latent representation centered around an EPICNET-derived disparity map. The results demonstrate that this method provides superior quality and comes closer to the quality of the original, uncompressed images than existing techniques, and it also significantly outperforms other model-based approaches in terms of compression efficiency and overall performance. Furthermore, the results show that by utilizing this model in combination with conventional entropy-coded hyper-lattice discretisation, it's possible to achieve compression ratios of up to 60:1 while preserving high-quality 4D light field images, and that these images can be used to generate various display formats such as 1.30 megapixels displays, 3D stereograms and hyperpanoramas. This technology has the potential to greatly expand the uses of light field technology in fields including advertising, journalism, medicine and virtual reality applications. Furthermore, the paper showcases the performance of the method by displaying a range of newly captured 4D light field datasets captured using a state-of-the-art R200 camera, and it highlights various example applications that use the generated compressed light field datasets to produce a range of photo-realistic formats. These examples effectively show how the technology can be used to capture and represent a wide range of visual data. Ultimately, the paper marks an important step towards using compressed optimisation methods for light field image compression, and it is an important step towards leveraging these methods in this field. Our framework integrates the advantages of independent and interactive models for cross-language image retrieval, combining users' initial search terms with users' and system-generated image features. To achieve this, we utilize two pre-trained models: a query translation model and an image similarity model. In our framework's non-interactive mode, we first obtain an initial list of images based on user input in the target language, then present a subset of images as options. Users can select one image, after which our framework refines the search by combining the target term translations with the selected image features. In the interactive mode, users are presented with two dropdown options – a list of potential images and a list of target term translations. By selecting an image or translation, the framework updates the top image list based on image-feature similarity. Through a search experiment conducted using 4000 images and 320 target terms in English and Spanish, we demonstrated that our framework's non-interactive and interactive implementations respectively achieved an 26.6% and 32.2% improvement in average precision compared to traditional baseline models. Moreover, our framework's non-interactive and interactive approaches respectively significantly outperformed existing related work, showcasing their efficiency in cross-language image retrieval. Average response times of our framework were recorded as 0.48 seconds in non-interactive mode and 1.07 seconds in interactive mode. These response times were faster and comparable to that of other related work. To validate our framework's efficiency, a user study was also conducted. Further development and optimization of our framework could potentially bring users closer to a fully immersive cross-language image searching experience. Our framework's and related work's source code and experiment data are available for further investigation at https://github.com/jaycis97/clic-rfi. Our framework won 1st place in the 2020 2nd Visual Information Retrieval Challenge at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. A related video demonstrating our framework's non-interactive and interactive modes is available at https://youtu.be/NQqU7TgVw8U. Our framework's non-interactive and interactive modes received the following awards: the 1st and 2nd positions in the non-interactive track and the 2nd and 3rd positions in the interactive track, respectively. When conducting surveys in low and moderate income countries, survey designers face two principal decisions, one involving expansion probability adjustment and the other relating to data model fitting. The first choice revolves around incorporating distinct estimation procedures for large and small regions, whereas the second is centered on models that recognize geographic divisions. The underlying rationale for distinct procedures in region-based estimation lies in the potential disparities between large and small areas in terms of variance and bias. The need for model-focused approaches stems from the fact that small regions tend to experience larger standard errors and negative estimates due to lower weights. The paper delves into these two distinct strategies for survey designers, analyzes their underlying logic, presents their practical implications, and provides recommendations for both designers and analysts based on extensive empirical evidence. The study's findings are grounded in the Dhaka Metropolitan Area fertility estimates, which serve as a primary case study. The research also draws upon the fertility estimates for 18 countries across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, operating under the Demographic and Health Surveys program protocol. The outcomes of the study will benefit not only survey designers but also analysts, whereas offering valuable insights for researchers to conduct thorough literature reviews and expand their understanding of region-based estimation methods and procedures. The study's key findings indicate that adjustment for regional expansion probability achieves better results when large and small regions share the same underlying population characteristics and density. In contrast, model-focused approaches yield more accurate estimates and reduce bias and error when accounting for regional characteristics and density variations. The study's recommendations are centered on the dual objectives of expansion probability adjustment and model fitting for region-based estimation. Specifically, the study advises survey designers to adopt a two-pronged strategy of incorporating distinct procedures for large and small regions, with the former focused on expansion probability adjustment and the latter centered on model fitting. The study also recommends that survey calculators leverage existing models to estimate small region values by incorporating adjustment for regional expansion probability. The study's analysis of the Dhaka Metropolitan Area fertility estimates is used to compare the performance of different estimation methods and models. The estimates indicate that small regions exhibit larger standard errors and negative bias. The study's analysis also shows that model-focused approaches yield more accurate estimates and reduce bias and error when accounting for regional characteristics and density variations. The study's key findings are summarized in the study's conclusion, providing valuable recommendations for survey designers, analysts, and researchers. The study's conclusion is grounded in the findings of the study, which are supported by the extensive empirical evidence from the Demographic and Health Surveys program protocol.
