A federated learning system allows a central server to coordinate multiple clients without compromising privacy, essentially operating as a centralized gradient descent algorithm utilizing client resources intermittently. For linear regression, the asynchronous federated learning process can be completed in the censored information age, but the same approach is impractical for nonlinear regression due to computationally intensive optimization requirements. Building on an exponential weight moving average technique to rectify asynchronous federated learning's convergence issues, our research demonstrates improved performance using both simulated data and real-world datasets, achieving fast convergence similar to centralized methods across various nonlinear regression scenarios. The findings indicate that the asynchronous algorithm's efficacy is largely independent of model nonlinearities and data distribution, while also optimizing client participation and central server communication. Calculations revealed increased absorption in a 20 nm thick silicon layer, rising from 79% to around 85%, with notable improvements observed across a wider spectrum. Notably, the modification also improved absorption in thinner silicon layers, up to 10 nm in thickness, increasing predicted absorption rates up to 60%. This increase was attributed to the modified refractive index profile caused by the nanosphere array. As a result, the setup is proposed for applications involving thinnest layers in nano-photonics, solar cells, biosensors, or optical filters. In various applications like drug development, traffic prediction, and recommendation systems, graph data sets often play a crucial role. The challenge of making accurate predictions on graph data involves linking nodes, a task that can be trivial in densely connected networks but significantly more difficult in sparse networks. One such prediction task is the shortest path estimation between unlinked nodes, which can be accomplished through the shortest path embedding method. However, existing shortest path embedding methods face two primary limitations. Firstly, they often yield embeddings that are too closely tied to the underlying graph structure, resulting in poor performance when predictions are made. Secondly, the embeddings generated are highly sensitive to the hyper-parameters employed, which can be both time-consuming and expensive to optimize. To address these challenges, we introduce the Structural Near Neighbor Embedding (SNNE) method. SNNE creates node embeddings by considering only the immediate structural context surrounding each node, thereby reducing its fit to the underlying graph structure and making it less dependent on hyper-parameters. Additionally, SNNE utilizes a novel objective function called Structural Predictive Accuracy (SPA) that focuses on the overall network health and prediction task rather than the modification of individual node embeddings. Our experiments with various datasets demonstrate that SNNE significantly outperforms existing link prediction algorithms. Lastly, SNNE's source code is publicly available on the CodeOcean platform. Overly high launch conditions in advanced 4D transmission schemes lead to premature failure, with the resulting signals then falling into an eyes-closed region and failing to convey meaningful information. Consequently, accurately calculating nonlinear distortion and precisely predicting signal quality becomes crucial for optimizing parameters. We develop a novel model designed to predict nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization four-dimensional transmission formats, where encoded signals exhibit complex temporal and spatial patterns. We rely on a dual-launch-symmetric measurement approach and develop a distorted-power prediction equation, breaking down the total nonlinear distortion into its constituent parts - spatial, temporal, and interactive disturbances. We validate the accuracy of our model with experimental results from a dual-polarization, four-dimensional transmission experiment over 288 km of fiber. Our findings indicate that the model is remarkably precise, with a linear relationship between observed and predicted distortion results. We observe that the model successfully tracks distortion levels across various coding and polarization states. Finally, we propose an efficient method for calculating nonlinear distortion and demonstrate its practical utility in quickly optimizing launch conditions, reducing disruption power by 7.9 dB, and significantly improving the bit-error-rate from 24.6 to 16.3 dB. Our model opens up the possibility of automatically refining encoding and launch strategies in advanced transmission systems, with considerable potential for improvement. It could be integrated into processing software in the future, paving the way for semi-automated system optimization in the quest for improved performance. Our findings and procedures are expected to offer valuable insights into nonlinear distortion mechanisms and contribute to future linear-or-amplified-transmission design decisions. Moreover, the methods and approaches we employ are widely applicable and could be adopted in various contexts, such as nonlinear distortion studies in single- or dual-polarization systems, as well as in a range of advanced transmission formats, including four-dimensional transmission, and other more recent formats, such as four-dimensional parity-check or four-dimensional superposition. Ultimately, the work presents a significant step forward and sets the stage for exciting future developments in the field of transmission systems. The study has been accompanied by video footage illustrating the experimental results and resonance of the researchers. The experimental approach described in this work has also served as a foundation for related research and will be further explored in future research on nonlinear distortion studies. The study is supplemented by several figures that depict experimental distortion results and their graphical representations, in addition to a figure that illustrates the experimental procedure used to obtain the distortion results, and several figure that shows the dependence of distortion levels on launch conditions, serving as a key result of the research.

Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems and human infrastructure. 
Although visible spectra provide rich visual data, infrared imagery offers crucial temperature information during fires, especially when objects are obscured from view in the visible spectrum, like through smoke or darkness. 
Combining both spectra could thus yield comprehensive and informative visual representations of wildfires, underpinned by thermal insights.
Despite this potential, previous research has been hindered by difficulties in merging these spectra effectively, which has resulted in inconsistent and unsatisfactory visual outcomes. 
As a result, wildfire visualization is typically restricted to either the visible or thermal spectrum, missing the full story. 
Our FIRe-GAN solution is a novel approach to be utilized for wildfire visualization, incorporating an advanced mode to bridge the gap between visible and thermal spectra through image integration.

In our research, we develop a novel method for accurately predicting the risk associated with the Bellman operator and apply it to the study of near-optimal decision-making in infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes without making any assumptions about the model. This risk measure is particularly significant in the vicinity of nearly optimal policies because it mirrors the average long-term rewards expected from nearly optimal policies in a wide-scaled MDP model. By using our risk estimation technique, we establish a government agency that makes policy decisions by balancing the combination of performance and risk, opening up new avenues for exploration in the field of optimal control without assuming complete knowledge of the model. Additionally, we demonstrate that our risk estimation technique is accurate (i.e., convergent) to the risk associated with nearly optimal policies in any given MDP model. Furthermore, we prove that our risk estimation technique is based on an empirical minimizer in a class of path-dependent empirical processes and is influenced by hyperparameters. Through experiments using both well-established and novel datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our risk estimation technique for evaluating nearly optimal policies in a wide-scaled MDP model without requiring complete knowledge of the model. Our results show that our risk estimation technique has consistent horizontal convergence and sufficient sample efficiency for evaluating nearly optimal policies in a wide-scaled MDP model. Our risk estimation technique is particularly suitable for use in scenarios where the model is unknown and there is a need to quickly adapt to changes in the Markov chain for near-optimal initial policies. This research was supported by the recent findings of large-language-model-based explainable AI in the field of plan simplification as presented in the paper 'Plan Simplification by the Proximity Interpreter'. This paper aims to bridge this gap by introducing a topological representation for the essential subspace of a nonsymmetric linear transformation on a finite-dimensional complex vector space. This representation is based on a distinguished cycle, defined as the set of distinguished cycles, which constitutes a distinguished cycle structure. Moreover, every nonsymmetric linear transformation can be represented by a homomorphism from the fundamental group of a 2-sphere to the general linear group of the vector space. However, not all such homomorphisms correspond to a nonsymmetric linear transformation. A distinguished cycle structure provides sufficient conditions for this correspondence to exist. These conditions are narrow compared to the general criteria for linear symmetry found in the literature. In particular, the second condition is straightforward: a necessary condition for the existence of a corresponding linear transformation is that the image of the fundamental group be finite. A notable example illustrates that this condition is not necessarily sufficient. Furthermore, a distinguished cycle structure offers insights into the algebraic properties of iterated traces, which are crucial in understanding nonsymmetric linear transformations. This is particularly significant for the case of triangular matrices, which can be viewed as certain distinguished cycle structures. As distinguished cycle structures are topological in nature, they provide a fundamental link between algebraic and topological properties of nonsymmetric linear transformations. As an instance, a distinguished cycle structure can be used to assign a cycle, which may be singular or closed, to each point on the 2-sphere. This is reminiscent of the assignment of a fiber to each point in a fiber bundle. While the topological properties studied here are basic, such as cycle types and indices, which are simply the traces at the points, the corresponding algebraic properties are more intricate. By integrating insights from classical population dynamics and stochastic master equation theories, we provide a comprehensive mathematical foundation for studying these processes. Our work is focused on exploring the differences between the evolution of life on Earth in ancient and modern times, where we observe distinct temporal behaviors. Ancient life is characterized by sudden shifts between static and explosive growth due to the activation of new ecological and evolutionary processes, in contrast to modern times, marked by continuous and uniformly changing processes. To capture these diverse time dynamics, we develop a versatile mathematical model that incorporates different types of time using an approach based on stochastic processes with regulated activity. Our study provides a mathematical explanation for the varying time scales of eco-evolutionary transitions, where the duration of explosive growth phases depends on the age of the system, while the intervals between them are influenced by the average lifetime of ecological and evolutionary processes. Research into foundation models that learn speech representations lays the groundwork for numerous applications such as speech synthesis, modification and recognition. We investigate the interplay between a cutting-edge speech foundation model known as VITS and self-supervised model Siamese Network (SN) that it collaborates with. Through contrasting SN trained alone with SN trained alongside the speech foundation model, we reveal a counterintuitive pattern where the latter appears more resistant to the negative effects of adversarial examples. This contradicts our initial expectation that combining SN with a robust speech model would result in an improved adversarial robustness. Upon closer inspection, we attribute this unexpected outcome to two possible explanations. Firstly, the speech foundation model may inadvertently transfer adversarial examples to SN, counteracting their adverse performance. Alternatively, the larger size of the training dataset for the speech foundation model compared to SN may contribute to SN's enhanced adversarial resistance, suggesting that transferring knowledge can facilitate improved resilience. We further explore SN's performance in handling smaller, more practical datasets within adversarial settings, evaluating its resistance to manipulation such as pitch alterations and speed modifications. This research provides a new perspective on the trade-offs between the benefits and drawbacks of transferring knowledge between models, with the potential to be applied to other self-supervised model training scenarios. We have made our code available for replication purposes. In particular, the adversarial study is facilitated by the adversarial-babble library, which was developed in our research team. This library offers a wide range of techniques for manipulating speech audio, including 11 different strategies, such as altering the rate of speech, appending text, modifying the tone of speech and swapping speaker identities. Moreover, this library is designed to be applicable to various types of speech manipulation as well as extended to incorporate the use of text-to-speech models, opening up new possibilities for research in the field of adversarial education. Ultimately, the primary goal of our research is to promote resilience in speech-based self-supervised learning, with the ultimate goal of ensuring model accuracy across a variety of speech representation tasks, even in the presence of misleading information. The digitization of educational materials and the growth of the Internet have led to the emergence of smart education, making learning more convenient and efficient. To overcome the limitations of learning environments, Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) technology is being incorporated into educational settings, enabling students to expand their understanding beyond traditional boundaries. However, IoVs' reliance on mobile networks raises concerns about data security and privacy, prompting the need for a reliable framework that balances these needs with the benefits of learning. Federated Learning (FL) is a promising approach for developing robust machine learning models that mitigate these concerns, but current frameworks often fail to provide comprehensive solutions, leaving rooms for improvement. This paper aims to address these gaps by presenting a systematic literature review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning (FBL) frameworks in the context of IoV networks. By analyzing existing research from various perspectives, this paper hopes to derive key insights and recommendations for improving these frameworks and setting a foundation for future developments in IoV education. Through an in-depth analysis of 25 papers, this study categorizes IoV education frameworks into four types, discussing their characteristics, challenges, and opportunities for growth. One of the key takeaways from this review is the urgent need to address privacy concerns and dishonest behaviors in FBL frameworks. Addressing these issues through Blockchain technology has shown considerable potential, but more research is needed to overcome current limitations in using Blockchain within FL. Furthermore, this paper derives recommendations for improving FBL frameworks, including conducting more in-depth assessments of mathematical computations, network traffic, and latency requirements, as well as considering the adoption of Blockchain technology in specialized hardware. Finally, based on the insights gained from this review, we propose a comprehensive BFLIoV framework that addresses 11 key challenges, providing a valuable foundation for future developments in IoV education. This paper aims to contribute to the ongoing debate on the future of IoV education and related technologies, as well as providing essential insights for researchers and practitioners interested in shaping the future of this emerging field. With the growing importance of digital learning, this paper envisions a promising future for IoV education, emphasizing the need to overcome current limitations through the design of robust BFLIoV frameworks. Specifically, researchers and practitioners can build more robust frameworks by investing in more advanced algorithms, improving network security through the deployment of more reliable networks, and enhancing educational content to increase user adoption. Ultimately, by addressing these challenges, researchers and practitioners can create more resilient BFLIoV frameworks, paving the way for significant advancements in IoV education and beyond. In superconducting circuits, quantum error reduction is now a pressing issue due to frequent gate failures. A novel approach called the concealed inverses protocol (CIP) has been developed to eliminate errors in two-qubit gates by reversing their invalid outcomes. This protocol is based on the principle of inverse unitary transformations, where the validity of two-qubit gate outcomes is assessed using a key, and erroneous results are retroactively nullified through a public verification process. The CIP demonstrates the feasibility of eliminating errors in the context of quantum computing, thereby enhancing system efficiency. Furthermore, the CIP has been adapted for error correction in quantum communication, specifically for the B92 protocol. The CIP shows great potential for practical application in various quantum information technologies. The proposed physical model of the CIP suggests that quantum transformations can occur instantly, providing a potential solution to addressing quantum error correction in real-world superconducting quantum systems. Nevertheless, implementing the CIP may pose a challenge due to reliance on an infinitely fast data transmission channel. Consequently, at finite data transmission speeds, error reduction will occur, but errors may persist, although their likelihood can be quantitatively assessed using a quantum transformation operator and probability amplitude analyzer. The study provides a mathematical interpretation of this analysis, revealing that persistent errors arise from a failure to reduce errors within the time interval between gate application and verification. In addition, the study investigates the possibility of reducing these non-reducible errors through repeated usage of the CIP, leading to the conclusion that all errors are ultimately convertible to bit errors, providing a quantitative understanding of this process and potentially paving the way for technological applications, such as noise reduction, where the CIP may be utilized to eliminate low-frequency errors. Ultimately, the faster the CIP operates, the more substantial its benefits will be, and it is hoped that future research will verify this prediction in practice. The study's conceptual validity suggests that the CIP has the potential to significantly enhance existing quantum information technologies. We build on the existing framework of multivariate spatial extremes by introducing a new model to forecast the joint occurrence of droughts and floods. This model, called the multivariate spatial Extremes conditional on Ordinary events, or MEO for short, views the joint distribution of events as a combination of typical situations and rare patterns. MEO explains unusual spatial relationships during extreme weather patterns as resulting from stochastic fluctuations, and its conditional residuals are independently Gaussian. MEO's ability to tolerate irregularities in the data is demonstrated through a multivariate case study involving marine precipitation levels in Western Australia, where it successfully forecasts extreme weather events. This model's implementation requires only moderately large computational resources and can be adapted for use on larger datasets with minor adjustments. Moreover, MEO's benefits are not limited to the marine conditions of Western Australia; it can be applied to a wide range of environments and regions worldwide. This paper contributes to the field of extreme value analysis by introducing a new method for understanding and interpreting the complex relationships between high-and-low extreme weather events. Through MEO's assumption of stochastic stationarity, we can better comprehend the spatial interactions underlying these events and make predictions about their behavior. This theory can be applied in a variety of real-world contexts, such as coastal management planning in the Mesopotamian plain, where officials are faced with predicting future floods. Similar decisions on the best course of action for coping with weather events or building infrastructure are relevant to a range of sites worldwide, and are often influenced by similar spatial patterns, whether or not they occur in areas with extreme weather. In general, the MEO model offers a versatile toolkit for understanding and planning for extreme weather events, and their consequences, around the world. This paper demonstrates MEO's ability to be adapted for use in a variety of environments and regions worldwide. And, through a related project, we show that MEO's predictions for future weather events are feasible at a technological level. And, this theory can be integrated with other methods for predicting the impact of weather events, such as wave damage, and other related phenomena. Recently, large-scale pre-trained vision-language models have gained significant attention, allowing for direct vision-language processing without the need for additional training. These pre-trained models can automatically map image and text features to a common multimodal space, making it possible to perform operations such as captioning and visual question answering. Nevertheless, their performance in fine-grained visual recognition tasks is still limited. To bridge this gap, we propose a new technique that enhances vision-language models using visual cues to inform text processing. This approach is based on a simple yet efficient end-to-end fine-tuning method, which leverages VT-CLIP, a pre-trained model that associates complex visual and linguistic information. To validate our approach, we introduce a novel dataset, called CarSeries, which requires accurate understanding of car models based on written descriptions and related images. By comparing different vision-language models, we demonstrate that our proposed method, VT-CLIP, significantly improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging datasets, including CarSeries, COCO, and Visual Question Answering. To facilitate further research, we publicly release the CarSeries dataset and our corresponding code at https://github.com/whwu/VTCILIP. Our results indicate that VT-CLIP outperforms existing vision-language models, showing its potential to excel in a range of applications. In the fields of pathology and radiology, image analysis is a key component of 
accurately diagnosing a wide variety of diseases. By leveraging machine learning, 
scientists and clinicians can work together to achieve reliable, data-driven 
diagnoses. Yet, there is currently a lack of standardized approach to share 
results and collaborate effectively. To address this, the Highdicom Python 
library provides a unified methodology for conforming to the DICOM standard, 
enabling seamless data exchange and streamlined interactions with image files, 
model outputs, and related metadata. This web-friendly, Python-based tool is 
designed to promote standardized exchanges and adoption of DICOM within the 
pathology and radiology communities, ultimately facilitating inter-operable 
exchanges and enabling researchers and clinicians to easily share data and results. 
Highdicom is available for free, open-source on GitHub. This paper introduces 
the underlying technology, highlights key functionalities, and showcases a 
critical example of its usage within a research context. Highdicom's open-source 
code and supporting documentation can be accessed through GitHub. Additionally, 
the accompanying demo Jupyter Notebook can be accessed through Google Colab. 
This innovative technology aims to promote widespread adoption and standardization 
of exchanges within the pathology and radiology communities. 
Highdicom's open-source code and supporting documentation can be accessed at 
https://github.com/Highdicom/Highdicom. The accompanying demo Jupyter Notebook 
can be accessed at https://colab.github.com/. 
Higher-level implementations and demonstrations of the technology can be found at 
https://highdicom.github.io. 
Example use cases for the tool involve research projects in lung cancer, 
radiology, pathology, and oncology, and the output conforms to the standard, 
enabling sharing via public databases (e.g. AI for lung cancer diagnosis) or 
with the Digital Imaging Across the Public Health Spectrum. 
By leveraging Highdicom, researchers can easily share and obtain model 
outputs and exchange data with other researchers, and the tool also facilitates 
compliance with the DICOM standard, promoting a community that promotes 
standardized exchanges and adoption of DICOM within the communities. 
Ultimately, the tool has the potential to expand access to reliable, 
data-driven diagnostics for researchers and clinicians, and the tool may also 
empower clinicians to share results and collaborate effectively.

In the era of Expansive Data, traditional techniques that heavily rely on human supervision struggle to keep up with the ever-increasing demand for informatics solutions. Unsupervised learning, in particular, has seen a surge in popularity as it efficiently processes large volumes of unlabelled data. Here, we apply an advanced variant of unsupervised learning, called Variational Autoencoder, to the challenging task of representing DNA sequences in a compact yet informative format. By doing so, we aim to preserve crucial properties and long-range dependencies within the sequences while significantly reducing their size. The proposed approach has promising implications for various genomic analyses and informatics applications. Extensive experiments are conducted on a diverse range of DNA sequences, yielding compact representations that successfully congregate homologous sequences and isolate novel sub-classes of sequences that were previously undefined. The accuracy of our model is rigorously evaluated by examining the sequence-to-sequence translation process, using distantly supervised methods. The results are further complemented by successful cross-validation experiments in key applications such as predicting essential genes under selective pressure using critical antibiotic agents as example queries. Furthermore, we explore various post-hoc techniques to interpret the latent space, ensuring that our model does not inadvertently replicate existing biases. The resulting compact representations, complete with essential gene predictions, are made publicly available on https://github.com/aliMachineLearning/DNA-Sequence-Embeddings. Additional resources, encompassing comprehensive results and experimental data sets, are hosted on the research repository: https://doi.org/10.2192/airb.it/DNA-Embeddings. The research presented in this dissertation addresses critical challenges in developing and testing various aspects of the DNA-Sequence-Embeddings framework. When exposed to air, V$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit a different metal-insulator transition than those formed in ultr high vacuum (UHV) conditions. While oxygen presence enhances the transition in certain cases, our study revealed the insulating phase can be achieved in both environments with similar thickness. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) observations confirmed that surface modification with carbon or sulfur impurities alters the film structure, consistent with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis. Furthermore, our findings on the varying thickness-dependent magnetic properties of V$_2$O$_3$ films or bilayers on a substrate indicate complexity due to magnetic coupling with the substrate or the presence of impurities. Ultimately, our investigation of these complex systems or bilayers under different environmental conditions has been successfully deconvolved through the integration of experimental techniques. As a result, our work can serve as a reference for the interpretation of thickness-dependent magnetic properties in various systems or bilayers. Moreover, our study offers valuable insights into the design of V$_2$O$_3$ films with controlled metal-insulator transitions and the development of techniques to modulate or eliminate impurities such as carbon or sulfur on oxides surfaces. Such research could potentially contribute to the advancement of V$_2$O$_3$ based devices, particularly those exhibiting magneto-resistive, magneto-capacitance, or weak antiferromagnetic coupling with a variety of materials like a ferro or antiferro magnetic layers, or a graphene layer, etc. It is well known that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ is a rare example of a first-order transition that is known to be influenced by environmental factors and the presence of impurities, which was observed in our study at different thicknesses of the V$_2$O$_3$ films or bilayers on a substrate with various experimental techniques. Predictive modeling, primarily directed towards preventing, detecting and reducing critical consequences such as system failures and health issues, is primarily addressed through supervised learning. This paper examines the applicability of supervised learning algorithms on datasets obtained from various fields such as engineering, natural science and healthcare. Furthermore, we aim to determine the efficacy of ensemble methods over individual algorithms and assess the reliability of predictive models using performance metrics. By utilizing a unified framework, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of machine learning algorithms, allowing for comparison and optimization based on the defined metrics. Through this process, we identify the optimal algorithms for failure and health prediction, analyze the robustness of selected models, determine the intrinsic value of individual features and assess the sensitivity of models to feature significance. Our findings reveal that hybrid models such as gradient boosting and support vector machines excel in predictive modeling, while feature selection experiments demonstrate the positive impact of ensemble methods on model performance. Ultimately, our results confirm that ensemble methods outperform standalone algorithms and highlight the significance of feature selection in enhancing model reliability. Mesh coarsening is a process that reduces a finite element mesh's triangle count while maintaining its overall structure. In mesh coarsening, the basis is composed of rigidity graph Laplacian matrices, which are transformed into integer matrices through the addition of randomly generated numbers. Using linear programming, the matrices are optimized to minimize the maximum ratio of off-diagonal to diagonal entries in each matrix. Due to matrix entries being whole numbers, the resulting matrices define compliant meshes whose elements are quad-triangles. In meshes with T triangles, the threshold for compliance in high-order meshes is given by $\frac{2k^2T}{d_{min}}<C_{max}$, where $k$ is the order of the meshes, $d_{min}$ is the minimum value in the diagonal of the matrix, and $C_{max}$ is the optimal cost $C$. In meshes where this threshold is violated, the method selects a subset of edges to remove in order to optimize the size of the resulting graphs while maintaining the overall structure of the meshes. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated in applications, including isogeometric analysis of elastic simulations and topology optimization. In topology optimization, the method is utilized in conjunction with materials to generate optimized structures using a scalar variable; due to matrix entries being whole numbers, the resulting designs are easily interpretable as physical materials. In isogeometric analysis, the method is utilized to determine properties of materials by reducing a highly detailed mesh to a coarser, more manageable form before performing analyses, resulting in improved results due to reduced mesh bias; due to the preservation of mesh structure, the coarsened meshes can be easily transformed to determine properties of fine meshes. In mesh reduction, the method is utilized to speed up simulations by reducing the size of highly structured meshes before performing analyses, resulting in improved performance. The resulting meshes are further utilized in topology optimization to generate detailed graphics of final structures. In graphics, the method is utilized to speed up processing of 3D models by reducing the size of highly detailed meshes in various fields such as visualization, film, and product design. The presented algorithm's performance makes it suitable for demanding applications in the fields of computer-aided design, engineering, and related fields. The results obtained from performing numerical experiments are presented; in these experiments, the method is applied to meshes with the same geometry and topology as the IBM Tetrahedral Mesh Flamingo benchmark, resulting in reduced execution times when compared to linear programming-based generation of coarser meshes. We present a novel approach to deriving quantum field theories for particles in curved spacetimes, relying on the concept of $S$-matrices that remain unchanged under general coordinate transformations. This method reveals the underlying symmetry of the derivations of $S$-matrices, consisting of units with specific spin and charge. For charge-minimal $S$-matrices, we derive tree-level field equations that accurately describe particles interacting in spacetimes that adhere to either Einstein's theory of general relativity or a specific alternative theory. The derived equations for general relativity replicate prior results and offer insights into the behavior of particles in gravitational fields. Furthermore, we present a potential solution to a long-standing inconsistency within quantum gravity that gives rise to an infinite number of negative energy levels, thereby suggesting an alternative $S$-matrix definition. By characterizing the set of possible $S$-matrices, we investigate the possibility of expanding upon Einstein's theory to develop novel gravitational models. Additionally, we demonstrate that $S$-matrices can be utilized to derive the effective field theory of gravitons, providing a new approach to studying quantum gravity and its potential application in modeling particle gravity. By reinterpreting known results in this novel context, we confirm that $S$-matrices for both general relativity and a specific alternative theory contain sufficient information to compute an infinite number of mass spectra of graviton quasiparticles, thereby resolving the aforementioned negative energy levels inconsistency. Notably, the derivations of particle gravity relying on the $S$-matrix formalism are consistent at both classical and quantum levels. Moreover, we demonstrate that $S$-matrices for general relativity and a specific alternative theory are respectively connected to Einstein's theory and a novel effective field theory of quantum gravity, thereby suggesting the existence of a gravitational "fixed point" that might potentially be generalized to other gravity models. The approach to deriving quantum field theories for particles in curved spacetimes, relying on the $S$-matrix concept, offers a fundamental tool for studying quantum gravity, its potential applications extending beyond Einstein's theory. Specifically, the method could be employed to investigate "short-distance" gravity, such as the formation of quantum black holes from particle collisions, in addition to "long-distance" gravity, such as the behavior of gravitons in cosmological settings (e.g., gravitational waves, inflation, and the cosmic string cusp effect). Achieving learning resilience in the presence of corruption is a pressing issue, given its potential to expand the applicability of machine learning methods beyond their original scope. We focus on the concept of corruption-insensitive learning, where a global model is trained on a diverse dataset incorporating various distribution parameters. However, it's often unknown which parameter applies in a given instance. To address this, we introduce the notion of corruption-insensitive learning as a regional problem. This approach necessitates a model that's effective across different distribution parameters within a specified range. We study the benefits and limitations of this method by analyzing its applicable regions and the conditions that minimize or maximize the advantage of this approach. Our empirical findings illustrate the practical implications of regional corruption-insensitive learning, revealing instances where this method is beneficial and not in other scenarios. Furthermore, we propose an optimization technique that enhances the resilience of traditional methods when they're trained globally. Our theoretical and experimental results validate the importance of understanding regional corruption-insensitive learning and its potential applications in practical scenarios. We hope this work contributes to a more in-depth comprehension of the generalization theory and promotes the development of resilient learning algorithms. The code for our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/jiaxiao/Regional_CorruptionInsensitive_Learning. Young stars with intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, affecting planetary mass-loss and distribution. Observing YPG systems is crucial to understanding this process, but the variability of young stars makes consistent long-term monitoring challenging. A recent study of AU Mic observed the star's far-UV radiation patterns over a nearly 20-day period, catching both active and dormant phases. This monitoring revealed that even in quiescent states, low-level far-UV radiation remains present, while intense eruptions produce a rapid increase in this radiation. Calculations suggest that this radiation could alter the AU Mic b and c exoplanetary atmospheres as follows. First, increased heating might lead to a thermal balance that shifts atmospheric features to the blue. Second, photoionization would create a significant ionized layer in the atmosphere of planet b, while ionization in planet c's atmosphere would be less pronounced. Lastly, a high-level far-UV flux would break down carbon dioxide and water vapor molecules in planet c's atmosphere, making its atmospheric composition more vulnerable to changes in the star's activity phase, whereas in planet b, a high-level far-UV flux would discover novel molecular species, such as CO molecular bands, in the star's spectrum. These atmospheric responses to varying levels of stellar radiation may offer a means to differentiate between distinct phases of activity in the YPG system of AU Mic. A superconvection zone is thought to drive the high-level X-ray radiation in AU Mic, and a similar zone may be present in other similarly active YPG systems, potentially leading to a massive atmospheric loss in their planets if not corrected for their star's activity phase. Such a phenomenon could result in a rare low-level far-UV radiation characteristic observed in planet b, and corresponding long-term atmospheric measurements are needed to verify this prediction. A unique monitoring project, the Planet-Host Galaxies Exploring Multidimensional Spectroscopic and Imaging Variability, is designed to investigate and characterize the low-level far-UV radiation in YPG systems. Recently, image generation models have gained traction, with a key focus on creating new images rather than manipulating existing ones. To fill the gap, we present a new category of models that can modify a single view to generate an arbitrary number of unique perspectives. By adopting a conditional diffusion model framework, we succeed in producing high-quality single-view generative models that outperform existing methods based on GANs. When evaluated across various metrics, our proposed model excels in both image quality and semantic consistency, yielding superior results. In addition, we create a new dataset for single-view generative models and demonstrate significant improvements over existing solutions, leading to more reliable and trustworthy outcomes. To ensure model robustness, we rigorously test our approach using multiple metrics and fail-safe techniques to minimize occurrence of unexpected 'black images'. The integration of image normalization in our pipeline effectively mitigates issues related to color consistency and semantic coherence, and we empirically validate the benefits of combined training methods involving supervised and self-supervised approaches on model performance. The source code and trained model parameters for our solution can be found on the repository 'DiffDreamer'. Furthermore, we have prepared a public dataset 'SVGAN' containing high-quality training samples for single-view generative models, which can be accessed through 'SVGAN'. The source code for this supplementary exploration can be found at a different repository 'ARDreamer'. We establish that solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation exhibit Lipschitz robustness, meaning that slight modifications in the initial condition result in correspondingly modified solutions. Furthermore, this robustness is demonstrated to be inherent from the perspective of the Helfrich energy, where we show that the variation in energy is equal to the Lipchitz norm of the initial condition and a real number. This research represents the first instance of robustness being proven for a HT equation without an additional dissipation term. As a consequence of this finding, we discover that without additional dissipation, the Helfrich energy is a well-defined and conservative quantity. We also prove the existence of global solutions for the HT equation within a specific space where the initial condition is Lipschitz and provide an estimate of the Lipchitz norm based on the Helfrich energy. Moreover, through the development of a new method inspired by recent work on interface dynamics, we show that the HT equation can be classified as a Hamiltonian system possessing robust solutions and a universal dissipation estimate in relation to the Lipchitz norm and energy. This innovative approach is expected to yield significant advancements in the study of interface dynamics in the future. Specifically, specific scenarios such as the formation of shocks from smooth initial conditions, the behavior at infinity in periodic domains, and the characteristics of traveling waves are all set to be explored in upcomng research. We leverage the power of a median-based normalization framework, where the length of synthetic speech is determined by the difference between an original and a medians-calculated utterance. Deep learning-based MIMO frameworks currently primarily rely on a straightforward
summing up of distinct features generated by individual CNNs through channel
expansion. To enhance interaction between these features, our study investigates
the effectiveness of exchanging features during the middle stage. To achieve this,
we introduce a novel MIMO architecture called the Collaborative MIMO network,
where alternate unit combinations are allowed for every CNN within the middle
layer. By doing so, this adaptation encourages collaborative learning among the
networks and facilitates the sharing of features at an earlier stage, allowing
for greater control over the passage of information between networks. Our
experiments with image classification and object detection have demonstrated the
superior performance of our proposed MIMO architecture, with achievement rates
comparable to or even superior to the current best performance, with reduced
computational requirements. Our code can be found at the repository link below,

To ensure precise movement and prevent damage, industrial robots require accurate position feedback systems. Despite the high precision of traditional position sensors, in practice, significant position errors can occur due to factors such as wear and tear in the sensors or drive systems. Since most robots operate within a two-dimensional or three-dimensional workspace with a relatively flat surface, a position error compensation method using supplementary sensors has been developed. By utilizing supplementary sensors like cameras or other position tracking devices, the proposed method calculates and compensates for end effector position errors caused by position sensor inaccuracies at each joint. To achieve this, a novel method for calculating the tangent vector of the joint axis has been developed using only joint angle data from the faulty sensor, and a robust algorithm for estimating the three-dimensional pose of the end effector from the perceived image has been created using only binary data from cameras. By incorporating these two new technologies into general robot control methods, more accurate movement is possible with reduced vibration, even in the presence of position sensor inaccuracies. Results from actual experiments using a two and a half axis robot with artificially introduced position errors demonstrate the effectiveness of this solution. With position errors of up to 1.7 times the resolution of the position sensor, accurate final position was achieved within 0.8 mm. Key to this success was the adoption of a regulation method based on flatness, allowing for uncomplicated integration of the position error into the planned movement. Furthermore, through the incorporation of the actual position error into the planned movement, complete position accuracy is achieved upon completion of movement, provided that actuator movement remains within the specified range. A novel approach for modeling the interaction between molecules and condensed phases is developed, where the system's free energy is split between two regions: a finite cluster of molecules that overlap with a continuum phase, and a continuum grand canonical reservoir that provides thermal equilibrium. The two regions' grand potential connections are calculated through two distinct sets of variational coordinates, one optimized at the atomic level for the cluster and the other at the grid level for the continuum. Upon convergence, the two potentials are set equal, yielding the total free energy of the system. Given that standard optimization techniques cannot be used concurrently due to differing coordinate spaces, a specialized procedure for calculating the free energy gradients and updating the positions of the floating region is developed instead. The effectiveness of this method in generating accurate binding curves for molecules interacting with water and carbon dioxide has been demonstrated through comparison with existing theoretical and experimental results. It has also been successfully extended to the study of peptide-helix unbinding transitions, peptoid $\beta$-sheet dissolution, and the binding of CO2 to a specific protein, allowing for the quantitative explanation of recently collected experimental data. Such approach opens up the possibility of modeling complex condensate-molecule interactions that cannot be explained by existing theoretical and computational models, including the binding of carbon dioxide to respiration proteins, where experimental data is already available. The developed code for this method can be easily accessed through public donation with the accompanying demonstration files included in the GitHub repository. In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the respective vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of a defined size is a crucial problem, especially when parameterized, which has applications across various domains. We examine the problem of determining whether a graph has a resolving set of a specified size k or smaller. By employing feedback vertex sets and feedback vertex groups, which are connected to the problem, we obtain a complex but structured recursive analysis. We also investigate the problem bounded below by the number of vertices in the largest component. Our results include a multi-component generalisation, showing that the problem remains hard, but we can reduce the complexity with selective pruning of the search space, which is defined via a gauge function. We also prove that the (k + 1)th power of any connected graph has a resolving set of size one less than the number of vertices, which is a simpler method but still applies across disconnected graphs. Furthermore, the problem of verifying whether the minimum size of a resolving set is less than a defined number, k, is a #P1-complete problem. This, along with our other findings, indicates that the problem of determining whether a graph has a resolving set of a specified size is a complex, highly computable function, which is exceptional in the graph problem space. We outline open issues related to graph resolving sets. Our study was performed to contribute to the development of efficient algorithms for graph and graph-related problems, particularly those that are parameterised in accordance with a specified metric attribute. We aim to further this goal within the graph and graph problem spaces, which ultimately benefits the field of comphex analysis and utility studies. In the process, we hope to facilitate contributions towards efficient algorithms for graph-related problems and ultimately resolve the long-standing open issue of determining whether a graph has a resolving set of a specified size. We also provide an additional contribution, a multi-component generalisation, which generalises our monolithic findings and enhances the overall understanding of the determining process. This article offers an algorithm that can calculate the genus of a weighted graph in almost polynomial time, making it a solution to a previously opened problem. The method involves assigning weights to the graph's edges based on their lengths and using a combination of Frankl-Winkler-West graphs and Harer's genus formula to obtain an approximation of the genus. The accuracy of this approximation can be adjusted by changing a specific parameter. Additionally, this algorithm can be used in some polynomial-time graph embedding procedures. The time complexity of this algorithm is tied to the number of variables in a related integer programming problem, which can be solved using a combination of the Ellipsoid algorithm and Harer's formula. Specifically, the discussion proposes two possible modifications: one could achieve an almost logarithmic increase in time complexity by utilizing a combination of the Harar-Jeronsky algorithms and 2-approximation of the surface's Euler characteristic, and another could reach a quadratic time complexity using a method of edge length counting. The adaptive spectral Koopman operator technique is a data-driven approach that uses the Koopman operator to discover the underlying dynamics of complex systems. Although the standard AKO operator technique works well for most problems with 2 to 3 intrinsic dimensions, it faces challenges with systems having more than 3 intrinsic dimensions. To address these limitations, a new approach called sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral Koopman operator technique has been developed to expand the applicability of AKO to such systems. The proposed approach is tested on the reduced three-dimensional Lorenz model and the unforced vortex flow. Compared to the standard AKO operator technique, it can handle systems with more than 3 intrinsic dimensions. Additionally, the proposed approach requires significantly fewer basis functions from $O(N^3)$ to approximately $N^2$, making it more computationally efficient by a factor of almost two. As such, it is well-suited for powering applications involving very large data sets. Finally, the proposed approach is shown to largely preserve the strengths of the standard AKO operator technique such as increased accuracy, improved adaptability, and robust Koopman operator discretization. To support these findings, a publicly available Python code of the proposed approach is provided. Several numerical examples are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed approach. Ultimately, the proposed approach provides a promising direction for future research on discovering the underlying dynamics of complex systems. The proposed approach can be viewed via a video demonstration at the provided URL. Machine learning models can mimic the way humans learn, but the reverse is less clear: can humans learn like the models? To address this, we investigated how people learn in scenarios similar to those studied in the brain, such as the mesolimbic dopamine system. The setting involved a basic task where animals associate actions with rewards in probabilistic conditions. We applied various learning techniques, including a conventional, an optimal, and several suboptimal variation of model-free Q-learning algorithms. The results showed that the suboptimal models share characteristics with human learning when faced with challenging tasks, while the optimal model does not. Notably, the suboptimal models rely on a concept known as off-policy violation, which the brain also utilizes. The off-policy violation refers to a situation where action values are estimated based on a policy that is different from the one being used. The presence of off-policy violation in these models correlates with human learning and the activity of the midbrain, pointing to its potential as an integral component of human learning processes. The study highlights the significance of optimizing machine learning algorithms to better understand the underlying brain mechanisms and their relevance to more effective learning techniques. The findings also support the use of empirical measures such as violation of off-policy evaluation as indicators of the efficacy of reinforcement learning methods, especially those that are human-compatible. Ultimately, the results point to the possibility of developing improved learning algorithms not only for computers but also for humans. The objective of collective autonomy is to facilitate cooperative endeavors among
agent clusters that are capable of autonomous decision-making. This theory has gained
preliminary attention in the fields of multi-robotic systems and autonomous vehicles. 
However, existing interactive methods are somewhat restricted. This paper proposes a
novel collection of algorithms and protocols for collective autonomy, which addresses
two key control challenges: multi-robotic system tracking and trajectory planning. 
These algorithms are underpinned by a theoretical framework incorporating
autonomously evolving behavior networks that are anchored on a cognitive map. 
Such behavior networks dynamically organize around a set of predefined cognitive 
landmarks, representing Robotic System Objectives. Also presented is a distributed
communication protocol, employing Time Delay Protocol, that facilitates agents to 
be aware of fellow agents' behavioral states, thus enabling informed decision-making. 
Multiple simulations and real-world experiments validate the proposed theories, 
demonstrating several scenarios, including tracking and trajectory planning around a 
set of moving cognitive landmarks. This research successfully integrates the theories 
of collective autonomy and behavior networking, showing their potential to tackle the 
control challenges of large-scale robotic systems. 
Furthermore, the framework is flexible, allowing users to customize the behavior 
networks in line with specific application requirements. 
This research contributes a comprehensive theoretical framework for collective 
autonomy, accompanied by various algorithms and protocols that can be applied in 
future robotic system designs.

This research is applicable in a broad spectrum of robotic systems, including those 
equipped with autonomous flight capabilities. 
Experimental testing of these ideas has shown promising results, with support from 
several technological demonstrations. 
One notable example is the successful navigation of the robotic system around a set of 
moving markers, albeit the cognitive map contained errors. 
Also, an experimental trial showed that the behavior network could adapt to a set of 
moving markers, without any prior knowledge of the markers' states or trajectories. 
These technological advancements have the potential to pave the way for the 
development of advanced autonomous systems, capable of cooperating in cohesive 
agent clusters.

In contextual named entity recovery, models are trained to predict entity names based on surrounding text, with results evaluated using a metric that ranks output entities according to their relevance to the actual entities. However, this approach can be problematic, as it treats all completed entities equally, regardless of their importance. To address this issue, our method employs an entity importance metric in conjunction with the standard relevance metric, and introduces a feedback mechanism that adjusts learning to emphasize shorter, more critical text spans containing key entities. Experiments demonstrate that targeting these shorter spans leads to substantial gains in entity recovery and overall F1 performance. Moreover, our findings suggest that incorporating the importance of recovered entities can enhance the accuracy of single-entity evaluation and provide more insightful insights. To facilitate future research, our code and data are openly available on our GitHub repository. This study examines why displaying multiple views of the same data simultaneously can be advantageous, while also identifying scenarios in which a single view is sufficient. Utilizing various datasets, we compare systems that display the complete data spectrum alongside systems displaying only a single view, finding that users prefer the former. To better comprehend user preferences, we conducted interviews and discovered that users appreciate the ability to easily access and compare different data views without needing additional selections. However, users also expressed difficulties in navigating the extra spectrum and associated overlays. Based on these findings, we propose the Spectral Navigation Framework, aiming to strike a balance between offering comprehensive data exploration and minimizing distractions and overload. The proposed framework is then put to a test through a remote usability study, demonstrating its effectiveness in streamlining data exploration and reducing user frustration. Ultimately, our approach is anticipated to inspire the design of systems capable of handling complex, screen-based explorations of various data types. A detailed analytical theory of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states relies on the electron spin function within a localized magnetic impurity and its surrounding conducting lead. Contrary to conventional depiction of YSR states as equally propagating forward and backward, we establish that their properties are entirely determined by the initial conditions and the relativistic Dirac equation governing the lead electrons must be taken into account. Our calculation indicates that both forward and reflective probabilities are insignificant in the non-relativistic scenario but become considerable in the relativistic case. We analyze dimer states comprising two Mn atoms on a 110 Nb surface using both theoretical and experimental methods. Our analysis demonstrates that accounting for the relativistic effect in YSR states is essential for correctly interpreting experimental results. Furthermore, evaluating the spin polarization of YSR states is carried out employing both the initial conditions of electron scattering and the magnetic field, and our calculations show that the polarization may be influenced by the initial conditions and magnetic field in opposite directions. Our predictions also reveal that the yield of Andreev states can facilitate the detection of ultra-small magnetic fields. Additionally, the properties of spin-polarized quasi-surface states generated by Mn dimer states are explored and found to be distinguishable from ordinary Yu--Shiba states produced by a single magnetic impurity. Our calculations of quasi-surface states produced by the radial symmetry of a dimer's wave function are also presented. In conclusion, the properties of a dimer's wave function containing two sites are found to exhibit pseudo-periodicity, and this phenomenon is independent of relativistic effects, whereas the characteristics produced by the spin function exhibit periodicity similar to that of a single impurity. Experimental data from x-ray absorption near-edge spectra (XANES) is often analyzed through calculations based on a quantum mechanical approach, utilizing electron groups derived from molecular orbital theory. Although guidelines for assessing the accuracy of these calculations exist, assessing the accuracy of individual calculations and identifying potential issues with divergent results from multiple calculations is often difficult. In high-intensity x-ray absorption spectra that show nonlinear effects, determining the initial electronic state of the target molecule or particle is also challenging. This work proposes a framework for quantifying the computational uncertainty associated with these calculations and selecting the most reliable results among a set of predictions. The framework's reliability estimates are based on metrics that quantify the alignment between experimental and computational data, as well as the consistency of the computational model with its own inherent principles. We apply this framework to a case study investigating the nonlinear XANES of a simple anion exchange compound that undergoes a significant structural change in the presence of intense x-ray radiation. This study reveals that the electron group approach can provide reliable results for linear and non-linear x-ray absorption spectra, but requires careful validation and post-processing to achieve accurate non-linear outcomes. The analysis also shows the significant structural transformation induced by intense x-rays can occur within a very short time frame. This work proposes a general approach for identifying and addressing potential issues with divergent models derived from the same basic methodology. The framework's flexibility and potential applicability to a wide range of applications make it a useful tool for the x-ray community. Furthermore, the study reveals that the structural transformation observed in the compound under intense x-rays occurs on a very fast timescale of tens to hundreds of femtoseconds. This observation suggests that scanning nonlinear XANES (SNXANES) can serve as a new method for detecting and studying fast structural changes in molecules and materials. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an essential component in clinical assessment. Despite achieving good results with well-established models, recent approaches question whether "continual learning" or starting over from scratch leads to better outcomes. To answer this, we developed multiple training strategies for the task, incorporating a new method called "semi-supervised incremental learning" that builds on existing knowledge. Our experiments focused on comparing these approaches with a baseline that re-trains the model from scratch on the entire original dataset. The results showed that our continuous learning strategies performed better than the baseline, with the "semi-supervised incremental learning" method demonstrating superior outcomes to other continuous learning methods. Moreover, the "semi-supervised incremental learning" method also performed favourably when compared to a model that re-trains from scratch on the entire dataset. Ultimately, our findings highlight that even in a well-established task like MS lesion segmentation, using existing knowledge effectively can enhance performance. reduce overfitting in image classification tasks by minimizing the contrast between
different image characteristics. The MC layer in the network forces pixels with high
similarities to have similar colors, resulting in a more uniform distribution of
values across images, which reduces overfitting by eliminating redundant pixel
information and and and and promoting generalizable pattern extraction through
novel and distinct features. The MC loss can be incorporated into existing
training frameworks and is demonstrated to yield comparable results with
state-of-the-art techniques on popular datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet).

large-scale training. Our work also provides theoretical insights into MC loss's role
in reducing overfitting through increased pixel heterogeneity and increased
interpixel correlations. The MC loss code is available at https://github.com/boyan-yang/Manic-Contrast. The IC dataset is available at https://boyan-yang.github.io/Manic-Contrast.   1. Clarifies the concept of model error. 
  2. Distinguishes between dynamic and parametric errors in partial and complete models.
  3. Reveals that some errors are resolved by enhancing model details, whereas others become evident with higher model complexity.
  4 Provides a framework for quantifying and locating model errors using the manifold structure of smooth dynamical systems.
  A crucial algorithm has also been created for finding the error manifold located beyond a given model's reach. This approach has been applied to a class of models called quadratic systems, allowing for a quantitative assessment of errors in this specific model class. Additionally, we demonstrate that some well-established numerical methods for solving two-form nonlinear systems introduce significant errors in their solutions that can only be rectified by enhancing model details. Finally, we illustrate the practical application of this framework by incorporating the error structure in a neural network designed to identify quadratic system parameters. This neural network, built with the Kantorovich's 2-Sphere geometry, exhibits superior performance and robustness in the face of perturbations not encountered during training. One of the key benefits of this approach is that it remains effective even when challenged with unforeseen perturbations during production. Such resilience is a critical attribute for autonomous AI operators, ensuring that models remain reliable across a wide range of untested environments. The presented methodology and associated algorithms for model evaluation and parameter identification have far-reaching implications and can be adapted for use in various applications. Furthermore, this work provides a methodological foundation for creating Machine Intelligence designed to augment and operate within theoretical and computational frameworks in a safe and trustworthy manner. This adapter strategy, successfully tested with modified versions of the BART model, yielded promising results across various sets of unique tokens, with the results appearing in the paper. As a result, this technique could find applications in scenarios such as tokenization for programming languages and translation. Machine learning model performance often benefits from set augmentation techniques that boost training flexibility. A proposed low-contextual embedding network, quantization and embedding (QnA), uses a unique binary encoding method to create set embeddings with minimal contextual interplay, preserving original element identities. By contrast, a best-effort contextual embedding method was developed for comparison purposes. Evaluation of QnA using contextual and non-contextual benchmark tasks reveals that its lack of contextual interplay leads to improved performance compared to the contextual approach, particularly in data retrieval, password generation, and face recognition tasks with the MNIST dataset. Interestingly, combining QnA with the best-effort contextual embedding yielded even more impressive results, underscoring the benefits of combining set augmentation strategies with diverse design principles. The study's open-source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/aachagard/QnA for further research. A comprehensive analysis is provided in the published paper. The term 'quantulation' is introduced to distinguish QnA's approach from quantitative methods, as well as from other contextual embedding techniques. Furthermore, a novel dataset was created for the face recognition benchmark, the '4digit digits with background' dataset, which is also hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/aachagard/QnA. The study was originally published in the Journal of Advanced Computational Intelligence (JACI) in 2021, volume 2021. Following the 2021 publication, multiple research papers based on the study were published in conferences in 2022. One of the research papers received a Best Paper Award at the I2CS 2022 conference. The study was presented at multiple conferences, including MDKDCs in 2021 and I2CS in 2022. A presentation based on the study was also delivered at the Department of Computational Logic at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam in 2021 as part of a course on fundamental machine learning topics. Moreover, a comprehensive research paper on the study is currently in press and will be published in the Journal of Systems and Software in 2023. A preliminary version of this paper was presented at the conference AAAData in 2021. A comprehensive doctoral dissertation based on the study was defended at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam in 2022. Following the completion of the research, a data science challenge was hosted by the data science company Digital Matter at least once in 2022, in which a unique binary encoding submission by the author was a top three finisher across all teams in the challenge

Our study examines the relationship between thermodynamics and dynamics in polymer liquids that exhibit glass-like behavior. By utilizing collective mode densities derived from neutron spin echo measurements, we have developed a method to calculate the thermal average of the thermodynamic factor and dynamic structure factor. These calculations confirm the presence of a significant correlation between the material's thermodynamic properties and high-frequency dynamics. Notably, this correlation is particularly strong when the system is close to the onset of glassy behavior. These findings enable us to assess the impact of thermal fluctuations on the dynamics of the glassy transition. Moreover, we have found that the thermodynamic factor can drive changes in the material's high-frequency dynamics, leading to two distinct transition scenarios: (1) two-step freezing, where a initial decrease in collective mode density is followed by a more pronounced slowdown; and (2) structural relaxation in a quasi-elastico state, characterized by an abrupt slowdown following a quasi-solid period. Overall, our results emphasize the importance of considering collective modes in understanding the glassy transition and further motivate the development of new experimental techniques to investigate these modes and the material's high-frequency dynamics. Lastly, our work also highlights the significance of neutron spin echo spectroscopy in exploring the material's collective behavior. Further investigation is recommended to clarify the dynamic instability in a certain state observed during a cooling process. If confirmed, this could mark the onset of a unique type of dynamical free volume driven by the material's high-frequency collective modes. A more in-depth theoretical analysis is needed to fully explore the implications of these findings. The essential concepts appear to involve a dynamic free volume related to the material's high-frequency collective modes, support for a quasi-elastico state hypothesis, and an extension of the geometric constraints model that can account for the material's high-frequency dynamics. Due to the current limitations in our understanding, additional experimental work is necessary to fully investigate the material's high-frequency dynamics and states observed during a cooling process. Furthermore, our results suggest that further investigation of this material's high-frequency dynamics and states observed during a cooling process in various glass-forming materials could lead to a deeper understanding of the relationship between thermodynamics and dynamics in these systems. In particular, it appears that the material's high-frequency dynamics could play a more significant role than previously thought in forming the configurations that contribute to its glassy transition. If this is the case, then the study of this type of dynamics could reveal new and crucial information that could lead to a deeper understanding of the material's glassy transition and further hypotheses for further investigation.

Motivated by this idea, we've developed a novel approach that mimics children's language development and can be used in transformer-based language models to generate human-like text. Our method relies on the idea that naturally occurring sentences may be unacceptable as children learn to speak, and we've designed a model that can analyze sentences based on their appropriateness in the context of their length and composition. Our experiments show that this approach yields benefits in several areas, including the quality of generated text, its coherence, and overall understanding. Additionally, our results indicate that our model is more relatable to child language development patterns than previous algorithms, and it's also more resistant to manipulations that artificially boost the coherence of generated text. Our source code and explanations are available for review. Overall, this study demonstrates that transformer-based language models can be improved by processing sentences as if they're being rejected, and this idea aligns with child language development principles. When analyzing generating models, researchers commonly use language models as a point of comparison. However, instead of merely comparing model outputs, a novel technique examines not only the models' behavior but also how humans interpret it. A recent study introduces the concept of "look-ahead focus" to better comprehend generating models from a human perspective. This approach investigates the visual arrangement of text and the sequential unfolding of a written sentence, modeling human reading habits and eye movement patterns. Focusing specifically on the FFP module, this investigation demonstrates that incorporating look-ahead focus into translation tasks enhances both the quality and clarity of machine-generated reports when compared to baseline models. Moreover, analysis of the obtained data suggests that benefitting from human-like focus patterns depends on the specific nature of the task in question. Training models with a focus on the sequence of ideas rather than individual words may be particularly advantageous in complex environments with many distractors. On the other hand, tasks involving explicit sentence construction may profit from models adopting a more expanded focus spanning multiple words. Overall, exploring machine interpretability through the lens of human visual processing appears to be a promising area of research, and subsequent studies are encouraged to apply this concept to a range of generating models, employing comparable methods of analysis. A proposed open-source toolkit, developed using the transformer decoder model, facilitates replication and extension of these experimental findings. Although great progress has been made, existing models are often hindered by their rigid structure, forcing all components to contribute equally regardless of their unique importance. In response, we introduce the TS2-Net structure, comprising a flexible and iterative token-shifting process to focus on crucial tokens and a selection transformer layer to distill image and text embeddings into a unified, discriminative space. Our experiments show that TS2-Net outperforms existing models on text-retrieval tasks, particularly in single-image and text-clips with text-clips' longer token sequences. Furthermore, we establish a new text-clips retrieval dataset, called TCR-10K, consisting of 10,000 pairs of 10-frame clips and labels. Our selection of tokens from text-clips is autolumosely controlled by image labels, ensuring sets of clips with uniform relevance. The TS2-Net's superior performance on this dataset significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art averages by 6.0 and 5.7 points. Notably, we find that specific tokens within the image and text sequences hold crucial information for retrieval, evident in the gradual increase in their relative importance as the length of the sequences grows. Current research mainly focuses on detecting disturbances caused by wireless communication with a single sensor, whereas our work investigates interference from multiple wireless transmission protocols, utilizing data collected using electromagnetic sensors. Given the diverse patterns of interference generated by various protocols, employing a multi-label classifier is necessary to identify the underlying transmission protocol causing the disturbance. In this research, we assess the efficacy of Convolutional Neural Networks as interference detectors, comparing their performance with other machine learning methods like Recurrent Neural Networks and the Fast Fourier Transform. Experimental results validate the superior performance of CNNs, achieving an average accuracy of over 90% in multiple testing scenarios. With our proposed approach, it is possible to automatically identify the source of interference without manual intervention, thus facilitating real-time interference analysis and diagnosis. To the best knowledge of our team, this is the first study to explore the application of CNNs for multi-label disturbance detection in Wireless Sensor Networks.
