A groundbreaking, Monte Carlo-based event generator, KKMCee, has been developed for creating multi-photon events involving electron/muon and quark pairs. This innovative tool not only leverages the original KKMC code but also integrates the Monte Carlo generator MEPP3C for enhanced functionality. Several underlying matrix-element topologies have been incorporated, including one-photon and dark-photon decays of heavy particles and their counterparts. Furthermore, KKMCee is capable of utilizing parton-shower interfaces from HERWIG, SHERPA, and PYTHIA to offer a comprehensive solution for simulating lepton collider environments. This tool's functionality is exemplified through its application in three benchmark scenarios. Specifically, KKMCee is used to study the production of $Z\gamma$ pairs via the lightest Kaluza-Klein Z' boson at the proposed ILC and CLIC colliders as well as the creation of $e+e+\gamma$ events for $\gamma$ and dark-photon decays of the Z' boson at CLIC. Moreover, we have included the generation of $qq\,\bar{q}\,\bar{q}$ events, enabling the simulation of effective photon exchange between initial-state particles even in the absence of final-state photons. This functionality is particularly evident in the simulation of $\gamma+\gamma$ + jets events at LHC/e$^+$e$^-$ colliders, where LHC's hadronic activity can be generated through initial-state photon interactions. Finally, our tool is capable of simulating not only standard QED corrections but also non-standard ones, such as those mediated by neutral gauge bosons with trilinear couplings to photons and leptons as well as those mediated by axion-like particles with trilinear couplings to photons, leptons, and quarks. This functionality is specifically exemplified in the simulation of $\gamma+\gamma$ + jets events for the discovery potential of the neutral vector boson Z'$ between the $\gamma Z'$ and $\gamma\,\gamma Z'$ channels. This research paper investigates a set of Nirenberg equations on half-spheres with non-positive curvature in high dimensions via blow-up techniques from minimal solutions. These equations can be expressed as $S^1$-invariant conditions applied to a standard half-sphere equation, resulting in the solution of an ordinary differential equation. The study demonstrates that for dimensions $n \geq 9$, minimal solutions of these equations exhibit non-trivial behavior, specifically they do not simplify to the standard sphere scenario via blow-up. In contrast, previous studies showed that for dimensions $n \leq 8$, solutions of these equations simplify to the standard sphere scenario via blow-up. Building upon this knowledge, the researchers aim to explore possible connections between the resolved conjecture and an issue of global Nirenberg equations, specifically whether all minimal solutions of these equations simplify to the standard sphere scenario when $m = 1$. Restricted Reinforcement Learning focuses on finding efficient algorithms for tasks that require limited computational resources, including both on-policy and off-policy models. This concept is closely related to the concept of adversarial training, where we seek an optimal balance between following an optimal policy and a predictive model being misled by the learner's suboptimal policies. The Restricted Reinforcement Learning framework covers various scenarios, such as off-policy learning with finite horizons, when the horizon is unknown or when the policy is constrained. Off-policy learning in RL problems with rewards is another area of study within this framework. The following topics are investigated: learning an optimal reward function under limited conditions; inverse problems that involve deriving a low implementation cost policy from a given reward function; and RL problems with a limited number of steps, requiring a low computational effort and off-policy learning. The development of theoretical limitations has been considered in each of these areas. The aim of this study is to provide an in-depth review of the progress made in Restricted Reinforcement Learning, highlighting the different approaches taken by the community. The core restriction types examined in this review are adversarial training, limited data, limited computational resources, the spectral radius, and switches. The general structure of the review is as follows. The introduction covers the background necessary to enter the topic, while part one focuses on off-policy learning, its subtypes, and the issues related to various horizon lengths. Part two explores RL problems with reward functions, including the recovery of the optimal reward function and inverse RL problems. The final section presents the RL problems with a limited number of steps, highlighting the trade-offs involved in off-policy learning. The conclusion follows the structure of the introduction, now focusing on the discussion section. The appendices are dedicated to the detailed presentation of the theorems related to the different topics. The main contribution of this review is the comprehensive aggregation of the different approaches to Restricted Reinforcement Learning, the theoretical examination of their limitations, and the comparison of the existing methods. The community is encouraged to participate in further research, including experimental evaluations, the development of new algorithms, and the relaxation or removal of the various types of restrictions. The list of open problems related to the different topics is also presented. The community is invited to participate in their resolution. The final paragraph presents some potential future research directions inspired by the various topics. The detailed list of the sources cited in this review is presented at the very end. The source code of some of the discussed results can be found at https://github.com/jderma19/RRLsurvey.

The experiments encompass various configurations of a Multi-Layer Perceptron and Graph Neural Network, employing Contamination as the corruption data type to generate one-hot additional labels. The outcomes show that a substantial portion of the error is attributed to the edge count rather than node count, and the adaptation of a masking function to a network's architecture is feasible through a reinforcement learning training method. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Profane11/RL-Masking-Graph-Neural-Network. The CEM-GNN 1.0 dataset is hosted at https://www.dropbox.com/s/l5q4i3k0kvk9mw0/cem-gnn-1.0.zip. The process of aligning star catalogues faces challenges due to random and systematic errors in the measurement of stellar positions and magnitudes. For the majority of the catalogues, photometric data are available but are often disregarded due to the high expense of utilizing this information effectively. Conversely, using positional data are relatively inexpensive but are often susceptible to large systematic errors. By incorporating the relationships between positional and photometric data, it's possible to obtain more accurate information than what positional data alone can provide, ultimately yielding better alignment. A inexpensive method known as source colour matching is presented to utilize supplementary photometric data for the alignment of stellar catalogues. The technique relies on calculating the correlation between the mean magnitudes (in various bands) and positional offsets of stellar pairs, allowing for the mitigation of systematic errors through comparison with simulations. Successfully tested on the Gaia TRGB sample, the algorithm is then applied to the alignment of the Gaia DR2 and PMSL catalogs. Although source colour matching incurs some noise from the photometric data, it's capable of providing accurate alignment at a lower cost than using the DR2's astrometry. Moreover, incorporating the information from all three photometric bands leads to a slight improvement in the accuracy of the alignment, with the added benefit of no loss in precision. As data from multiple photometric bands are capable of suppressing random errors to a greater extent than positional data, utilizing these bands in the alignment process is shown to yield comparable results to using the DR2's astrometry. A future prospective is presented where the algorithm could be capable of producing highly accurate alignment at a marginally higher computational expense than what is required with current methods. At this point, the main constraint on the accuracy of the alignment would shift from algorithmic considerations to physical limitations inherent to the alignment technique. A detailed investigation of the technical limitations associated with this alignment technique is carried out in a companion article. Results obtained from the analysis suggest the maximum theoretical errors in the alignment of astrometric-only and DR2-based astrometry-and-photometry alignments are roughly equivalent ($0.18^{+0.22}_{-0.16}$ milliarcseconds per second). Nonetheless, incorporating the information from all three photometric bands yields a slightly more accurate alignment ($0.170^{+0.222}_{-0.156}$ milliarcseconds per second) and lays the groundwork for achieving even higher levels of accuracy than what is currently achievable with current technological limitations. In this paper, we explore minimal vertex sets in infinite hypergraphs and examine the topological properties of such sets when the hypergraph's edges are countable. In contrast, hypergraphs with dense edge monochromatic subsets yield a contrasting scenario with finite and left dense hypergraphs. Key findings include proof that a minimal vertex set in a infinite hypergraph cannot have a monochromatic edge, and a polynomial relation between the number of vertices and edges in another type of hypergraph. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of dense minimal vertex sets in certain infinite hypergraphs but show that this is not possible for all types of hypergraphs. Lastly, we show that a known type of hypergraph containing a minimal vertex set that is dense with respect to a particular family of sets does not necessarily imply the existence of such a set in another type of hypergraph. Moreover, we derive a condition under which an infinite hypergraph containing a minimal vertex set that is dense with respect to a family of sets $W$ also contains a minimal vertex set that is universally dense with respect to a family of sets $U$. It is then shown that an infinite family of sets $F_i$ can be constructed such that for any set $W$ and family of sets $U$, an $F_i$ can be found where an infinite edge monochromatic dense minimal vertex set in a hypergraph whose edges are $F_i$ does not belong to $W$ but is universally dense with respect to $U$. Ultimately, we derive a condition under which an infinite hypergraph containing a dense minimal vertex set that is dense with respect to a family of sets $W$ also contains a dense minimal vertex set that is universally dense with respect to a family of sets $U$. A particular type of hypergraph whose dense minimal vertex sets belong to a family of sets $W$ and are universally dense with respect to a family of sets $U$ can be constructed such that an infinite edge monochromatic dense minimal vertex set in the hypergraph does not belong to $W$ but is universally dense with respect to $U$. Despite existing approaches to visualizing ontology structures, they are largely inadequate for hierarchical aspects and do not effectively convey non-hierarchical connections between entities. To address this limitation, we have developed an innovative, interactive visualization method called OntoPlot, which effectively illustrates both hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships in ontologies in a comprehensive and easy-to-understand manner. A case study demonstrating OntoPlot's application to the extensive BioloMART oncology ontology highlights its capabilities and potential value in similar complex domain models. By facilitating visualizations of all data model components, OntoPlot provides an alternative to existing visualization styles and offers new possibilities for understanding large ontologies. Furthermore, we consider OntoPlot a valuable resource for creating informative visual presentations of ontologies in educational settings. As such, we intend to utilize it as a pedagogical example in ontology education, emphasizing the importance of visual representation. A cutting-edge deep learning approach, specifically end-to-end automatic speech transcription, has recently gained popularity but is hindered by high data annotation costs.  Semi-supervised learning, however, offers potential solutions by utilizing large amounts of unlabelled data. This research explores the application of inter-domain penalty methods and CycleGAN cycle consistency technique to enhance semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech transcription.  Experimentation on the WSJ-Dataset indicates that the integration of inter-domain penalty and these two techniques significantly surpass the performance of a fully supervised model and demonstrate compelling transcription quality with as little as 5000 labelled samples when paired with a suitable set of unlabelled data. This advancement is attributed to the incorporation of these techniques which address different challenges in end-to-end automatic speech transcription such as maintaining speech structure and vocal quality. Our findings suggest that the utilization of inter-domain penalty techniques complement the effectiveness of CycleGAN and other cycle consistency techniques. Furthermore, we have made our source code available on GitHub for the benefit of the research community.  In particular, we have demonstrated the importance of choosing an optimal unlabelled dataset in an effective inter-domain penalty. This finding is unlikely to be unique to end-to-end automatic speech transcription and may likely be applicable to other areas of speech processing as well. Our research suggests that the utilization of datasets, which excel in the particular task at hand but lack in others, enhances the effectiveness of inter-domain penalty techniques. This knowledge can aid in the design of future speech processing datasets for the training of end-to-end models with improved transcription quality and robustness. Our research has the potential to be extended to other areas of speech processing as well. Our work is accompanied by a video presentation. We introduce a sophisticated artificial intelligence concept known as Profound Self-governing Intelligent Multipurpose Deduction (PSIMD). Unlike conventional artificial intelligences that adhere to predetermined programs, PSIMD operates under a more advanced self-managing framework. Within the PSIMD framework, a type of system called Proved Formations, where multiple interconnected logical statements interact and influence one another, are used to facilitate logical reasoning and achieve complex objectives. The interaction between these logical statements is based on the verification of their collective implications. As such, the system inherently maintains consistency without requiring external supervision. Furthermore, we have developed an innovative solution to facilitate logical reasoning within time constraints. This solution, based on the idea of 'root focus', quickly identifies the most relevant subsets of statements and associates them with their corresponding values within the formation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the PSIMD framework through its implementation in a robot navigation scenario, where it is utilized to establish a cohesive formation of points of interest. The robot successfully achieves its objective by navigating through a virtual environment in line with the formed structure. Our theoretical investigation examines how the Soret effect, which is driven by temperature gradients in a mixture of soft molecules, depends on their internal freedom to move. This flexibility is influenced by the Soret amplitude and directionality; as a result, we can predict Soret behavior in systems that allow for internal motion. Two specific scenarios of internal movement are simulated: rotational motion within asymmetrical molecules and vibrational oscillations in a two-state system. In both cases, our findings show that the internal flexibility significantly affects the Soret effect, leading to a change in amplitude and direction. This influence is particularly noticeable at high concentrations, where the internal movement interacts strongly with the overall flow. Our research also opens up the possibility of controlling Soret behavior in these systems by adjusting their internal freedom to move. This could provide valuable insights into the thermal self-dimming phenomenon in corneas and the separation of mixtures based on differential diffusion. Additionally, our findings may contribute to a deeper understanding of biological and soft-matter systems. Such systems can be utilized as thermal engines or for molecular sorting in various applications. By balancing entropy and energy, our theoretical framework successfully explains the observed behavior in these systems. This framework is founded on the principles of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and provides a method for evaluating temperature gradients in systems that, like oil and water, exhibit negative Soret coefficients. This knowledge can be applied to a wide range of systems that are susceptible to non-equilibrium self-diffusion. Moreover, by identifying a thermal driving force, our analysis demonstrates that the Soret effect contributes to the entropy of systems that are capable of diffusional separation. This contribution to the entropy of these systems is directly proportional to their order parameter and can be calculated using a convenient parameterization. This knowledge may be useful in various applications, such as the thermal self-dimming phenomenon in corneas and the separation of mixtures based on differential diffusion. By examining Soret coefficients in systems that are capable of diffusional separation, our analysis demonstrates that the thermal self-dimming phenomenon in corneas is the result of a complex interplay between rotational diffusion in melanin and vibrational oscillations in protein molecules. The versatility of generative music models through automated composition creation has significant potential in enhancing musical creativity; nonetheless, overcoming the hurdles in automatic evaluation of compositions is crucial for their advancement. By adapting a standardized critique into a measurable assessment, artists can engage with these models in a more informed manner, ultimately driving computational music creativity forward. To address this challenge, researchers proposed the development of an automated evaluation method for compositions that mimics human criticism and reflects on a piece's musical qualities. By leveraging a large-scale text dataset of expert piano critiques, they employed a BERT-based model to incorporate explicit musical notions into an innovative criticism metric. Through a multifaceted evaluation involving both human judges and musical experts, the researchers demonstrated that the model has attained reliability in composing music and proved capable of replicating an expert music critic's assessment, offering valuable insights that could be applied in future research on automatic composition evaluation and potentially impacting the development of music generation models. The researchers made their evaluation model available to the public in the form of a Python package, allowing other scientists to build upon their work for the benefit of the computational musicology community. Supervised learning methods for object detection are hindered when training on annotated datasets with significantly less data than available positive and negative samples. The resulting models often label positive targets as false positives at a high rate. This paper presents an innovative technique that seamlessly integrates supervised learning approaches into domain shift scenarios between annotated and unlabeled input domains, using density-based rejection of false positives post-classification. The proposed method first synchronizes the distribution of negative samples between the two domains using a variant of the adaptive cross-domain mapping (ACDM) algorithm. It then uses an unsupervised clustering approach to isolate false positives in the target domain, utilizing the negativized target scores and the mean target density estimates of each cluster. Comprehensive experiments on the challenging semantic target class of pedestrians demonstrate the method's ability to reduce false positives up to $90\%$ in a realistic automotive domain, while maintaining high target detection rates. Notably, the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches with $70\%$ fewer annotations required in a critical safety application. Our method is available as an open-source contribution. Furthermore, an extended version of this work is available on arXiv:2105.13434. Lastly, relevant data and model resources are available through the Box Reordering repository on GitHub: https://github.com/jderoziere/boxreordering. \\

\noindent \textbf{Contributions.} \\

\noindent This paper addresses the challenge of domain adaptive pedestrian target identification by introducing the Box Reordering technique that effectively removes false positives in an unsupervised setting. The key concepts underlying this method are (a) using an adaptive domain mapping (ADMM) to align negative samples across domains; (b) incorporating the ACDM algorithm to utilize pseudo-target labels for negative sample alignment; (c) incorporating density information to improve the rejection of false positives; and (d) utilizing the PyCAT framework for unsupervised clustering. Our method is evaluated extensively, demonstrating its ability to reduce false positives up to $90\%$ in a realistic automotive domain with minimal domain adaptation. The method performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches with $70\%$ fewer annotations required, showcasing its utility in critical safety applications. \\

In virtual environments, the simulation of object movements is typically determined by the actions of the simulated user. Specific movements, like throwing, are often used in these simulations to convey human-like behavior. Our study investigated the impact of incorrectly representing the point at which a throwing motion peaks when rendering such movements to observers. We found that in certain situations, where the simulation is observable by other characters who are also simulated entities (agents), the point at which the peak occurs can significantly affect these agents' actions. Moreover, our results indicate that agents can potentially exploit this information to carry out malicious actions against their human opponents. It is only when the simulation is viewed directly by a human, as opposed to being perceived through the actions of other simulated entities, that the peak of the throwing motion appears to be consistently anticipated by the system. This discovery implies the existence of a flaw in the current mechanisms used for simulating throwing motions. To further explore the issue, we have dubbed this phenomenon, where erroneous simulations can be exploited by other simulated entities, FauxThrow. To enable machines to understand language, we combine tree structure extraction with syntax analysis. Our novel parsing model incorporates a new decoding method that uses syntax-based connections. This unique approach allows the incorporation of multiple tree structures during decoding and uses syntax-based connections to refine tree selection. In experiments, we improve upon state-of-the-art results in the WSJ test by parsing the 02 corpus, achieving a 2.1% reduction in errors compared to a similar method without syntax-based connections. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model is effective in interpreting machine language through an evaluation of text summaries generated by machines. Our model is also capable of making human-like syntax-based connections, providing a machine interpretable layer. Finally, we use attention mechanisms to reveal which parts of the input sentence each word in the summary is looking at, and we find that our model is more sensitive to input sentence components compared to a similar method without syntax-based connections. Instead of relying solely on previous words as context, our model is more responsive to rare words and distant context. For complete results and code, see our public GitHub repository at: https://github.com/AllaGemati/Top-down-tree-structure-parser-with-syntactic-links. We observe, albeit briefly, a power-law distribution with an exponential tail emerging from a multiplicative stochastic model where the lower limit of sample selection is considered. Furthermore, there's a discussion on how this model can be used to analyze the distribution of earthquake magnitudes and the waiting times between successive earthquakes in specific seismic regions. Specifically, we contend that the differences in magnitude distribution and interearthquake interval dynamics between various regions can serve as distinct identifiers, much like folkloric fingerprints. Moreover, we are able to reconstruct the region corresponding to a given data set using this method. The associated code is freely accessible online at the specified repository. 

The primary findings are:

1. A multiplicative stochastic model incorporating a lower limit $M_0$ for sample selection generates an heavy-tailed distribution of earthquake magnitudes even when the lower limit is close to zero.
2. The model is able to capture the characteristic exponent $\alpha$ of an earthquake magnitude power-law distribution, but only up to a certain point.
3. The model is unable to reconstruct the entire distribution of earthquake magnitudes when the lower limit of sample selection is far removed from the minimum possible value.
4. There's a distinct, albeit short, period during which the model is able to capture the fluctuating behavior in interearthquake interval sequences.
5. Sequences of interearthquake intervals and earthquake magnitudes fail to demonstrate independence or uncorrelatedness in correlation function calculations.

Our model and methods have been successfully applied to sequences of earthquake magnitudes and interearthquake intervals in three seismic regions: Southern California, Scotland, and Costa Rica. The replication of our results in these different regions using our publicly available code indicates that the model is robust and generally applicable. However, there's an upper limit beyond which the model can no longer accurately capture either earthquake magnitude or interearthquake interval data. These upper limits correspond to a point in time beyond which the distribution of magnitudes ceases to be power-law-like and the interearthquake interval sequence exhibits significant statistical correlation structures that cannot be explained by conventional stochastic models. These findings reveal that there's a significant link between earthquake behavior and the complex systems of humans. These interactions can launch earthquakes and affect the timing of their occurrence in regions with high seismic activity. Therefore, the model is not only a tool for analyzing seismic data but also for understanding the intricate connections between earthquake activity and the systems of human beings that inhabit these regions. 

The relevant code for our analysis is freely accessible at https://github.com/andreacimino/earthquake

Our goal is to evaluate quantum states of light via shallow circuits. To achieve this, we design a low-depth random Clifford circuit that accepts input quantum states of light and produces a classifiable output. The circuit incorporates a random rotation on each qubit, accompanied by a random beam splitter that assigns qubits to either the transmission or reflection path. We demonstrate that a two-qubit circuit with specific parameters can accurately determine the quantum state of light by analyzing the output's two-particle correlation functions. With these correlation functions, one can determine if the input state was a maximally entangled two-photon state or a two-photon mixed state with a specific probability distribution. To verify our findings, we apply our protocol to a real-world experiment involving spontaneous parametric down-conversion, showing that the data matches our theoretical predictions well. This study not only provides a method for evaluating quantum states of light but also explores how quantum circuits, even with limited depth, can determine nonlocal properties of quantum states. Additionally, one can extend this protocol using our theoretical framework, enabling the evaluation of more complex quantum states and increasing the circuit's depth accordingly. Nonetheless, it is crucial to note that there is a threshold for the circuit's depth beyond which the determination becomes difficult, which is related to the efficiency of our classifying circuit. To apply this protocol in practical settings, one should ensure that the quantum states of light used in the experiment have good overlap with the desired state being tested. Ultimately, one can use this protocol as a tool to generate specific quantum states of light by selecting the appropriate input state of the first photon and applying our determination procedure. To validate our findings, one can conduct experiments multiple times and calculate the fidelity of the output state for various initial states, showing that the results match our theoretical predictions. Additionally, the generated sibylvariants of Large GPT(2) models exhibit near identical performance levels on various text classification tasks, with some even outperforming their original counterparts in three out of four tasks. Finally, a performance metric called the sulfulence ratio is introduced to quantify the benefits gained from sibylnoise additions, revealing improvements of up to 4.71% in classification accuracy for large language models in several tasks. Our findings indicate that sibylvariants offer a useful strategy for improving the resilience of large language models. Utilizing this representation, we investigated whether a CNN could be trained without explicit supervision during an object recognition task, allowing it to instead learn by trial and error in an unsupervised setting. We further demonstrated that this linear depiction can facilitate more effective object recognition, especially when paired with a simple, linear classifier. Notably, our method outperformed traditional pre-training techniques and yielded comparable results with significantly reduced computational requirements, being suitable for deployment on edge devices such as smartphones. Previous studies on leveraging multilingual and cross-lingual models for low-resource machine translation have focused primarily on small-scale and high-labeled contexts, which is impractical for real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose utilizing large pre-trained multilingual translation models and reducing large, high-parameter models such as the mMBART translation model through distillation and quantization. Our goal is to detect which approach yields more resilient models when translated across non-English languages. We examined various quantization techniques, including a model specifically designed for low-resource contexts, and evaluated its performance against traditional approaches for obtaining resource-efficient MT models. To simulate real-world scenarios with low resource availability, we conducted experiments using 5 languages with different levels of available parallel data. The results show that distillation offers better performance, robustness, and transferability than the currently available models and quantization techniques, even when dealing with limited data. However, we found that some quantization techniques can occasionally surpass traditional approaches in performance, particularly when there is an insufficient number of available training data. To this end, we are open-source providing our code for reproducing the results and facilitating future advancements in this area of research. Consider a hypergraph consisting of only one edge that connects n vertices, denoted as $V_1 \times \cdots \times V_n$, where each subset $V_i$ contains at least two elements. For a function $f$ defined on this hypergraph's vertices, we examine the validity of illogical consistency for the following expression: $\sum_{i=1}^n \prod_{j=1}^n f(j) = 1$. Surprisingly, we find that when $f(x)$ equals $x^k$ and $k$ ranges from 0 to n-1, the expression is always true, indicating a contradiction to the illogical theorem's requirements. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the Carleman condition is not necessarily satisfied in this scenario, resulting in the illogical function's existence and fulfilling the requirements for hypergraph illogicality. Finally, to resolve this anomaly, we propose an alternative, more stringent definition for the illogical function, achievable only if the inclusion properties of the subsets $V_i$ exceed a certain threshold, specifically when each subset contains at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ elements. With this revised definition in mind, the expression $\sum_{i=1}^n \prod_{j=i}^n j^{i-1} = 2^{-n+1}$ holds true, presenting a compelling explanation for the prior anomaly. The research presents a crucial generalisation of the illogical theorem, applicable to hypergraphs, with specified inclusion requirements on the subsets $V_i$. The detection and segmentation of pulmonary congestion or edema in CT scans of the chest is an essential component of diagnosing certain cardiopulmonary conditions. Commonly used machine learning-based segmentation models, such as U-Net, require substantial labeled data to operate efficiently, which can be costly to acquire or mark. Recent research has explored the potential of utilizing unlabelled images through unsupervised and semi-supervised techniques. This work proposes an innovative method to enhance the performance of a basic U-Net model using image enhancement techniques and demonstrates that performance can be improved with minimal supplementary annotated data. Experimental outcomes on our in-house cardiopulmonary CT dataset showcase the efficacy of these techniques in reducing required annotated images from 799 to 50, while maintaining a high Dice coefficient. Furthermore, it was discovered that the greatest contributions to improved performance came from GAN-based image enhancement rather than the specific augmentation technique employed. These findings offer an efficient, low-data solution for developing a pulmonary congestion segmentation task, which could prove particularly valuable in institutions lacking extensive cardiopulmonary imaging expertise. The versatility of language models is widely recognized due to their ability to adapt to various tasks with minimal modification in model architecture. This paper reveals that such adaptability also applies to image description tasks, enabling the adjustment of a single general-language model with relatively simple image preprocessing techniques and prompt engineering methods. We develop different prompting strategies and evaluate their performance across multiple datasets, and our results indicate that (1) brief description prompts yield better results on the COCO dataset compared to longer prompts, and (2) prompts complemented by low-cost image enhancements such as token deletion and replacement significantly boost performance on the SQuAD and COCO datasets. This prompting approach is essentially a form of image preprocessing by token composition. Furthermore, we apply GPT-2 outputs to generate description prompts, and experimentally verify the stability and manageability of this method, along with its significant performance improvement on the COCO dataset. Our findings emphasize the significant impact of prompting strategy and image preprocessing techniques on the performance of pre-trained general-language models in image description tasks. Moreover, with the advancement of large language models, the necessity for sophisticated fine-tuning datasets may decrease, potentially leading to a more sustainable concept of lightweight, task-specific fine-tuning. The code for our technique is publicly available at https://github.com/sudhanshu5/prompting. Different fields, including physics and biology, use the concept of damage to describe systems that can be affected or harmed. In this study, we offer a broader understanding of damage that is not only limited to physical harm and can also be applied to various disciplines. Damage is defined as a reduction in a system's ability to behave predictably due to a disruption caused by one entity and experienced by another. This definition in terms of causality highlights that damage is not just a result of physical collisions but can also stem from interventions such as modifying system parameters or introducing new information. Using the latent variable model, we demonstrate that our definition of damage consistent with structural equation models and can be applied to analyze various instances of damage across different fields such as information security, online advertising, and biological systems. Furthermore, we illustrate that altering certain parameters in a system can lead to counterintuitive outcomes where the introduced disturbance seemingly reduces damage or makes it dependent on the intensity of the disturbance. These findings stress the significance of utilizing causal language when discussing damage and highlight the need for precise definitions in order to effectively utilize this concept in different fields. Additionally, these causal considerations can offer valuable insights for optimizing system functions, for example, by identifying "good" disturbances that can reduce damage suffered by a system, such as utilizing "white noise" to improve the security of cryptographic systems. A comprehensive exploration of the principles governing damage in various systems may reveal such beneficial disturbances and contribute to the development of innovative strategies for optimizing system functioning. Moreover, by examining the principles of damage, applications may be discovered where the concept can be applied and could potentially lead to advancements in fields such as medicine and theoretical physics. Ultimately, the application of the definition of damage and the utilization of the latent variable model may facilitate interdisciplinary discussions and collaborations, for example, discussions between physicists and biologists, and may lead to common ground among these disciplines. Such common ground could lead to new approaches and methods for investigating damage and the various systems in which it occurs. Furthermore, the most effective approaches for optimizing system functions may arise from the integration of concepts from different fields. For instance, in the past concept of gradients has been applied across various systems but our findings also indicate that certain instances of damage do not adhere to the gradient structure and therefore require unique solutions that take into account the specific characteristics of the system in question. Therefore, the exploration of damage and the search for optimized system functioning may heavily rely on interdisciplinary collaborations and integration. This research provides a comprehensive review of the current Spark ecosystem and offers valuable insights for developers seeking to leverage MMLSpark within Java context. Furthermore, our experimental findings illustrate the library's performance advantages, showcasing the benefits of using MMLSpark when running on Java instead of Python. The system of equations consisting of Laplace operator and surface dynamics equations, modified by integrating out surface dynamics and replacing boundary conditions with distributed sources and fluxes, can be rewritten in a simplified manner within a flat spacetime framework. This new form facilitates the integration of the developed theory with classical phase-field models. Specifically, it demonstrates the integration with the sharp interface model. Furthermore, it explores the integration with the modified Caginalp phase-field model, which incorporates heat transfer and includes a heat source and boundary conditions that rely on the temperature and heat flux on the boundary. In the exploration of the modified Caginalp model, two scenarios are considered: one in which the heat source is confined to the boundary and one in which the heat source is distributed across the domain. In the first scenario, the developed theory results in a simplified system of equations consisting of Laplace operator and surface dynamics equations. In the second scenario, the developed theory introduces surface dynamics equations with source terms representing the distributed heat source and flux boundary conditions. In both cases, the developed theory exhibits accurate results that replicate the first-order approximation of the modified Caginalp model's sharp interface limit as predicted. In addition to the exploration of the modified Caginalp model, the developed theory is applied to consider thermocouple signal modeling, comparing the theoretical outcomes with existing literature in this area. This work provides evidence of the feasibility of incorporating active boundary conditions into phase-field models, which may have potential for use in modeling real-world phenomena such as melting/solidification problems with internal heat sources and sensors. Moreover, the developed theory provides first- and second-order approximations of various interface problems, thereby broadening our understanding of these phenomena. The theory is implemented in the form of publicly accessible code at the following repository: https://github.com/williamcalhoun/Coleman-Gurtin-with-active-boundary-conditions. The repository serves as the complementary source for the provided images in this dissertation. In addition to the work described in this document, the developed theory is also applied to model growing seeds and growing crystals. Images demonstrating the results of this modeling process are available at the following website: https://calhoun-phdconfirmation.wixsite.com/home. The CGP model without active boundary conditions is not applicable to this type of behavior, which is why the developed theory is utilized instead. By combining the developed theory with the sharp interface model, the developed theory yields a precise system of equations that accurately replicates the behavior of seeds growing in a vertical plane.

To effectively manage daily peaks in low voltage grid load, we must incorporate seasonal factors into our forecasting models. By examining a decade's worth of UK dataset from the low voltage grid, we have found that a statistical approach using ARIMA can accurately predict daily load outputs and also captures the relationship between highest daily loads and their preceding timeframes. Our model consistently provides precise forecasts over short and extended periods, including specific hourly predictions up to 12 hours in advance. Utilizing historical and meteorological data, we have obtained consistent forecasting performance during various seasonal periods. Our model's success in achieving minimal prediction error results in an enhanced mean squared prediction error (MSE) reduction of approximately 10% in comparison to a basic arima model. Additionally, in scenarios involving heightened weather conditions, we have observed a 20% decrease in MSE when our model is used alone, as opposed to incorporating meteorological data. Therefore, as part of a broader strategy to minimize forecasting inaccuracies, combining models such as arima, which is based on past consumption behavior, and other arima models that are driven by meteorological conditions, demonstrates considerable potential in producing accurate forecasts. Our findings are supplemented by a web-based interactive browser work, which enables users to visualize and understand the relationships between a decade of daily peak load and their preceding timeframes. This platform is accessible via https://lvforecast.web.columbia.edu. Our model's code and data are also available for further analysis at https://github.com/grupodl/arima_weathercombo. Our research demonstrates that by leveraging statistical analysis of a decade of daily peak load and incorporating seasonal factors into our forecasting models, we can substantially minimize forecasting inaccuracy. Additionally, our model's code and data are contributed to the research community with the aim of advancing the development of accurate probabilistic forecasting methods for low voltage grid load and, more broadly, advanced metrological applications. Our joint analysis of consumption behavior and meteorological data provides novel insights into the relationships between highest daily loads and their preceding timeframes, which are made publicly accessible for further research. Our research can serve as a benchmark for assessing the accuracy of probabilistic forecasting methods for low voltage grid load and may inspire researchers to explore new approaches to model daily peak load. Our findings indicate that by leveraging historical data and a range of statistical analysis methods, we can develop highly effective probabilistic forecasting models for low voltage grid load that are well-suited for a variety of applications. Recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning have led to a surge in automated model creation, but the integration of domain expertise still poses a significant challenge. From a practical perspective, this issue often results in the problem domain being unclear, with unclear or no boundary settings for input and output data. This paper aims to provide a general framework for integrating domain knowledge, highlighting various forms of domain expertise and their corresponding representations. We also discuss how domain knowledge can be utilized at different stages of the machine learning process. A critical analysis of existing research revealed that many studies fail to effectively incorporate domain knowledge, with some attempting to embed rules directly within models or using time-consuming and often ineffectives experiments to adapt pre-existing models to specific problems. To resolve these issues, this research proposes a structured approach for representing domain knowledge, enabling a more systematic integration of domain expertise in machine learning models through methods such as transfer learning. An empirical evaluation using two real-world datasets demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework in producing data-driven boundary representations and models that require minimal computational resources to train. Ultimately, this research seeks to provide practical guidelines for integrating domain knowledge, facilitating a more systematic research in this area and potentially opening new avenues, such as the exploration of transfer learning and semi-supervised learning. Identifying vertebrae in the spine is a key problem in medical imaging. We've developed an efficient method for this task by improving the initial detection of vertebral bodies and then applying a straightforward characterization of vertebra positions. Since the spine isn't always perfectly straight in real CT scans, we've incorporated a correction process to restore a standard, upright position. Additionally, we've created a new anatomically-based model to improve vertebra recognition accuracy. This innovative approach has yielded better results than previous techniques, achieving top-notch recognition rates with relatively minimal user interaction. Comprehensive testing across various spinal conditions and types has been carried out to validate the effectiveness and robustness of our method. It successfully aligns the spine with a straight, normal orientation and accurately assigns vertebral labels while tolerating diverse vertebral appearances. Researchers investigated the interaction of a high-speed electron beam and a strong, low-frequency electromagnetic field within a vacuum cavity.  By adjusting the electron beam's energy and the vacuum cavity's size, they managed to increase the electron's effective mass significantly.  Observing the electron beam's transmission at the cavity's boundaries, they discovered that the electron's effective mass was influenced not just by the external electric field but also by the dynamic changes in the electromagnetic field and the electron's own time-dependent aspects.  This leads to the formation of a resonant, stable state that occurs near a specific point in the electron's energy and the electromagnetic field's energy, known as aacc.  Inside this stable state, the electron's effective mass becomes even larger due to the strong electromagnetic field and can approach the order of the energy required to break the vacuum.  The aacc stability is known to occur due to a dynamic back-and-forth effect between the electron's movements and the electromagnetic field, which amplifies the electromagnetic field's role in the vacuum.  This stability's origin is therefore multi-faceted and tied to the strong interactions within the vacuum.  The present study is meant to be a starting point for exploring the electrical and magnetic aspects of vacuum phenomena, particularly at the points of intense light-matter and matter-matter coupling.  It also sets the stage for potential applications in constructing intricate optical and sub-electron devices, such as gates and lenses, the concepts of which are being actively researched at the research and theoretical levels. In non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, a pivotal issue arises in the study of certain measures that supposedly quantify the influence one quantum system may exert on another. A notable claim in this area states that the effects of a reduced quantum system should be representable as a density matrix for the combined system, under the condition that the initial states of the two systems are uncorrelated. Conversely, opposite outcomes have been obtained in subsequent studies. This paper aims to provide a new approach to the issue by developing a non-equilibrium extension of the Gaussian optimization principle. Utilizing this variational method, it is demonstrated that the effects of a reduced quantum system are indeed representable as a density matrix for the combined system, under the condition that the initial states of the two systems are uncorrelated. Nevertheless, it is found that the scenario is non-trivial and depends heavily on the quantum channel in question. Consequently, lower bounds for certain entropy measures are derived in terms of the relevant correlations. The results are then exemplified through the study of a linear quantum system responding to an external periodic force. It is shown that in this specific instance, the effects of the reduced quantum system are precisely representable as a density matrix for the combined system, under the condition that the initial states of the two systems are uncorrelated. Moreover, it is observed that under specific conditions, the R\'enyi entropy of order 2 for the reduced quantum system exhibits a decay consistent with a Gaussian process. Finally, it is found that in the general scenario, the rate of decay is positively correlated with the strength of the external force applied. The methodological approach to the issue is overall non-trivial and depends on the type of quantum channel in question. Nonetheless, it is evident that in the study of open quantum systems, where monotonically increasing measures are of the utmost importance, the effects of the reduced quantum system are indeed representable as a density matrix for the combined system, under the condition that the initial states of the two systems are uncorrelated. A thorough comparison with the issue itself is conducted, highlighting the respective differences and similarities between the two approaches. A key goal of fashion image retrieval involves pinpointing a fashion item's style, qualities, and accessories to understand its overall fashion value.
However, images of low-fashion items often lack sufficient context, making them difficult to classify.
This study presents a novel context-aware approach that uses feature-level trait manipulation to boost a image's contextual information when its original quality is insufficient.
A novel quality and context loss function is also proposed to map the embedded context onto a unit sphere for classification, using which the model can successfully transfer the learned features from a labeled dataset to an unlabeled test image.
This innovative semi-supervised framework was tested on a dataset consisting of low-fashion images and multiple context classes and demonstrated superior performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the study involved Amazon Mechanical Turk evaluations which validated the model's contextual understanding. A comparative analysis of our approach with existing state-of-the-art methods is presented showing the benefits of our context-aware framework. The framework's implementation can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/stergiosit/FashionImageRetrieval-CVFRC18. Additionally, the dataset used for the study can be found at https://www.dropbox.com/s/2jlnsir0ewt0kgp/fashion_lowquality_context_8400p.csv. A video presenting the findings can be found at https://youtu.be/4hjyvzgkx3E. A Press Release for the study can be found at https://stergiopoulosresearch.medium.com/cvfrc18-context-ensemble-axiom-in-cvpr-2018-keyvision-journal-2018-a9 [online]. The task of finding the optimal dual solution in variational problems that involve infinite-dimensional spaces with ill-defined problems is a crucial and challenging one, where conventional methods run into difficulties due to the non-existence of a surjective linear operator. This paper addresses this issue by developing a dual gradient ascent technique that incorporates penalty and smoothing methods to tackle the problems raised by ill-defined problems in Banach spaces with sparse constraints. Numerical experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of this technique in the context of dual imaging problems have been presented. Up to now, a comprehensive analysis of the convergence of the proposed algorithm in the context of Banach spaces with ill-defined problems has been provided, where robust estimates for the rate of convergence have been established in terms of the penalty parameter and the step size. Specifically, it has been shown that under certain conditions, both the primal and dual sequences associated with the proposed algorithm converge under certain conditions for sufficiently small step sizes and penalty parameters. The technique has been successfully illustrated through numerical experiments that involved real-world applications, such as a computed tomography reconstruction problem and a problem related to optimal control. Where numerical solutions to such problems that involved dual constraints were previously intractable, the technique has been shown to yield sparse solutions of satisfactory quality. These new formulas are consistent with known solutions and offer a novel, unified approach to solving these equations, while also providing a new quadratic solution formula for the Fokas-Lenells equation. Through the Euler integrals method, our first solution formula for the Fokas-Lenells equation features Euler integrals of the type S_+(u,v). Interestingly, the Fokas-Lenells bilinear equation with enhanced nonlinearity yields combined solution formulas of the type S_+ and S_- as well as a new triple product of Euler integrals. Lastly, applying the bilinear method to the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy yields a new solution formula featuring a quintuplet of Euler integrals. In recent years, the deployment of Extended RAN technology has significantly increased the number of access points within a typical home network, enabling the creation of a separate wireless network when the main network becomes congested. Currently, the decision to use a main access point or an extension is made randomly by the device, which may result in poor performance due to the high activity on the main access point. To address this issue, we propose using IEEE 802.11k/v to inquire about channel load and then selecting the most suitable access point or extension based on that information. Our proposal is validated through simulations which demonstrate a notable improvement in performance metrics such as video streaming bitrate and online backup upload speed when utilizing our proposed strategy compared to the existing method. To further optimize the results, we also present an additional idea for adjusting the configuration of extension access points. To the best knowledge of our team, this work presents a novel method for leveraging IEEE 802.11k/v to allocate resources efficiently and enhance the performance of Existing RAN technology. To achieve this goal, we also developed the "Netinfo" inquiry method, a complementary part of the IEEE 802.11k/v standard, for inquiring about network information such as traffic load across a certain channel. This information can then be used by the device to select the most suitable access point or extension and configure the optimal transmission parameters, such as transmission speed, channel, etc. for optimal performance. To evaluate the performance characteristics of the proposed concept, a series of simulations were conducted based on a real-world scenario. To further develop the concept, we also present additional ideas for integrating the feature into a popular next-generation home network standard, Multi-AP. To achieve this goal, we also proposed two possible approaches, one of which involves modifying the existing IEEE 802.1Q multilink standard to collect and aggregate the traffic information from all access points before transmitting it as part of the IEEE 802.11k/v inquiry signal. This information can then be used by the device to select the most suitable access point or extension and configure the optimal transmission parameters, such as transmission speed, channel, etc. for optimal performance.
